Article.Title: Lifespan Trajectories of Resting State Bipolar EEG Power
Article.Authors: Chorlian, D. B.; Kamarajan, C.; Meyers, J. L.; Anokhin, A.; Pandey, A. K.; Zhang, J.; Kinreich, S.; Porjesz, B.
Article.Abstract: Normative trajectories of resting state bipolar EEG power over the lifespan were derived from a sample of 5781 participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA), a large multi site study, using 12,906 observations from ages 12 through 70. Trajectories were analyzed using the means, variances, and correlations of data in seven frequency bands (from low theta to high beta) and 24 bipolar channels obtained from 17 electrodes of the 10-20 system. In order to make the study more useful for understanding EEG in the general population, only subjects never having an alcohol use disorder (AUD) diagnosis were included in the study. Bipolar EEG data is derived from the differencing of the signals in adjacent electrodes, either in a lateral (left-right) or sagittal (anterior-posterior) orientation; each difference is called a channel. The power values for the individual observations were calculated by standard Fourier transform based methods. In all cases there are sharp decreases in EEG power from ages 12 to the early 20s after which there are number of divergent patterns: general increases in the beta frequencies, and mixed patterns of increase and subsequent decrease in the theta and alpha frequencies. In these characteristics the lifespan trajectories presented here are similar to the monopolar trajectories described in our previous study \citet{Cho2026}. Sagittal and lateral bipolar trajectories are similar within each sex and between sexes; the primary difference is the much lower degree of regional difference in the sagittal trajectories as compared to the lateral trajectories. The pairwise inter-frequency (within channel) correlation trajectories between the four theta and alpha frequency bands and the four high alpha and beta frequency bands at each channel show striking sex differences unlike the corresponding monopolar correlations. There are a number of features in the bipolar power trajectories that suggest that the differencing procedure reduces not only local phase synchrony, but also effects of global and regional phase synchrony present in the monopolar data from which the bipolar signals are derived. The inter-frequency correlations at the individual channels are much higher in the bipolar data than the monopolar data, suggesting that global and regional phase synchrony components retained in the monopolar data have greater frequency specificity than the more purely local components in the bipolar data. Further analyses to examine many other features of the data will be undertaken in our subsequent work.

Article.Title: Intra-uterine position modulates lifelong hippocampal neurogenesis and anxiety-related behavior
Article.Authors: grieco, f.; Vilademunt, M.; Ali, M.; Sprenger, T.; van Gelderen, P.; Gallart-Ayala, H.; Ivanisevic, J.; Holub, A.; Yoo, J.; Bedrosian, T.; Larrieu, T.; Toni, N.
Article.Abstract: Individual differences in vulnerability to disease are a defining feature of biology and are especially prominent in mood disorders, where susceptibility to stress varies markedly across individuals. Strikingly, such individuality also emerges in inbred mice despite genetic homogeneity and controlled environments, suggesting that early non-genomic factors can durably shape behavioral trajectories. Yet the developmental origin of this variability remains largely unknown. Here, we identify the intra-uterine position (IUP) as a potent source of inter-individual variability in emotional behavior by showing that it influences prenatal steroid exposure, hippocampal development, adult neurogenesis, and anxiety-like traits in inbred mice. At embryonic day 18.5, embryos adjacent to one or two male siblings (i.e. 1M/2M) exhibited altered brain steroid profiles, coinciding with increased proliferation of neural stem and progenitor cells in the dentate gyrus, as compared to 0M mice. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing further revealed that IUP leaves a transcriptional imprint on hippocampal development, with 1M/2M neural stem cells showing reduced stemness and activation of a neurogenic transcription program. In adulthood, 1M/2M mice presented reduced hippocampal and dentate gyrus volumes, diminished radial-glia-like cell counts, lower cell proliferation, and impaired dendritic maturation of immature neurons. Behaviorally, both juvenile (PND22) and young adult (8-week) 1M/2M mice displayed increased trait anxiety, and 1M/2M males exhibited heightened stress reactivity. In vitro, testosterone, but not progesterone, directly enhanced proliferation of adult rat hippocampal stem/progenitor cells, whereas corticosterone reduced it. In vivo, administration of the androgen receptor agonist dihydrotestosterone (DHT) to pregnant dams recapitulated IUP effects by increasing embryonic dentate gyrus (DG) proliferation in female embryos, whereas antagonism reduced progenitor proliferation in male embryos. Together, these results indicate that IUP has long-lasting effects on hippocampal development and anxiety and may underlie natural variations in trait anxiety.

Article.Title: Neural networks as decision trees: an analytical solution for learning and neural selectivity
Article.Authors: Tissot, H.; Ranft, J.; Boubenec, Y.
Article.Abstract: Nonlinear neural networks develop structured internal representations, yet how their geometry is determined by the tasks being learned remains poorly understood. Here, we develop an analytical framework for piecewise-linear feedforward and recurrent networks that links learning, activation-region structure, and neural selectivity. We show that, at any stationary point of gradient-aligned learning, a nonlinear network decomposes into local linear regressions over its activation regions. Deviations from the corresponding least-squares solutions are jointly constrained by network weights shared across regions and vanish in the low-error regime, yielding an approximate piecewise least-squares decomposition of the task. This structure admits a decision-tree interpretation, which we recover numerically by fitting trees to predict network activation patterns from the input. We further derive how the regions in which neurons are active determine the task statistics they capture, thereby organizing neural selectivity into distinct subpopulations. The resulting predictions closely match the selectivity geometry observed in simulated networks and two empirical neural datasets. Finally, we show that neural baseline regulates activation pattern diversity, placing networks along a continuum between coarse, generalizing representations and fine-grained, expressive representations. Together, these results establish activation regions as a unifying framework for describing how nonlinear networks decompose task structure into local computations and how those computations can be revealed through neural activity.

Article.Title: Sparse coding at the input stage of the hippocampus enables fast learning
Article.Authors: Sasan, A.; Mok, R. M.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampus is crucial for fast learning, a capacity commonly attributed to the sparse code of the dentate gyrus (DG), the input stage of the trisynaptic circuit. However, this has been assumed rather than demonstrated, and we lack a principled account of when sparsity helps or hurts learning and what is traded off along the sparse-to-dense continuum. We characterize sparse coding in neural networks trained on nonlinear tasks and show that the level and position of sparsity determine learning speed and the memorization-generalization trade-off. Learning speed follows an inverted-U function, peaking at capacity-sufficient codes. Critically, sparsity must be implemented at the input stage, mirroring the DG. Sparsity speeds learning by producing high-dimensional, pattern-separated representations, but at a cost: models learn through memorization and fail on new examples. Our work establishes principles linking sparsity to learning, casting the DG's sparse code as a mechanism for episodic snapshots rather than general structure.

Article.Title: Reelin Deficiency Alters the Directional Orientation, Apical Localization and Length of Primary Cilia in Principal Neurons in the Cerebral Cortex
Article.Authors: Akter, S.; Mirhosseiniardakani, S.; Takekoshi, Y.; qiu, l.; Baker, K.; Jiang, K.; Lyon, M.; Hattori, M.; Chen, X.
Article.Abstract: The primary cilia of pyramidal neurons in inside-out laminated regions are oriented predominantly toward the pia, a pattern reflecting reverse soma movement during postnatal neurodevelopment. However, the mechanisms that regulate the directional cilia orientation remain unknown. Here we show that the primary cilia of neocortical pyramidal neurons are localized at the base of the apical dendrites and aligned distally and opposite to the axon initial segment (AIS). However, this pattern is not observed in atypical pyramidal neurons in the deep neocortex, excitatory neurons in non-laminated regions, or interneurons, where cilia are randomly positioned around the nuclei and lack preferred orientation. In Reelin-deficient mice (reeler), the directional orientation and apical location of cilia in late-born neocortical and CA1 neurons are altered. However, the initial impairments are partially corrected during early postnatal development. In contrast, Reelin deficiency disrupts the directional orientation and apical localization of primary cilia in early-born neocortical neurons and principal neurons in evolutionarily conserved laminated regions, where lack postnatal correction. Reelin deficiency also increases the cilia length in principal neurons across the cerebral cortex at a developmental stage when cilia length stabilizes in wild-type mice. In contrast, cilia elongation is not observed in interneurons, GFAP-positive astrocytes, or excitatory neurons in non-laminated reeler regions. Together, Reelin regulates the directional orientation, apical localization, and length of primary cilia in principal neurons in the cerebral cortex. This study underscores the cilium as a key apical domain, particularly prominent in late-born pyramidal neurons.

Article.Title: Templated seeding induces the formation of Alzheimer paired helical tau filaments in human brain organoids
Article.Authors: Bacioglu, M.; Katsinelos, T.; Schweighauser, M.; Gallo, F.; Mueller, K.; Christou, R.; Brandes, J.; Lovestam, S.; Cowley, S. A.; McEwan, W. A.; Scheres, S.; Goedert, M.; Spillantini, M. G.
Article.Abstract: The prion concept postulates that seeded aggregation results in the recruitment of soluble protein monomers and their assembly into amyloid filaments with the same structures as those of the seeds. Here we show that this concept applies to tau filaments formed in cortical organoids obtained from human iPSCs of control subjects. Tau seeds were extracted from the frontal cortex of individuals with Alzheimer disease. When added to human cortical organoids expressing endogenous levels of three-repeat tau, they gave rise to filaments of three-repeat tau whose formation required endogenous tau expression. By cryo-EM, these seeded tau filaments were identical to the paired helical filaments of the seeds. This novel finding demonstrates the faithful templated seeding of tau in human nerve cells expressing endogenous levels of tau and opens the way to studying the mechanisms of paired helical filament formation and their downstream effects in a human system amenable to genetic modification.

Article.Title: Templated paired helical filament formation and tau fold-dependent inclusion morphologies in primary neurons
Article.Authors: Huang, M.; Lövestam, S.; Cheam, K. A. X.; Ghetti, B.; McEwan, W. A.; Scheres, S. H. W.; Goedert, M.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies are characterized by the abnormal assembly of tau into amyloid filaments with distinct, disease-specific folds. These filaments are proposed to spread in a prion-like manner, thus underlying the progression of pathology in diseased brains. A prediction of this hypothesis is that tau filaments will induce progeny filaments identical to the input seed material, yet cellular models of templated tau assembly have failed to fully recapitulate brain-derived filament structures. Here, we show that mixed primary mouse cortical neurons overexpressing full-length human tau via adeno-associated virus transduction propagate Alzheimer's disease paired helical filaments upon exposure to human brain-derived seeds. Using minimal tags and core mutations, we were able to unambiguously differentiate induced aggregates from the original seeds. Super-resolution microscopy and live-cell imaging revealed progressive inclusion formation in neurons. Moreover, seeding primary neurons with brain extracts from individuals with Pick's disease, corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy induced the formation of morphologically distinct inclusions. Together, these findings establish that primary neurons provide an environment for the faithful propagation of paired helical filaments and show that tau filament folds dictate higher-order inclusion morphologies within neurons.

Article.Title: Chronic Intermittent Ethanol Exposure Produces Physiological Tolerance and Distinct Behavioral Alterations Across Abstinence in Female Mice
Article.Authors: Eberle-Reddington, M. R.; Walker, A. M.; Vaidya, S. P.; Ritchie, J. L.; Taxier, L. R.; Materia, B. R.; Coleman, L. G.; Vetreno, R. P.; Kash, T. L.; George, B. E.
Article.Abstract: Chronic ethanol consumption produces long-lasting effects on the brain that contribute to persistent behavioral changes. This has been modeled in animals using the chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) paradigm, which induces escalation of consumption and alterations in affective and cognitive behavior. While this model has been well characterized in male subjects, the effects of CIE in females and long-term effects that persist beyond the acute withdrawal remain relatively underexplored. Here, female C57BL/6J mice were exposed to four weeks of chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) vapor to induce dependence. Following CIE, mice were evaluated for physiological tolerance to ethanol and alterations in anxiety-like behaviors and memory processing. Using the ethanol responsivity battery (ERB) assay to assess physiological tolerance, we found blunted responsiveness to the intoxicating effects of ethanol in the CIE-exposed females, indicating heightened ethanol tolerance that persists beyond the acute withdrawal phase. A cohort underwent behavioral testing following CIE to characterize changes in anxiety-like behavior, exploration, and memory across abstinence. In early abstinence (<5 days post-CIE), CIE-exposed females showed increased exploratory behavior compared with Air controls. After one week of abstinence, CIE-exposed females displayed impaired object recognition memory. CIE-exposed females also showed increased anxiety-like behavior at protracted abstinence time points, exhibiting hyponeophagia in the novelty-suppressed feeding test at 2 weeks post-CIE. In addition, following cued fear conditioning, we found reduced extinction recall at 4 weeks post-CIE. Together, this work indicates that chronic alcohol exposure leads to increased alcohol tolerance and distinct, persistent alterations in memory and anxiety-like behavior in female mice.

Article.Title: Restoration of (nor)adrenergic-like Ca2+ signalling counteracts age-related motor decline
Article.Authors: Horvat, A.; Cerne, U.; Dahse, A.-K.; Brodmerkel, L.-S.; Bratanic, A.; Matz-Soja, M.; Schirmeier, S.; Zorec, R.; Scholz, N.; Vardjan, N.
Article.Abstract: Aging disrupts neural function, but whether impaired noradrenergic control of brain metabolism contributes to functional decline remains unclear. Using genetically encoded fluorescent sensors we measured metabolic and signaling responses in neurons and glia of living Drosophila brains following stimulation with octopamine, the invertebrate analogue of noradrenaline. Aging was accompanied by neurodegeneration, reduced locomotion and enhanced oxidative whole-brain metabolism. Octopamine increased D-glucose uptake selectively in astrocytes and elevated L-lactate in both astrocytes and neurons, consistent with astrocytic glycolysis coupled to neuronal L-lactate uptake; monocarboxylate transporter inhibition caused selective astrocytic L-lactate accumulation. In aged animals octopamine-evoked metabolic responses in astrocytes and neural Ca2+ transients were markedly reduced. This impairment was associated with lower expression of adrenoceptor-like tyramine 1 receptor (Tyr1R). Selective Tyr1R overexpression in (nor)adrenergic-like Tdc2 neurons prolonged lifespan, restored Ca2+ signalling and improved locomotor performance. These findings identify Tyr1R-dependent Ca2+ signalling as an age-sensitive regulator of brain metabolism and motor function.

Article.Title: Extended amygdala function is governed by threat probability, not uncertainty
Article.Authors: Okhan, M.; Kalinova, K. N.; DeYoung, K. A.; Didier, P. R.; Scott, Z. S.; Ewing, D. B.; Hassani, J.; Cunneen, J. V.; Liu, E.; Earp, J. K.; Castro, G. B.; Oler, J. A.; Roseboom, P. H.; Christensen, C. W.; Drzewiecki, C. M.; Chavez, J. I.; Boorman, E. D.; Smith, J. F.; Kalin, N. H.; Shackman, A. J.; Fox, A. S.
Article.Abstract: Anxiety is a universal experience that arises as we anticipate negative events that may or may not happen. When extreme, anxiety is a major cause of distress, suffering, and disability-adjusted life years, with nearly one in four individuals experiencing clinically relevant anxiety in their lifetime1-3. Elucidating the biological basis of anxiety has the potential to help people understand, cope with, and ultimately receive improved treatments for their anxiety. The canonical neuroscientific model of anxiety posits that distinct regions of the extended amygdala (EA) elicit distress that is conditional on threat uncertainty4. Here, we refute this model using a precise computational framework to disambiguate specific dimensional facets of threat uncertainty in a racially diverse sample of 104 individuals. We show that self-report, psychophysiological, and neural correlates of threat anticipation are much more strongly associated with threat probability than uncertainty per se. Importantly, EA regions, including the central nucleus of the amygdala (Ce) and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST), were most reliably associated with threat probability--contrary to the canonical model. Re-examination of the pioneering experiments that motivated the canonical model reveal a previously unappreciated confound between probability and uncertainty, suggesting the novel hypothesis that EA regions differ in their sensitivity to low-probability threats. Our fMRI data support this, showing that BST is more sensitive to low-probability threats than Ce. Moreover, lesion experiments in rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) demonstrate that BST causally contributes to defensive behavior in low-probability threat contexts. Together, these data reconcile previous empirical inconsistencies, provide a fresh theoretical perspective on the neurobiology of anxiety, and underscore the theoretical importance of a formal lingua franca for coordinated cross-species emotion research.

Article.Title: Myelinated mechano-nociceptors encode noxious cold and underlie hypersensitivity in pulpitis
Article.Authors: Ronan, E. A.; Wan, S.; Perry, S.; Jha, A.; Gandhi, A. R.; Xu, J.; Wang, S. T.; Wu, L. L.; Pipe, K. P.; Emrick, J. J.
Article.Abstract: The ability to identify dangerous temperatures is critical, but the neural basis for cold sensation remains enigmatic. By combining in vivo functional imaging with tissue-specific spatiotemporal cooling, we unveil myelinated high threshold-mechanonociceptors (HTMRs) as the neural origin of tooth cold sensitivity. Critically, this neural encoding is driven by threshold noxious cold temperature, not cooling rate and remains independent of the cool receptor TRPM8 or pain transducer Nav1.8. Furthermore, while Bmpr1b-Cre captures the intradental HTMRs, it further reveals myelinated HTMRs mediate trigeminal cold encoding in soft tissues. Finally, we determine that inflammation potentiates intradental HTMRs, providing functional basis for clinical hypersensitivity in pulpitis. Collectively, our results reveal a new neural mediator of cold sensation and provide insight into painful transformation of cold sensory encoding in inflammation.

Article.Title: Communication as a Two-Person Neural Process: fNIRS Hyperscanning in Adults with and without Post-Stroke Aphasia
Article.Authors: Magee, G.; Colwell, J.; Kelley, S.; Mohammad, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Boas, D. A. A.; Kiran, S.; Varkanitsa, M.; Meier, E. L.; Yucel, M. A.
Article.Abstract: Communication is inherently interactive, yet most neuroimaging studies examine individuals in isolation. Here, we used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning to investigate interbrain synchrony (IBS) during naturalistic communication. In Study 1, 13 healthy familiar dyads completed Joint Singing, Joint Reading, and Picture Guessing tasks. IBS was quantified using wavelet transform coherence across bilateral frontal and temporoparietal regions. Joint Singing produced higher IBS than the other tasks in several regions, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and temporoparietal junction, and selected effects were greater in true than pseudo-dyads. In Study 2, we applied the same paradigm to five individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia interacting with trained speech-language pathologists. IBS could be estimated in all dyads after lesion-informed channel exclusion, although regional coverage varied with lesion location. These findings demonstrate that fNIRS hyperscanning can capture task-dependent interpersonal neural coupling during spoken interaction and can be extended to communication involving individuals with aphasia. This approach provides a foundation for studying how neural coordination between communication partners relates to functional communication and partner-supported interaction.

Article.Title: Structure-function coupling in the human brainstem
Article.Authors: Farahani, A.; Koley, S.; Hansen, J. Y.; Hannanu, F. F.; Garcia Gomar, M. G.; Singh, K.; Cauzzo, S.; Milisav, F.; Liu, Z.-Q.; Bazinet, V.; Bianciardi, M.; Misic, B.
Article.Abstract: The nuclei of the brainstem modulate neuronal activity throughout the central nervous system. Yet connectome reconstructions typically do not include the brainstem because it is notoriously difficult to image. As a result, the influence of the brainstem on structure-function coupling in the brain is unknown. Here we use high-resolution 7 Tesla magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to reconstruct structural and functional brain connectomes encompassing cortex and 58 brainstem nuclei spanning the midbrain, pons, and medulla. We identify structural connectional profiles of individual brainstem nuclei to the cortex and find that they align with a spectrum of functions, spanning sensory and motor processing to higher-order cognition. Structural and functional connectivity in brainstem-augmented connectomes are positively correlated, and pairs of regions with direct anatomical projections display greater functional connectivity than pairs without. Structure-function coupling is heterogeneous across brainstem nuclei, with strong coupling in both modulatory and relay nuclei. Collectively, this work presents an initial step toward understanding how the brainstem shapes structure-function relationships in the brain.

Article.Title: Perceptual sensitivity is explained by optimization for ecological tasks
Article.Authors: Saddler, M. R.; Dau, T.; McDermott, J. H.
Article.Abstract: When asked to discriminate between two stimuli that differ along some dimension, such as intensity, frequency, or orientation, humans exhibit a smallest stimulus difference, or threshold, below which discrimination becomes impossible. These limits on perceptual sensitivity have traditionally been explained by internal noise. Contemporary theories instead link perceptual sensitivity to efficient coding of the natural environment but have not been comprehensively tested. Here, we measured the psychoacoustic sensitivity of a computational model optimized for everyday sound localization and recognition tasks. We used linear classifiers operating on the model's learned representations to estimate 1632 thresholds spanning the perceptual dimensions of sound. These model-derived thresholds closely matched thresholds measured behaviorally in humans on the same test battery. The results show that many classical psychophysical phenomena emerge from representations optimized for natural behavior and suggest that discrimination thresholds are determined by linear separability in these optimized representations, rather than intrinsic neural noise.

Article.Title: Odor-evoked activity outside canonical areas of olfactory information transmission is visualized by ODORTRAP and modulated by diet-induced obesity
Article.Authors: Mitra, S.; Pacheco, F. A.; Fadool, D. A.
Article.Abstract: Enhanced excitability of output neurons in the olfactory bulb (OB) has been linked to regulation of energy homeostasis. The mechanism by which the olfactory system can drive metabolic state while processing odor information remains elusive yet must depend upon integration and relay to the rest of the brain. Herein, we screened brain-wide neuronal ensembles that preferentially engaged during odor stimulation (referred to as ODORTRAP) utilizing FOSTRAP activity mapping. Mice were exposed to the odor isopropyl tiglate (IPT), a preferred ligand for the olfactory receptor 160, previously shown to be vulnerable to diet-induced obesity. Odor activation resulted in elevated labelling in the olfactory bulb (ODORTRAP) (p < 0.001), as well as in higher olfactory cortices including anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex, and cortical amygdala (p < 0.05). Interestingly, IPT differentially recruited hypothalamic feeding areas, namely the arcuate (ARC), dorsomedial (DMH) and lateral (LH) hypothalamus (p < 0.001), while the ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus and the suprachiasmatic nucleus exhibited no change in ODORTRAP activity (p > 0.05). In mice that were maintained on moderately high-fat (MHF) diets, we discovered that obesity re-models the activation pattern across the brain. Obese mice exhibited loss of ODORTRAP activity in the ARC (p < 0.0001), whereas in the DMH and LH increased baseline activity that obscured any odor-linked neural activity. While IPT activated the nucleus accumbens and medial septum in control mice (p < 0.01), obese mice demonstrated no changes in ODORTRAP activity (p > 0.05). Our study identifies key brain regions linking chemosensation and metabolic state, specifically demonstrating alteration in activity in hypothalamic domains upon obesogenic diet.

Article.Title: A Semi-Dry, Visually Comfortable c-VEP BCI with Short Calibration, Conservative Idle-State Behavior, and a VR Proof of Concept
Article.Authors: dehais, F.; Maggi, E.; Cabrera-Castillos, K.
Article.Abstract: Background and Objectives: Code-modulated visual evoked potentials (c-VEPs) provide fast and reliable control signals for reactive brain-computer interfaces (rBCIs). However, deployment beyond laboratories remains limited by visually intrusive stimulation, reliance on wet electroencephalography (EEG), and false activations during non-control periods. We introduce a usability-oriented c-VEP rBCI combining low-salience textured stimulation, slow flashing codes, asynchronous evidence accumulation, and semi-dry EEG acquisition. Methods: Thirty participants evaluated the system on a standard screen using an 11-class keypad typing task. Two identical online typing sessions were separated by a 2-min video-viewing period serving as an explicit idle condition. Feasibility was then assessed in virtual reality (VR) through a proof-of-concept shell-game task involving head movements and immersive rendering constraints. Visual comfort, peripheral distraction, and fatigue were assessed subjectively in both conditions. Results: In the keypad task, the system achieved 99.8% accuracy with 33 s of calibration data and a mean decoding time of 4.3 s. No spurious commands occurred during the tested 2-min idle condition. In VR, online accuracy reached 100%, with a mean decoding time of 5.6 s. Participants reported high visual comfort and minimal peripheral distraction in both conditions, although fatigue was higher in VR. Conclusion: The proposed c-VEP rBCI combines short calibration, high accuracy, comfortable stimulation, semi-dry EEG, and asynchronous decision-making. Performance during the explicit idle condition and VR implementation support the feasibility of wearable and practical c-VEP systems for self-paced interaction beyond laboratory environments. These findings encourage evaluation in longer idle periods and real-world tasks.

Article.Title: Asymmetric Adaptation of Catch-up Saccades with Artificial Central Scotomas
Article.Authors: Dore, S.; Black, J.; Blohm, G.; Khan, A. Z.
Article.Abstract: In fully-sighted individuals, pursuit and saccadic eye movements work together to foveate moving targets; pursuit attempts to match target velocity, while catch-up saccades re-align the fovea to the target if it deviates during pursuit. Although saccade-pursuit interactions are well understood in healthy individuals, much less is known about how these mechanisms adapt in the presence of central vision loss. Here, we simulated central vision loss in healthy young adults to examine plasticity in saccade-pursuit mechanisms and investigated whether and how catch-up saccades adapted over five days of visual tracking. Twenty-five fully sighted participants performed a task in which they pursued a moving target that stepped position randomly (designed to elicit catch-up saccades) while viewing with a gaze-contingent central scotoma. The scotoma was shaped like a bitten cookie to encourage use of a specific preferred retinal locus (PRL) corresponding to the peripheral location with the highest acuity. By the end of the five days of repetition, most participants showed catch-up saccade endpoints shifted towards the PRL rather than the fovea. On average, endpoints shifted 0.5 deg towards the PRL between days 1 and 5 (range=0.3-1.5 deg), with significant shifts in 13 of the 25 participants. Adaptation was asymmetric; shifts were largest when the target moved in the direction opposite the scotoma bite and smallest when it moved towards it. In summary, we observed adaptation of saccade-pursuit interactive mechanisms through the re-referencing of catch-up saccades from the fovea to PRL. These results provide a promising avenue for rehabilitation in central vision loss aimed at improving eye movements and encouraging PRL use. Ultimately, such an approach may enhance residual visual function and quality of life.

Article.Title: Magnetic Field Enhanced Docosahexaenoic Acid Delivery for Acetylcholine Restoration in Alzheimers Disease an In Silico Study
Article.Authors: Dasgupta, M.; Konar, A.; Nagar, A. K.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimers Disease (AD) is characterised by the progressive depletion of Acetylcholine (ACh), a neurotransmitter essential for cognition and synaptic communication. Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), the predominant omega 3 polyunsaturated fatty acid in neuronal membranes, raises cerebral ACh and supports cholinergic transmission, but its therapeutic efficacy is limited by poor blood brain barrier permeability and slow passive diffusion. This work addresses these limitations through a closed form mathematical model coupling the spatiotemporal dynamics of DHA diffusion and ACh synthesis under an externally applied static magnetic field. Because DHA is diamagnetically anisotropic, it aligns along the field axis through diamagnetic torque while body cells form field aligned linear arrays; together these effects raise the effective diffusion coefficient of DHA. At a representative observation point, 0.5cm, magnetic field assisted transport reduces the time for ACh to reach a therapeutic threshold by 83.3%, from 10.55 s to 1.76 s. This reduction is spatially uniform across the modelled range of 0 to 3.0 cm from the source, with the absolute saving growing from 6.71 s at the source to 19.21 s at 3.0 cm. Co-evolution analysis reveals the mechanism: by the end of a 2.0 s window the field elevates DHA 7.39 fold relative to baseline, driving ACh to 133.7% of threshold versus only 18.1% without the field. A Brain Computer Interface (BCI)-based closed loop dosing framework is additionally proposed for future clinical validation. These findings establish a quantitatively grounded theoretical basis for magnetically enhanced DHA therapy as an approach to cholinergic restoration in AD.

Article.Title: Respiration and individual differences shape behavioral and inter-brain synchronization
Article.Authors: YI, W.; Palmer, C.
Article.Abstract: Humans coordinate their actions while their bodies and brains synchronize in social interactions, yet how behavioral, physiological, and neural dynamics interact during interpersonal coordination remains largely unknown. We investigated how respiration and individual differences influence behavioral and inter-brain synchrony in a musical synchronization task, which requires precise temporal alignment. Eighty-eight individuals first produced a familiar melody at their most comfortable rate to measure their spontaneous production rate (SPR). They then synchronized the melody with a randomly assigned unfamiliar partner under natural (unpaced), instructed in-phase, and instructed anti-phase breathing conditions, while hyperscanning 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), respiration, auditory-motor timing, and perceived social connectedness were recorded. Relative to natural respiration, both in-phase and anti-phase breathing increased inter-brain phase-locking and perceived social closeness but reduced behavioral synchrony; the instructed respiratory phase relationship was mirrored in their inter-brain relative phase. Differences in phase of respiratory cycles (inhalation and exhalation) also influenced coordination: Inhalation was associated with stronger inter-brain synchronization but less precise and stable behavioral coordination than was exhalation. Moreover, Individual differences influenced coordination: Partners with the faster SPR consistently preceded the slower partners and exhibited an alpha-band inter-brain phase advance in synchronization, whereas dyads with similar SPR showed greater behavioral synchrony and smaller inter-brain phase difference. Our findings identify respiration as a previously overlooked factor that organizes behavioral and neural synchronization, while individual intrinsic rhythms constrain how interacting partners align in time. Together, these findings reveal a dynamic interplay between the rhythms of the body and brain during human social interactions.

Article.Title: Distinct EEG microstate signatures across different pain types
Article.Authors: Rabiei, P.; champagne, a.; Barrette, L.-E.; Fakhry, N.; Masse-Alarie, H.; Coll, M.-P.
Article.Abstract: Pain is associated with dynamic brain reorganization. Electroencephalographic microstates can characterize transient large-scale brain states, yet findings across pain studies are inconsistent. Two features may contribute: conditions have been studied in isolation, and analytical pipelines vary widely. We applied a harmonized analysis pipeline across three pain conditions: capsaicininduced pain, assessed within participants against a pain-free baseline, and non-chronic and chronic back pain, each compared with matched controls. Using a five-minute resting-state electroencephalographic recordings we examined microstate topography, temporal expression and transition probabilities, and directly compared pain related differences across pain states. We identified five microstates (A-E), corresponding to auditory, visual, salience, and attentional networks. Capsaicin pain showed increased expression of microstate C and reduced expression of microstates A, D and E. Transitions were redistributed towards microstate C, indicating a shift toward salience-related processing at the expense of sensory and attentional dynamics. In clinical back pain, effects were smaller and diverged by pain type: non-chronic back pain showed lower microstate C occurrence, opposite in direction to the capsaicin effect, whereas chronic back pain showed lower microstate D global explained variance, suggesting salience and attentional differences in clinical pain. Direct comparisons showed weaker pain-related increases in microstate C expression in both clinical back pain groups than capsaicin pain, with additional differences involving microstates A, D and E. These findings argue against a unitary EEG microstate signature of pain and instead reveal pain-type-specific patterns of large-scale brain dynamics, with microstate C providing the clearest distinction between experimental and clinical pain.

Article.Title: Imputation-Based Harmonization Mitigates Site Effects Without Data Leakage in Machine Learning Studies
Article.Authors: Hillman, N.; Chen, A.; Hu, F.; Vandekar, S.; Melhem, R.; Beason-Held, L.; Satterthwaite, T.; Davatzikos, C.; Shou, H.; Shinohara, R.
Article.Abstract: Neuroimaging studies that pool data across clinical sites often suffer from site effects --- variability in imaging measures that arises from technical heterogeneity across sites as opposed to true biological signal. While numerous harmonization methods have been proposed to remove site effects from imaging features, less attention has been placed on how to incorporate harmonization models into common machine-learning pipelines. We demonstrate that current approaches for integration either suffer from data leakage, fail to fully remove site effects from the target data, or attenuate true biological associations during the harmonization process. To address these issues, we propose Multiple Imputation for Removing Technical Heterogeneity (MIRTH), which uses imputed outcomes to harmonize the test data. We benchmark MIRTH's performance using both simulated and real-world volumetric data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, demonstrating that MIRTH can achieve high predictive accuracy while avoiding inflated performance when the outcome is imbalanced across clinical sites.

Article.Title: Spatial Sampling and Temporal Dynamics Shape Motor Decoding from Broadband Intracortical Signals
Article.Authors: Zheng, C.; Xiao, Y.; Cui, H.
Article.Abstract: Objective. Neural decoding performance depends strongly on neural signal representation; however, how the informative components of broadband intracortical activity vary with electrode configuration and decoding strategy remains unclear. We systematically compared the neural features spanning multiple temporal scales to identify the factors underlying robust motor decoding. Approach. Neural recordings were obtained from the dorsal premotor cortex, primary motor cortex, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of rhesus monkeys performing delayed-reaching tasks toward static or moving targets. Signals were recorded using 64-channel linear S-probes or 96-channel planar Utah arrays. We compared spiking-band power (SBP), local motor potential (LMP), and local field potential (LFP) power across multiple frequency bands using linear and nonlinear decoders. We further characterized the spectral and temporal components contributing to LMP decoding and evaluated the channel redundancy. Main results. The decoding performance of the SBP and high-frequency LFP features scaled with the number of recorded single units, whereas the LMP performance was more strongly influenced by the electrode geometry. LMP achieved a higher decoding performance with planar Utah arrays than with linear S-probes, accompanied by lower inter-electrode correlations and greater variability in preferred directions. Spectral analysis showed that LMP decoding was dominated by low-frequency components overlapping the delta band and movement-related cortical potentials, with an optimal decoding range of approximately 0.1-8 Hz. Nonlinear temporal decoders, particularly the convolutional neural network and gated recurrent unit models, further improved LMP decoding. Significance. These findings demonstrate that the neural features most informative for motor decoding depend on both the spatial sampling configuration and the temporal structure of the recorded activity. The results highlight the importance of low-frequency population dynamics and provide principles for optimizing neural-signal representations and reducing redundant neural data for scalable and wireless brain-computer interfaces.

Article.Title: Learning continuous updating and control of neural population activities from sparse time samples
Article.Authors: Wu, Z.; Zhang, M.; Qian, N.
Article.Abstract: The brain frequently updates or controls its internal representations of sensory or motor variables over time. An example is transsaccadic updating of stimuli's retinotopic positions: When the eye moves in one direction, the positions are updated continuously in the opposite direction, and the process is controlled by the corollary discharge (CD) of the saccade motor command. We previously trained neural networks to perform such updating using the desired time courses of stimuli's positions at every time step. However, this may not be biologically plausible because, before a system learns to perform the task, it may not have access to complete time courses and the actual visual inputs are delayed and thus incorrect. Here we show that by adding the continuity equation to the loss, we can train neural networks with only stimuli's pre- and post-saccadic retinotopic positions (without specifying the intermediate transitions), and with heavily down-sampled time courses. Moreover, both the connectivity patterns and the CD control signal can be learned simultaneously. Since the continuity equation can be applied to waves of neural population activities that are distributed representations of variables, our work also suggests an advantage of distributed representations which are ubiquitous in the brain.

Article.Title: Psychedelics Restructure the Global Workspace of Consciousness
Article.Authors: Yousefi, P.; Shinozuka, K.; Vizeli, P.; Holze, F.; Becker, A. M.; Muller, F.; Liechti, M. E.; Hasler, G.; Rodriguez, C. I.; Luppi, A.; Mediano, P. A. M.
Article.Abstract: Psychoactive drugs profoundly alter consciousness, but the neural mechanisms by which they do so remain poorly understood. Global workspace theory may provide a framework for investigating these mechanisms. The global workspace, a candidate neural substrate of consciousness, is a set of brain regions that integrate and disseminate information to the rest of the brain. According to a recent model, the integrators, or 'gateways,' are characterized by synergistic interactions with other brain regions, while the disseminators, or 'broadcasters,' exhibit redundant interactions. Here, we measured the effects of various psychoactive drugs, including 'classic' psychedelics like LSD, mescaline, and psilocybin, 'atypical' psychedelics (entactogens) like MDMA, and the stimulant D-amphetamine, on the global workspace. In a secondary analysis of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data on all these drugs, we found that classic psychedelics are associated with significant increases in the number of gateways in the frontoparietal control and dorsal attention networks. Meanwhile, MDMA and amphetamine reduced the number of gateways in the visual and somatomotor networks. The regional topographies of both synergy and redundancy distinguished classic psychedelics from other drugs. Finally, drugs producing similar changes in synergy and redundancy also produced similar profiles of subjective effects. Overall, our findings provide the first direct evidence that psychedelics may alter the synergistic and redundant interactions that characterize the global workspace of consciousness.

Article.Title: Diffusion MRI of cortical organoids reveals protocol-associated spatial reproducibility and increasing diffusivity with diffusion time
Article.Authors: le Boeuf Flo, A.; Taskin, E.; Lavielle, O.; Grigoriou, A.; Pierzchala, K.; Le, T. P.; Jelescu, I.; Krsnik, Z.; Ribierre, T.; Thiran, J.-P.; Rafael Patino, J.; Canales Rodriguez, E. J.; Fischi Gomez, E.
Article.Abstract: Early human cortical development involves rapid changes in cytoarchitecture that remain difficult to interrogate non-invasively. Biophysical diffusion MRI models provide a potential window onto this microstructure, including water exchange across cell membranes, but their assumptions are difficult to validate directly in developing human tissue. Human cortical organoids provide a tractable biological model in which diffusion measurements can be related to tissue architecture within the same specimen. We scanned six fixed cortical organoids at 9.4~T, three grown under a directed and three under an undirected differentiation protocol, at three diffusion times and b-values up to 7000~s/mm$^2$. Center-to-periphery profiles of DKI-derived diffusion metrics were reproducible across the directed organoids but more variable across the undirected organoids, while nuclear staining revealed greater variability in the internal architecture of the undirected organoids. Unexpectedly, mean diffusivity increased with diffusion time in more than 80% of tissue voxels in both batches, opposite to previous organoid measurements. Across 12,348 simulated two-compartment substrates, this increase was reproduced only with permeable membranes and an extracellular diffusivity substantially exceeding the apparent intracellular diffusivity, a regime that challenges assumptions commonly used in current gray-matter exchange models. These results support cortical organoids as biologically realistic platforms for probing early cortical microstructure and testing diffusion models under controlled conditions, while remaining amenable to post-MRI histological validation.

Article.Title: Hippocampal granule cells balance energy and function along the Pareto optimal front
Article.Authors: Mittag, M.; Bird, A. D.; Mongiat, L. A.; Roth, A.; Cuntz, H.; Jedlicka, P.
Article.Abstract: The dentate gyrus' principal neuron, the granule cell (GC), plays a key role in pattern separation, transforming similar inputs into dissimilar outputs. We used a new measure based on information theory to evaluate this transformation in an experimentally derived in silico GC model with realistic ion channel distributions across its dendrites. We found that model performance aligned well with current-clamp recordings from mouse brain slices. However, it was also possible to find artificial parameter combinations in the model that functionally outperformed the recorded cells while matching their action potential shapes. Rather than maximising computational power, the biologically realistic GC model balanced energy efficiency against increased functionality in a Pareto optimal way: No possible parameter combination was found to improve one of the objectives without impairing the other. Interestingly, immature GCs adopted a different weighted trade-off with a stronger emphasis on energy efficiency than pattern separation, but they remained Pareto optimal over their putative developmental trajectory. Our results support the idea that evolution favours neurons that can satisfy functional and energetic demands simultaneously.

Article.Title: Continuous Rod Noise and Nonlinear Synaptic Filtering Shape Signal Detection in the Primary Rod Pathway
Article.Authors: Bocchero, U.; Pahlberg, J.
Article.Abstract: Rod photoreceptors are optimized to detect single photons, but their performance near absolute visual threshold is limited by intrinsic phototransduction noise. The two major components are discrete single-photon-like events and continuous fluctuations in outer-segment current. Although spontaneous rhodopsin activation is established as the source of discrete noise, the molecular origin of continuous noise remains controversial, and how these distinct noise sources influence signal processing at the first visual synapse is not fully understood. To address these questions, we combined genetic manipulation of rhodopsin, phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6), and glutamic acid rich protein 2 (GARP2) with single-cell recordings from rods and rod-bipolar cells (RBCs) and pharmacological manipulation of mGluR6 signaling. Continuous noise was unaffected by reduced rhodopsin concentration but was strongly influenced by PDE6 expression and regulation, supporting basal PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise. Reducing either discrete or continuous noise increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in rods, but these changes were differentially processed at the rod-to-RBC synapse. In WT retina, the nonlinear transformation increased SNR, whereas elevated continuous noise limited this increase. Conversely, reduced continuous noise increased rod SNR, which was maintained in RBCs and associated with a lower detection threshold. Pharmacological reduction of the mGluR6-dependent nonlinearity altered these genotype-dependent differences, indicating that nonlinear filtering is well matched to normal signal and noise distributions but does not fully compensate when presynaptic noise is experimentally altered. Together, our study identifies spontaneous PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise and demonstrates that continuous noise interacts with nonlinear processing at the first visual synapse to determine the fidelity and detection threshold of dim-light signals.

Article.Title: No Evidence of tACS-Primed Enhancement of Alpha Neurofeedback
Article.Authors: Turner, C.; James, L.; Bakhtiari, M.; Learmonth, G.; Fracasso, A.; Vuckovic, A.
Article.Abstract: Neurofeedback shows promise as a clinical intervention, but its effectiveness is hindered by variability of response across individuals. One factor influencing neurofeedback success may be endogenous brain states, particularly the baseline power within target frequency bands. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) provides a potential mechanism to modulate these baseline frequency bands. This study explored whether tACS could effectively enhance participants' ability to gain neurofeedback control by increasing lateralised posterior alpha activity prior to engagement in a covert spatial attention-based neurofeedback task. Participants completed three counterbalanced sessions: 1) alpha tACS and active neurofeedback, 2) alpha tACS and sham neurofeedback, 3) gamma (40Hz) tACS and active neurofeedback. Neurofeedback performance was assessed via lateralised posterior alpha power shifts and Posner task reaction times. We identified no difference in reaction times or lateralised alpha power shifts across conditions. While participants reliably demonstrated lateralised posterior alpha patterns, consistent with the covert spatial attention neurofeedback protocol, no advantage of active neurofeedback over sham was observed. The lack of significant effects underscores the need for further rigorous tACS studies to identify the parameters essential for successful neural entrainment, and to evaluate its potential in enhancing neurofeedback efficacy.

Article.Title: Glycosaminoglycan presentation-dependent regulation of glial responses by Orion during Drosophila neuronal pruning
Article.Authors: Gal, C.; Perron, C.; Vallet, S.; Gout, E.; Weber, M.; Ezzahra, O. F.; Ji, H.; Han, C.; Lortat-Jacob, H.; Dura, J.-M.; BOULANGER, A.
Article.Abstract: Neuronal pruning refines neural circuits by eliminating unnecessary connections to ensure proper nervous system function. In Drosophila mushroom body gamma-neuron remodeling, the chemokine-like protein Orion is required for astrocyte infiltration and phagocytosis. This study investigated whether glial responses depend on how Orion is presented. We found that Orion interacts with glycosaminoglycans (GAG) associated to proteoglycans, which are essential for proper axon pruning. Tethering Orion to the gamma-neuron plasma membrane, mimicking glycosaminoglycan binding, was sufficient to induce astrocyte infiltration into axon bundles. However, membrane-bound Orion alone could not efficiently support phagocytosis, which additionally requires a soluble and mobile Orion pool. We also identified exosomes carrying GAG-bound Orion as potential mediators of neuronal remodeling. These findings provide the first evidence that glial infiltration can be uncoupled from phagocytosis, demonstrating that the mode of Orion presentation regulates distinct glial mechanisms during neuronal remodeling.

Article.Title: Structural integrity moderates the cognitive bearing of dopamine clearance in aging
Article.Authors: Esmaeili, A.; Preti, G.; Bittner, N.; Woodman, M.; Caspers, S.; Hashemi, M.; Petkoski, S.; Marinazzo, D.; Jirsa, V.
Article.Abstract: Age-related cognitive decline in humans is well established, yet how neurobiological variations influence brain dynamics, and subsequently behavioral performance, remains insufficiently explored. Microscale accounts of cognitive aging revolve around attenuations in dopamine (DA) receptors and transporters (DAT). In contrast, macroscale accounts associate individual declines in cognitive performance with functional brain networks' reorganization and white-matter tracts' deterioration. We endeavor to bridge this gap with an amortized dopaminergic aging model (ADAM) which assembles aging brain twins by coupling dopaminergic modulation with structural connectomes to constrain emergent whole-brain dynamics. ADAM thereby augments established DAT decline with personalized estimates, through a reusable and generalizable estimator capable of disentangling neuromodulatory from structural contributions to age-related decline within each individual. To that end, we embed structural connectomes into a low-dimensional space exhibiting high reconstruction fidelity and -pseudonymized- individual identifiability. The spectrum of structural embeddings is subsequently updated with fMRI observations to estimate DA clearance timescales in 3,650 adults aged 36 to 95 years across five independent aging cohorts. Our analysis reveals an age-related elevation of DA clearance timescales. Critically, low performers exhibit elevated clearance in adults with marked structural degradation, and only within sliding age windows centred between 56 and 76 years. This supports a contribution of dopamine to aging, and reveals a structure- and age-conditional association between its clearance and cognitive performance. Our findings suggest that structural connectivity gates the macroscale reach of dopaminergic modulation, thus rendering the gain-control framework of neuromodulation mechanistically explicit across individuals and cohorts. ADAM therefore provides a biologically plausible framework that anchors interindividual variability in cognitive aging to perturbations in the dopaminergic system by learning cohort-scale mappings which can be shared across sites, establishing a transferable testbed for precision neuromodulation and future in-silico pharmacological trials.

Article.Title: Simultaneous multi-area recordings in macaque frontoparietal cortex during a manual object-interaction task
Article.Authors: Liu, K.; Guan, S.; Luo, S.; Li, Y.; Dong, Y.; Chen, W.; Chen, M.; Zhang, D.; Chen, L.; Huang, S.; Chen, Y.; Jiang, H.; Wu, L.; Li, R.; Zhu, F.; Xie, Y.; Sui, Y.; Min, B.; Guan, S.; Li, C.; Wang, T.; He, T.
Article.Abstract: Dexterous hand control is essential for daily activities and a top restoration priority for people with tetraplegia, yet neurophysiological datasets suitable for studying and decoding naturalistic hand behavior remain scarce. Most available recordings constrain movements to a small number of degrees of freedom or cover only a single stereotypical grasp-and-hold structure. Moreover, previous brain-computer interface (BCI) studies have largely relied on signals from a single cortical area, even though dexterous hand control is distributed across an interconnected frontoparietal network. To address these limitations, we designed a paradigm that elicits rich hand movements across 40 distinct hand-object interaction conditions. We recorded simultaneous frontoparietal activity with hand kinematics from a rhesus macaque performing them. Neural activity was recorded from the primary motor cortex, anterior intraparietal area, and ventral premotor cortex using microelectrode arrays spanning 1,920 channels, while a multi-camera markerless motion-capture system acquired video from which kinematics were extracted offline. The dataset comprises data from 20 sessions, including processed neural features, synchronized 3D coordinates of hand and elbow keypoints, and trial-level metadata including task conditions and event timing. We further provide technical validation, including a neural decoding benchmark with multiple algorithms for continuous keypoint coordination reconstruction. We found that cross-day and cross-task decoding performance varied among algorithms. Variation in channel availability leads to different performance degradation curves in different algorithms. This task-rich dataset offers a valuable resource for investigating the neural mechanisms of dexterous hand control and for advancing the performance of motor BCIs.

Article.Title: An information-borrowing Bayesian method for inferring high-dimensional population-level brain connectivity from small samples
Article.Authors: Pu, Z.; Zeng, C.; Ge, S.
Article.Abstract: Estimating population-level dependence between brain regions is challenging when the number of regions greatly exceeds the number of individuals. We introduce an information-borrowing generalized Bayesian method for high-dimensional covariance estimation from region-level brain measurements. A divide-and-conquer parameterization separates marginal variances from correlation calibrations: an empirical \emph{pilot} correlation matrix--by default, obtained by standardizing a sample covariance matrix (SCM)--provides a reference structure that is adaptively calibrated through region-specific parameters shared across pairwise correlations, reducing the number of free parameters from $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(d)$ ($d$ is the number of regions) while guaranteeing a positive-definite covariance through the inclusion of a ridge term. Horseshoe priors on the calibration parameters enable selective borrowing and shrinkage of pilot information. Under suitable conditions on pilot accuracy, we establish theoretical guarantees for covariance estimation while retaining scalability in ultra-high-dimensional settings via a low-rank likelihood representation and a Woodbury-accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm. Simulations showed lower estimation error than the SCM, bagging and iteratively refined principal orthogonal complement thresholding (POETRY). Applications to a semi-synthetic cortical-thickness and ADHD resting-state fMRI data revealed significant group differences in the default-mode--visual network and somatomotor network--limbic network blocks after Benjamini--Hochberg correction.

Article.Title: Behavioral arousal organizes visual cortical population micro-states across the sleep-wake cycle
Article.Authors: Wang, J.-Y.; Huis in 't Veld, G.; Takahashi, K.; Tijsseling, K.; Bassler, M.; Knoben, A.; Pennartz, C. M. A.; Olcese, U.
Article.Abstract: Brain states are conventionally defined as discrete categories, such as wakefulness, NREM sleep and REM sleep. Yet, whether these labels fully capture the organization of cortical population dynamics remains unclear. Using large-field-of-view two-photon calcium imaging of layer II/III pyramidal neurons in mouse primary visual cortex (V1), we show that population activity organizes into recurring micro-states that span conventional sleep-wake boundaries. A Hidden Markov Model fitted independently of behavioral state labels identified temporally stable micro-states with structured transition pathways. Micro-state organization was more strongly aligned with a continuous behavioral arousal axis, indexed by pupil diameter and orofacial motion, than with discrete NREM-wake categories, a relationship confirmed by mediation analysis. At the circuit level, two spatially intermingled but functionally opposing neuronal ensembles tracked this arousal axis in opposite directions. These findings establish behavioral arousal, rather than discrete wake-sleep state, as the primary organizing dimension of V1 population dynamics.

Article.Title: Preconception stress in mice alters maternal behavioral, neural, and endocrine outcomes, and produces sex-specific disruptions in offspring
Article.Authors: Nicodemus, M. M.; Luther, L. A.; Linton, I. M.; Foual, M. A.; Maynard, K. Y.; Morrison, K. E.
Article.Abstract: Disruptions to maternal behaviors that emerge during the peripartum period have been shown to have lasting physiological and behavioral consequences for offspring. In addition to effects on offspring, disrupted maternal behaviors have been associated with peripartum mood and anxiety disorders. Therefore, it is critical for the wellbeing of both mother and offspring to identify upstream risk factors for the disruption of maternal behavior. We have previously found that pubertal stress leads to a blunted hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis response in peripartum humans and mice. Given that dysfunction of the HPA axis is associated with both PMADs and disrupted maternal behavior, we examined how pubertal stress influenced maternal behavior throughout peripartum in mice using a pup retrieval test. We found that pubertal stress led to faster pup retrieval, but a less predictable pattern of maternal behavior, as well as a blunted HPA axis response during pregnancy. We also examined whether maternal pubertal stress influenced offspring behavior in adolescence and adulthood. We found sex-specific differences in risk-taking behavior during adolescence that are no longer present in adulthood. Finally, we used in situ hybridization to examine gene expression during pregnancy in the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus, a region implicated in maternal behavior. Following pubertal stress, we found cell-type specific changes in the expression of genes necessary for the expression of maternal behavior. Collectively, these findings contribute to our understanding of upstream risk factors for peripartum disruptions to maternal behavior and the lasting effects of pubertal stress on both mother and offspring.

Article.Title: Hyperexcitable primary somatosensory cortex in the MitoPark mouse model of Parkinson's disease
Article.Authors: Zhang, R.; Qi, R.; Emanuel, A. J.
Article.Abstract: The majority of Parkinson's disease patients suffer from decreased tactile acuity or neuropathic pain, both of which contribute to low quality of life and likely exacerbate motor dysfunction. How Parkinson's disease pathology relates to altered somatosensation remains unclear. One potential contributor is the progressive degeneration of dopamine neurons. To assess the extent to which gradual dopamine neuron loss contributes to altered somatosensation, we recorded spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the primary somatosensory cortex of the MitoPark mouse model of Parkinson's disease. MitoPark mice experience progressive dopamine neuron degeneration that is independent of -synuclein. We found that MitoPark layer V regular-spiking (largely pyramidal) neurons, but not fast-spiking (largely parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory) neurons, had elevated spontaneous firing rates relative to littermate controls at late stages of symptom progression. Regular-spiking neurons also became hyperresponsive to tactile stimuli -- more neurons were recruited by stimuli across a wide range of intensities, and these neurons responded with higher firing rates. Fast-spiking neurons, but not regular-spiking neurons, became desynchronized at late stages of symptom progression. These physiological changes coincided with pronounced degeneration of dopamine neurons and axons, which we measured with tyrosine hydroxylase immunostaining in the midbrain, striatum, and primary somatosensory cortex. Altogether, this characterization revealed cell-type-specific changes in the primary somatosensory cortex that are consistent with both decreased tactile acuity and hyperalgesia in Parkinson's disease patients. This suggests that the loss of dopamine neurons, potentially including those that innervate primary somatosensory cortex, contributes to somatosensory impairments associated with Parkinson's disease.

Article.Title: Two components of rapid temporal recalibration: a stimulus-driven shift and a decisional carryover dissociate across the senses
Article.Authors: Cass, J.; Van der Burg, E.
Article.Abstract: Multisensory synchrony judgments depend on recent history: the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) shifts toward recently experienced timing relationships. This shift, known as rapid temporal recalibration, is almost always interpreted as perceptual, a change in when events appear simultaneous. Yet serial dependence in such judgments can arise from two mechanistically distinct sources that a raw PSS shift cannot separate: a genuine perceptual realignment, which slides the psychometric function sideways along the multisensory asynchrony axis (an odd effect), and a decisional carryover, a bias to repeat the previous verdict, which lifts the function vertically without moving the PSS (an even effect). We re-analysed eight published datasets investigating rapid recalibration spanning audiovisual, audiotactile, and visuotactile pairings and audiovisual speech, decomposing serial dependence into these two components within a single mixed-effects model. The components dissociated by modality: perceptual recalibration was robust for audiovisual pairs but weak for audiotactile and absent for visuotactile pairings, whereas the decisional carryover was largest for the tactile pairings and weak for audiovisual pairings, so that the two traded off across the senses. In audiovisual speech, the decisional carryover was gated by the spoken syllable but not by the talkers identity and did not persist beyond one trial, identifying it as a content-specific, one-step decision memory rather than a motor habit or a multi-trial store. Separating the perceptual and decisional contributions to a timing judgment thus re-draws the map of temporal recalibration and revises several conclusions drawn from the undecomposed PSS.

Article.Title: Neurons in the lateral spinal nucleus give rise to the spinotectal component of the anterolateral system in the mouse
Article.Authors: Abu Hajer, M.; Yadav, M.; Ma, W.; Dickie, A. C.; Polgar, E.; Bell, A. M.; Todd, A.
Article.Abstract: The anterolateral system (ALS) originates from neurons in various regions of the spinal cord and conveys somatosensory information related to pain, skin temperature and itch to several brain targets. One component of the ALS is the spinotectal tract, which projects to the superior colliculus (SC) and is thought to underlie directed movements of the head towards a painful stimulus. Using anterograde and retrograde tracing, we demonstrate that the input from the spinal enlargements to the SC originates predominantly from neurons in the lateral spinal nucleus (LSN), many of which express calbindin. This input, which mainly targets the caudal and lateral parts of the SC, is somatotopically organised, and is associated with the clusters of Pitx2-expressing neurons that have been identified in previous studies. Since activation of Pitx2 neurons drives directed head movements, input from LSN neurons to the Pitx2 cells is likely to be a critical component of orientation and attention towards a noxious stimuli. We also provide evidence that spinotectal LSN cells receive excitatory synaptic input from neurons in superficial dorsal horn that express substance P or the gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR). Since GRPR neurons are strongly implicated in itch, our findings raise the possibility that the SC has a role in coordinating movements in response to pruritic stimuli.

Article.Title: Shared Fine-Scale Functional Organization in the Human Subcortex Revealed by Connectivity Hyperalignment
Article.Authors: Tu, J. C.; Feilong, M.; Zhang, Y.; Gobbini, M. I.; Haxby, J. V.
Article.Abstract: Subcortical structures are central to cognition, emotion, and social processing, and their dysfunction underlies a wide range of neurological and psychiatric conditions. Yet subcortical fine-scale functional organization has remained largely inaccessible to group-level fMRI analysis: nuclei are small and low-SNR, and their functional topography varies idiosyncratically across individuals in ways that anatomical alignment cannot resolve. This idiosyncrasy carries real stakes. For example, deep brain stimulation targets with more variable functional connectivity across individuals show correspondingly less consistent clinical outcomes. Here we show that this seemingly idiosyncratic subcortical organization in fact reflects shared, fine-grained structure that can be recovered by modeling each individual's connectivity in a common functional space (connectivity hyperalignment, CHA), rather than relying on anatomical correspondence. Applying CHA to fMRI data collected during naturalistic movie viewing, we found that aligning subcortical voxels by their cortical connectivity, rather than their anatomical location, sharply increased cross-subject correspondence in both stimulus-evoked response and connectivity profiles. Critically, this alignment sharpened rather than blurred local structure: neighboring voxels became more functionally distinct from one another, and cortical connectivity targets became substantially more decodable across subjects. These results indicate that human subcortical nuclei possess a common fine-scale functional architecture that is masked by anatomical variability but recoverable at the individual level. This reframes a central methodological constraint in subcortical neuroimaging: rather than trading spatial resolution for signal quality via smoothing, group-level analyses can achieve voxel-level precision by aligning function rather than anatomy, opening a path to studying cortical-subcortical circuit organization in greater detail.

Article.Title: Distinct Hippocampal Cellular Pathologies Influence Cognition Across Diagnostic Categories and Distinguish Schizophrenia from Affective Psychoses
Article.Authors: Ruby, E.; Gonen, O.; Walsh-Messinger, J.; Lotan, E.; Tal, A.; Rusinek, H.; Clemente, J. C.; Robinson-Papp, J.; Lafont, E.; Karlsgodt, K. H.; Malaspina, D.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: Cognitive deficits are key endophenotypes for psychosis, but targeting these in clinical trials has been unsuccessful in improving functioning. The admixture of schizophrenia and affective psychosis cases could be a roadblock if these forms of psychosis differ in cellular pathology. Methods: We examined cognitive functioning (MATRICS) and metabolite biomarker concentrations for cellular pathologies from whole hippocampal proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (1H-MRSI), using categorical and transdiagnostic classifications in 80 participants: 22 with non-psychotic affective disorder (NP-aff), 25 healthy controls (HC), and 33 with psychosis (Psy), including 20 schizophrenia and 13 affective psychosis (aff-P) cases. Results: NP-aff and HC had similar total cognition (46.64{+/-}12.01 vs 41.10{+/-}17.88), both superior to Psy (28.34{+/-} 12.34; p's<0.01). Mean metabolite concentrations were similar across all groups but showed significant within-group associations with cognitive tests. FFor HC, overall cognition, working memory, and reasoning deficits were associated with reduced neuronal integrity ({rho}=-.414, {rho}=-.422, and {rho}=-.433, respectively; all p's<.05), although no biomarker predicted overall cognition in the clinical groups. For NP-aff, elevated myelin/membrane concentrations accompanied cognitive deficits, significantly so for verbal learning deficits ({rho}=.446, p<.05), which were also associated with decreased glia ({rho}=-.503, p<.05). Opposite to NP-aff, reduced myelin/membrane concentrations predicted cognitive deficits in Psy, specifically visual learning deficits ({rho}=-.514, p<.05). Separating schizophrenia from aff-P evealed distinct abnormalities for social cognition deficits; reduced glutamate/excitation in schizophrenia ({rho}=-.673, p<.05) but increased levels of the biomarkers for myelin/membrane turnover and neuronal integrity in aff-P ({rho}=.575 and {rho}=.581, respectively; p's<.05). Conclusions: Schizophrenia and affective psychosis significantly differed in biomarkers of cellular pathology related to social cognition. Distinct underpinnings for cognition were also identified for other groups, aligning with DSM-5 and ICD disorder-based categories. These findings include support for heterogeneous, but not transdiagnostic, conceptualizations of cognition and psychosis.

Article.Title: Adolescent alcohol consumption differentially alters sexually-divergent behaviors and infralimbic cortex function in mice
Article.Authors: Seemiller, L. R.; Unsal, H. S.; Xie, Y.; Hossain, M. S.; Sicher, A. R.; Griffith, K.; Tuttle, K.; Johnson-Dendy, B.; McDonald, E.; Beloate, L. N.; Drew, P. J.; Zhang, N.; Crowley, N. A.
Article.Abstract: The cortex is one of the last brain regions to fully mature, making it particularly sensitive to early life drug use. Both human and rodent studies find long-lasting behavioral changes after adolescent alcohol exposure that implicate underlying disruptions in cortical development, including structural abnormalities and altered functional connectivity. Few rodent studies have been conducted across biological scales (from single cell, whole brain network, to behavior) to understand the comprehensive implications of these disruptions. We assessed how adolescent binge-like alcohol consumption in a drinking in the dark (DID) model affected adult alcohol consumption, behavioral exploration, brain-wide functional connectivity, and intrinsic cellular excitability in mice. Only female mice exposed to alcohol during adolescence exhibited aversion-resistant alcohol preference, as well as increased exploration in the elevated plus maze. Resting state neuroimaging revealed broad sex-specific changes in brain-wide networks. Finally, we identify ex vivo intrinsic excitability alterations in key brain regions known to be susceptible to adolescent perturbations identified in neural networks, with greater effects in males, allowing biological and mechanistic targets to be further explored for future study and interventions. Our results show that females may be more vulnerable to lasting addiction-related behavioral and brain connectivity consequences of adolescent alcohol exposure, corroborating human and rodent studies demonstrating that adolescent alcohol use may increase risk for adult alcohol use more strongly in females. We further show that while males do not show identical behavioral changes, they critically show alterations in intrinsic excitability and cellular function, suggesting divergent sex-specific adaptations to adolescent binge drinking.

Article.Title: Predictive processing for sensory and action neural representations
Article.Authors: Iwama, G.; Bresk, A.; Helfrich, R. F.
Article.Abstract: Prior information, such as predictive cues, shape perceptual decisions. Predictive theories make conflicting claims about whether the brain preferentially processes expected, as proposed by Bayesian accounts, or unexpected information, as proposed by cancellation accounts. These conflicting mechanisms may co-exist if they differ across sensory and action systems, or if their influence changes as the decision unfolds. To test these alternatives, we tracked sensory and action representations in EEG during a motion-discrimination task with changing cue validity. Cross-temporal decoding revealed distinct stabilization of sensory and action representations. Under strong priors, stabilization of unexpected actions predicted stronger bias by the cue, consistent with cancellation accounts. Unlike action, stabilization of expected sensory information was both positively and negatively correlated with precision-weighted prior bias, depending on the decision stage (before or after stimulus onset), compatible with both Bayesian and cancellation accounts. Together, these findings suggest that predictive processing does not uniformly favor expected or unexpected information. Instead, its effects depend on representational domain and decision stage.

Article.Title: Seeing at Will: Shared Neural Representations of Motion Perception and Intention
Article.Authors: Si, W.; Choe, E.; Heller, N. H.; Kohler, P. J.; Cavanagh, P.; Stoermer, V. S.; Tse, P.
Article.Abstract: Intention can bias perception in cases where two or more interpretations of a stimulus are possible. The neural mechanisms whereby intention influences perception are poorly understood. Here we investigated whether the intention to perceive horizontal or vertical motion in a bistable apparent motion stimulus pre-activates motion axes representations in sensory cortex before the position shift occurs and before motion in consciously perceived. Twelve participants underwent fMRI scanning under three conditions: (1) passively viewing quartet stimuli moving continuously along veridical trajectories; (2) passively viewing bistable apparent motion quartet stimuli induced by two pairs of squares alternately flashing at diagonally opposite corners of an invisible rectangle; or (3) while actively intending to perceive a single-shot apparent-motion stimulus as moving either vertically or horizontally. Multivariate decoding analyses revealed that activity patterns during the intention period of (3) generalized to patterns evoked by both (1) physical and (2) ambiguous motion perception. Cross-decoding was strongest within dorsal/lateral visual regions, including hMT+, V3AB, and the intraparietal sulcus, but was largely absent from ventral visual cortex. Widespread overlap was also observed between intention-related and perceptual motion representations throughout the dorsal/lateral visual cortex. Our findings suggest that intention may bias prospective sensory representations prior to the stimulus-driven processing that results in perceptual experience and that these representations closely resemble those associated with illusory motion perception. The fact that intention-related representations were mostly found within dorsal/lateral visual regions is consistent with top-down influences from attentional control systems.

Article.Title: Tofacitinib overrides first-line drug resistance in a pre-clinical model of epilepsy
Article.Authors: Koehler, J.; Hoffman, O. R.; Harvey, Q. R.; Schoenike, B. A.; Espina, J. E. C.; Roopra, A.
