To address this, we combine topological analysis of representational manifolds with neuroscientific analyses of reactivation. We find that event-level causal relations modulate temporally structured neural reactivation in the human brain, particularly in the angular gyrus, precuneus and prefrontal cortex. By contrast, LLMs express these relations through positionally structured representational reactivation. Despite these differences, the resulting reactivation patterns exhibit similar intrinsic manifold structure across the two systems. Together, these findings suggest that the human brain and LLM share a common principle for organizing causal knowledge.

Article.Title: Spontaneous slow waves index multiple dimensions of recovery in Disorders of Consciousness
Article.Authors: Ruyant Belabbas, A.; Boullet, A.; Manasova, D.; Le Coz, A.; Valente, M.; Lejeune, F.-X.; Sitt, J. D.; Naccache, L.; Rohaut, B.; Andrillon, T.
Article.Abstract: Whether and how residual awareness is expressed in patients with Disorders of Consciousness (DoC) depends on the severity of brain damage and the transient functional state of the cortex at assessment. Classically, DoC are associated with electroencephalographic (EEG) slowing, marked by high-amplitude slow waves, even during the day. Yet, slow waves are also a hallmark of healthy sleep, where they are thought to serve restorative functions and to help maintain network homeostasis. Here, we asked whether slow waves in DoC can provide insights into the severity of cortical dysfunction or, conversely, into the preservation of residual awareness and recovery potential, by characterizing their spatial, temporal and morphological properties. We analyzed 256-channel EEG recorded during the Local-Global auditory paradigm in 236 DoC patients, including 123 in Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (UWS), 62 in a Minimally Conscious State minus (MCS-) and 29 in MCS plus (MCS+). High-amplitude slow waves were detected as local events, and their density, amplitude and slopes were quantified scalp-wide and channel-wise, by mean level and temporal variability across the recording. Slow-wave features were related to concurrent (Coma Recovery Scale-Revised - CRS-R, Local-Global paradigm) and follow-up (one-year Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended - GOS-E) assessments of consciousness and functional recovery. Associations with MRI-derived measures of cortical integrity and structural connectivity, and differences between anoxic and traumatic etiologies, were also examined. Slow waves were more frequent in less severe DoC patients (i.e., MCS) compared to UWS. Slow-wave slopes were also steeper frontally and increased at a faster rate in patients exhibiting higher levels of consciousness and/or markers of conscious access during the Local-Global paradigm. More frequent and steeper slow waves at baseline further predicted recovery of consciousness and of functional independence at one year. At the individual level, slow-wave features classified states of consciousness above chance (AUC = 0.62 and 0.71 for MCS- and MCS+ versus UWS), whereas outcome prediction remained modest (0.56-0.58). These clinical associations had a structural basis: slow-wave occurrence was greater after traumatic than anoxic injury and scaled with the integrity of subcortico-cortical projection fibers and consciousness-related cortical networks. Contrary to the classical view of delta activity as a non-specific marker of impaired consciousness, prominent spontaneous slow waves indexed behavioral and neurophysiological signs of awareness and better recovery. Beyond reflecting a propensity for pathological bistability, they may also signal the integrity of the networks required to generate them, together with their residual capacity for dynamic regulation.

Article.Title: Task demands shift motor learning from adaptation to feedback control in an unconstrained bimanual task
Article.Authors: Varghese, R.; Rossi, C.; Malone, L. A.; Bastian, A. J.
Article.Abstract: Bimanual actions are common in daily life, yet how task demands shape reliance on learning and control mechanisms remains largely unknown. We examined this in 73 participants who lifted a plate in virtual reality while we distorted visual motion of their right hand. During right-hand-only lifting, aftereffects were present but incomplete. Bimanual lifting with the same right-hand perturbation shifted learning further from adaptation toward feedback control: participants developed compensatory hand adjustments and showed smaller aftereffects. Relaxing precision demands improved success but neither restored aftereffects nor reduced compensation. Removing interlimb conflict by perturbing both hands did not improve success but eased compensatory adjustments and restored plate aftereffects to unimanual levels. Success rate during learning did not correlate with aftereffects, but faster movement speed did. This demonstrates that precision demands and interlimb conflict independently shift learning strategy in bimanual contexts.

Article.Title: Hippocampal extracellular matrix remodeling and temporally distinct glial reorganization following peripheral injury
Article.Authors: Ge, C.; Kausar, V.; Xu, L.; Maghsoudi, A.; Shtudland, G.; Amrami, M.; Betancourt, M.; Niaz, A.; Zirkiyev, J.; Alvarado, S. G.; Abzalimov, R.; He, Y.; Tajerian, M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic pain is frequently accompanied by anxiety and other affective disturbances, but the molecular and cellular changes linking peripheral injury to persistent alterations in brain function remain incompletely defined. The hippocampal extracellular matrix (ECM) regulates synaptic plasticity, cellular signaling, and neuroimmune interactions and may therefore contribute to pain-related central plasticity. We used a tibial fracture/cast immobilization model to examine temporal changes in hippocampal ECM, glial morphology, and affective behavior following peripheral injury. Behavioral testing was performed at 3, 7, and 20 weeks after injury, while high-dimensional morphometric analysis of microglia and astrocytes was performed at 1, 3, 7, and 20 weeks. Hippocampal ECM associated molecular signals were mapped at the chronic stage using decellularization coupled with MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry imaging. Injured mice developed mechanical hypersensitivity and reduced exploration in two anxiety related paradigms during the early and chronic stages, with these behavioral phenotypes no longer detected at 20 weeks. At 7 weeks, injury was associated with changes in hippocampal ECM-associated peptide signals, including reduced signals corresponding to four ECM-associated proteins. Microglia and astrocytes exhibited distinct, time-dependent changes in density and multidimensional morphology, with some alterations persisting after behavioral measures returned toward control levels. In vitro, BV2 microglia exhibited rigidity-dependent changes in morphology, phagocytic behavior, and calcium signaling. Together, these findings define a temporally evolving hippocampal ECM and glial phenotype following peripheral injury and identify matrix biomechanics as a candidate regulator of microglial function.

Article.Title: Immediate cortical responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation of the human motor leg area
Article.Authors: Beck, M. M.; Nuyts, M.; Sakalauskaite, L.; Rothwell, J.; Siebner, H. R.; Christiansen, L.
Article.Abstract: Background: Immediate transcranial evoked potentials (iTEPs) are ultra-early electroencephalographic responses elicited by single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the primary motor cortical hand area (M1-HAND). Their characteristic latency, waveform, and sensitivity to short-interval intracortical inhibition suggest a close relationship to the cortical generators of indirect corticospinal volleys (I-waves). Here, we tested the hypothesis that iTEPs constitute a fundamental physiological response of human motor cortex and therefore generalize across motor representations, including the leg representation (M1-LEG). Methods: Single-pulse TMS was delivered over the motor cortical representation of the right tibialis anterior (TA) in 16 healthy volunteers. In a subset of participants (n=10), stimulus-response curves and paired-pulse short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) measures were obtained. Results: TMS of M1-LEG elicited reproducible iTEPs consisting of a slow positive deflection with superimposed high-frequency peaks with topographic maxima in electrodes adjacent to the stimulation site. M1-LEG iTEPs emerged close to active motor threshold and increased in prevalence and amplitude with increasing stimulation intensity. Paired-pulse stimulation produced consistent SICI of the second and third iTEP peaks. M1-LEG stimulation also evoked conventional later TEPs with latencies and polarities closely resembling those recorded after M1-HAND stimulation. Conclusions: TMS of the human M1-LEG elicits robust iTEPs that closely resemble those recorded from M1-HAND in their timing, intensity dependence, and sensitivity to intracortical inhibition. These findings indicate that iTEPs are not specific to M1-HAND but reflect a general physiological response of human motor cortex closely linked to corticospinal I-wave generation. This broadens their utility as a non-invasive probe of excitatory and inhibitory circuit dynamics throughout the human motor system.

Article.Title: Aging reshapes odor-evoked dynamics in central olfactory circuits
Article.Authors: Chapman, I. F.; Bolding, K. A.
Article.Abstract: Olfactory decline is among the earliest signs of aging and predicts later cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Age-related impairments in odor identification and discrimination implicate central olfactory brain regions in both mice and humans, but it remains unclear where in the processing hierarchy aging alters neural function relating to these cognitive and perceptual deficits. To resolve this, we acquired simultaneous Neuropixels recordings from olfactory bulb (OB) and piriform cortex (PCx) in young and old mice during awake, head-fixed odor presentation, allowing us to probe multiple levels of odor response features within each animal. Our recordings revealed a shift toward greater excitation in both regions and reduced inhibitory neuron activity in PCx. Aging also restructured odor-evoked local field potential (LFP) oscillations within and across regions, with strongly elevated beta power and coherence. Population odor representations were less discriminable in OB, but not in PCx. Thus, our results point to reduced discriminability of OB population odor representations as the clearest neural analog of previously reported discrimination deficits. Single-unit, LFP, and population measures did not collapse onto a single axis using dimensionality reduction, indicating that several partly independent processes reshape the dynamics of odor responses in central olfactory circuits with aging. Together, these findings identify central circuit excitation/inhibition (E/I) and oscillatory imbalances that parallel age-related olfactory dysfunction despite largely preserved odor responsivity.

Article.Title: Model-based pupil deconvolution reveals latent attentional dynamics
Article.Authors: Maity, S.; Mathot, S.; Ray, S. B.
Article.Abstract: Changes in pupil size have been widely used as an indirect measure of attention. However, attention engages on a faster timescale than the pupillary response. Therefore, the slow time course of the pupil response makes it difficult to distinguish attentional responses to stimuli presented in close temporal succession. Although signal deconvolution has been used in previous research to estimate latent attentional responses from the pupil signal, existing methods primarily model dilation without considering the visual stimulus evoked constriction phase of the pupil. Here, we introduce a dual-kernel deconvolution model that models constriction and dilation using separate impulse response functions. Using an RSVP paradigm with emotional faces as target stimuli, we demonstrate that the proposed model estimates latent attentional response despite substantial overlap in the measured pupil signal. Importantly, the recovered attentional response resembles the time course of attentional allocation previously predicted by several models of Attentional Blink. Together, these findings demonstrate that the dynamics of latent attentional episodes can be recovered from the pupil response with a temporal resolution previously obscured by the sluggishness of the pupillary response. The proposed method is also provided as a usable software package that serves as a general tool for investigating the temporal dynamics of attention in rapid visual paradigms.

Article.Title: Eyes on the prize: a neural basis of perceptual choking under pressure
Article.Authors: McDonnell, M. E.; Chandrasekaran, A. N.; Ki, C. S.; Smoulder, A. L.; Miyata, H.; Yu, B.; Batista, A. P.; Smith, M. A.; Chase, S. M.
Article.Abstract: Even professional athletes sometimes fail to perform when it matters most. This phenomenon, known as choking under pressure, has been observed in a variety of motor and cognitive tasks. Can inordinately large rewards influence even sensory processing, and if so, what might be its neural basis? To probe this, we studied rhesus monkeys performing a challenging color change detection task and recorded from populations of neurons in visual area V4. We found that monkeys underperformed when offered rare "jackpot" rewards and uncovered associated detrimental alterations in V4 population activity. These findings were consistent with misallocated spatial attention, providing a potential neural basis for perceptual choking under pressure.

Article.Title: Biophysical modeling of excitation/inhibition imbalance in Alzheimer's disease
Article.Authors: Deng, Q.; Chen, C.; Zikopoulos, B.; Yazdanbakhsh, A.
Article.Abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves early sensory and perceptual changes that can precede memory decline. We developed a two-layer rate-based neural model of early and higher visual areas with feedforward, feedback, and recurrent connections to examine how excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance shapes visual motion perception in AD. METHODS: Using Motion-Induced Position Shift and Altered Motion Repulsion stimuli, we factorially manipulated excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) subfield power and connectivity to examine their effects on illusion representation across visual layers. RESULTS: Increased E, decreased I, and increased E/I reduced illusion representation, consistent with reduced illusion susceptibility in AD, whereas the converse increased illusion representation, reflecting neurotypical processing. Higher-level layer 2 representations were more resistant to E/I perturbations than lower-level layer 1. Illusion representation was less affected by E/I increases in intra-areal (recurrent) connectivity than in inter-areal (feedforward/feedback) connectivity. DISCUSSION: This mechanistic framework links E/I balance and connectivity to altered visual motion illusion representations in AD and suggests that E/I and connectivity measures may provide probes of early AD neurobiology. The framework may also generalize beyond vision.

Article.Title: Retinotopic organization of head-orienting vectors in the pigeon ventral lateral geniculate nucleus
Article.Authors: Severin, D.; Reynaert, B.; Vega-Zuniga, T.; Letelier, J. C.; Marin, G.; Karten, H. J.; Mpodozis, J.
Article.Abstract: The ventral lateral geniculate nucleus (GLv) is a conserved retinorecipient structure positioned between visual and premotor systems, yet its role in visuomotor transformations remains poorly understood. Here, we examined whether the pigeon GLv contains a spatially organized motor representation linking visual-field locations to orienting movements. Anatomical tracing identified descending projections from neurons in the GLv inner lamina (GLv-li) through pretectal and tegmental regions toward pontine targets. GLv-li projection neurons are GABAergic, yet electrical microstimulation of GLv-li in awake pigeons evoked rapid head movements followed by smaller eye movements. Each stimulation locus produced a reproducible characteristic motor vector whose direction and duration were largely insensitive to stimulation parameters, whereas movement amplitude and velocity approached site-specific plateaus. Movements initiated from different head positions were better explained by repetition of a fixed displacement than by convergence toward a common spatial goal. Critically, motor-vector direction was systematically related to the direction of the visual receptive field represented at the same GLv locus, while motor-vector amplitude covaried with receptive-field eccentricity. These defining features persisted after optic tectum ablation. Together, these findings reveal a retinotopically-organized map of fixed-vector head movements in the avian GLv and identify a tectum-independent route through which visual spatial representations can access descending orienting circuitry.

Article.Title: Focal drug uncaging for the precise control of endogenous nicotinic receptors in behaving mice
Article.Authors: Guyon, N.; Mohayyaei, M.; Bergel, A.; Grellier, G.; Jehl, J.; Pietrancosta, N.; Rebola, N.; Francois, A.; Faure, P.; Ellis-Davies, G. C. R.; Mourot, A.
Article.Abstract: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors shape diverse brain functions, including reward, aversion, and pain, but dissecting their roles in vivo requires drug delivery with spatiotemporal precision that conventional pharmacology cannot provide. Here we establish in vivo photopharmacology of endogenous nicotinic receptors: two complementary, highly-potent agonists, administered systemically in an inactive caged form, are photoreleased locally in target brain circuits of behaving wild-type mice. Despite irreversible photochemistry, photoactivation can be repeated over many trials on a minute timescale, for hours following a single injection. Local uncaging evokes circuit-specific dopamine release, drives place preference from the ventral tegmental area and aversion from the interpeduncular nucleus, and, in pain circuits, reveals a pronociceptive effect masked when the same agonists are given systemically. By controlling where and when nicotinic signaling acts, this approach exposes circuit-specific drug effects invisible to conventional pharmacology, and outlines a general strategy for on-demand control of endogenous receptors in vivo.

Article.Title: Synaptic density imaging associates with performance but not self-report in autism
Article.Authors: Naples, A. J.; Cayir, S.; Cukar-Capizzi, C.; Wolf, J. M.; Mcclelland, J. E.; Robertson, E. C.; Sawant, S. S.; Matuskey, D.; McPartland, J. C.
Article.Abstract: Autism is a common neurodevelopmental condition with considerable between-person variability and unknown biological etiology. Diagnosis of autism in adults relies on measurement of performance (e.g., clinician rating of social behavior, standardized assessment of cognition) and self-report of autism features. Our prior work revealed a strong relationship between clinician ratings of social function in autism and in vivo measures of synaptic density as measured by [11C]UCB-J PET (Matuskey et al., 2025). However, it is not understood how the measured aspects of the autism phenotype index underlying biology. Here, in a sample of 12 autistic adults, we address this question by relating synaptic density imaging to a range of performance measures, such as cognition and face recognition, in contrast to self-report measures. Our results identify a dissociation between these measurement types in that synaptic density correlates strongly with measures of performance but shows virtually no relationship with self-report. These findings suggest that, while self-report and performance measures share variance in characterizing phenotypes in autism, they diverge when mapping onto the underlying biology. Results suggest that higher synaptic density may index a general mechanism that facilitates social and cognitive performance across a range of tasks. These data also indicate that performance and self-report measures are not interchangeable in capturing brain-behavior correspondences in autism, a finding that can guide measure selection in future biomarker studies and clinical research.

Article.Title: Impaired astrocytic Cx43 syncytial network in lateral habenula affects synaptic connectivity and drives adolescent stress-induced depression
Article.Authors: Li, H.; Wang, Q.; Su, Y.; Chen, H.; Wu, Z.; Chen, X.; Wang, C.; Zhao, Y.; Li, D.; Huang, X.; Fu, R.; Huang, W.; Tang, Y.; Niu, J.; Verkhratsky, A.; Yi, C.
Article.Abstract: Adolescent depression is a major neuropsychiatric disorder induced by early life stress; the underlying cellular mechanisms instigating pathological circuit malformation remain unclear, and, consequently, effective therapeutic strategy is limited. Here, we analysed the contribution of astrocytes to early life stress-induced adolescent depression using a mouse model of parental separation. We identified a previously unrecognised regional specialisation of lateral habenula (LHb) astrocytes, characterised by compact cellular domains, abundant leaflets, and enhanced Cx43 gap junctional coupling. Parental separation selectively reduced astrocytic Cx43 expression and gap junctional communication in the LHb, which was accompanied by profound astrocytic atrophy and loss of leaflets. Single-cell sequencing further revealed that parental separation induces a broad reorganisation of LHb astrocyte transcriptional states, including metabolic, stress-response, and inflammatory programs; moreover, it specifically reduces astrocyte-neuron communication. Consistent with this, we found that structural remodelling of LHb astrocytes affected tripartite synapse geometry, resulting in impaired excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission, and neuronal Ca2+ hyperexcitability, all ultimately associated with depressive-like behaviours. Selective knockdown of astrocytic Cx43 in the LHb recapitulated these pathological changes and translated into depressive-like behaviours. Mechanistically, we found that impaired Cx43 gap junctional communication is associated with excessive astrocytic Ca2+ dynamics, resulting in Rac1-GTPase activation and decreased p-Ezrin levels. In vivo inhibition of LHb astrocytic Ca2+ signalling rescued astrocytic atrophy and depressive-like behaviours following parental separation. Together, our findings establish a Cx43-Ca2+-Rac1-p-Ezrin pathway that links gap junction malfunction to structural remodelling of astrocytes and disruption of neuron-astrocyte interactions in the developing LHb. Our study reveals astrocytic Ca2+ dysregulation as an active downstream effector of Cx43 dysfunction and identifies a regionally specialised astrocytic mechanism through which early-life stress disrupts synaptic transmission and neuronal function during adolescence, providing a potential cellular target for intervention in adolescent depression.

Article.Title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles
Article.Authors: Broor, M.; Ogunniyi, K.; Williamson, L.; Liu, C.
Article.Abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

Article.Title: Dorsomedial striatal Bmal1 deletion in medium spiny neurons alters EPSCs and dendritic morphology after chronic exposure to alcohol in female mice.
Article.Authors: Darvishmolla, M.; Courtemanche, R.; Amir, S.; Chapman, A.
Article.Abstract: Circadian clock genes in the striatum modulate alcohol drinking behavior in female mice, but the underlying synaptic mechanisms remain unknown. Medium spiny neurons (MSNs) of the striatum express D1- or D2-type dopamine receptors, which are differentially modulated by alcohol. Here we used whole-cell patch-clamp recordings to examine how deletion of the clock gene Bmal1 affects spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in electrophysiologically identified D1 and D2 neurons of the female mouse dorsomedial striatum (DMS). Prior intermittent access to alcohol increased sEPSC amplitude in putative D1 neurons of wildtype mice without affecting sEPSC frequency, and this increase was accompanied by greater dendritic branching and complexity in biocytin-filled D1 MSNs. Bmal1 knockout had the opposite effect in D1 neurons, reducing sEPSC amplitude in both alcohol-exposed and alcohol-naive animals. In D2 neurons, alcohol produced only a non-significant trend toward increased sEPSC amplitude in wildtype mice, but a significant increase in Bmal1 knockout mice. Thus, local disruption of Bmal1 appears to block the alcohol-induced enhancement of sEPSCs in D1 neurons while unmasking a similar enhancement in D2 neurons. These findings may help explain how Bmal1 deletion in the DMS reduces alcohol consumption in female mice.

Article.Title: Cross-Tissue Inflammatory Convergence Supports a Putative Muscle-Brain Axis in Alzheimer's Disease
Article.Authors: Zhang, A.; Shen, W.; Yan, S.; Chen, J.; Liu, X.; Zou, J.; Li, S.; Hu, S.; Liu, Y.; Pan, C.; Lan, Z.; Peng, G.; Zhang, Q.; Peng, W.; Ahmadizar, F.; Zhang, J.
Article.Abstract: Background Reduced muscle strength is associated with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that skeletal-muscle aging and AD-related neurodegeneration may share biological mechanisms. Vascular dysfunction, immune activation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling have been implicated in both tissues, but the extent of shared cellular and molecular programs remains unclear. We investigated cross-tissue transcriptional programs in aging skeletal muscle and AD-related brain tissue and evaluated whether related signals are detectable in peripheral blood. Methods We analyzed independent, unpaired human transcriptomic datasets from skeletal muscle (23 donors), the SEA-AD middle temporal gyrus atlas (84 donors), and peripheral blood. Donor-aware models identified age-associated changes in muscle and transcriptomic changes across continuous pseudoprogression score (CPS) in brain. Cross-tissue comparisons focused on 30 brain donors within an early CPS window. Shared tissue-derived programs were assessed in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and independently tested in frailty bulk-blood and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) whole-blood datasets. CellOracle simulations were used to prioritize candidate transcriptional regulators. Results Aging muscle showed increased inflammatory, extracellular-matrix, and stromal communication programs. During early AD-related brain progression, vascular and immune populations showed increasing inflammatory and matrix-associated activity together with shifts in intercellular communication. Cross-tissue analysis identified six concordantly enriched pathways comprising 109 leading-edge genes in endothelial populations and four pathways comprising 51 genes in myeloid populations. Related peripheral-blood signatures varied across cohorts and cell types. However, in independent frailty and ADNI mild cognitive impairment and AD datasets, 23 of 30 predefined tissue-derived pathway-subset tests showed significant positive enrichment after false-discovery-rate correction, whereas individual gene-level bulk-blood associations did not survive correction. CellOracle analyses prioritized ETS2 and BHLHE40 as exploratory endothelial regulators whose simulated perturbation consistently reduced selected shared program scores across tissues. Conclusions Aging skeletal muscle and AD-related brain tissue exhibit convergent endothelial and myeloid inflammatory programs, with related pathway-level signals detectable in peripheral blood. These cross-tissue programs and candidate endothelial regulators provide testable hypotheses for mechanisms linking systemic aging, muscle dysfunction, and AD-related neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Bone regulates locomotion by sustaining motoneuronal mitochondrial function
Article.Authors: Romeo Guitart, D.; Tirani, T.; Milunov, D.; Torres-Juacida, A. K.; Lamotte, B.; Arenas-Plascencia, C.; Durand, S.; Nemazanyy, I.; Moriceau, S.; Saha, S.; Karsenty, G.; Oury, F.
Article.Abstract: Body-brain communication is crucial for optimal neuronal performance across the lifespan, yet whether peripheral organs regulate spinal cord motoneuron (MN) function through circulating molecules remains unknown. The expression of hormone receptors by spinal MNs raises the possibility that circulating cues allow the spinal cord to sense the body's energetic state and sustain motor activity. Here, we show that the bone-derived hormones osteocalcin (OCN) signals on spinal MNs via its receptor GPR158. GPR158 is selectively enriched in spinal cholinergic MNs, and its loss, globally or specifically in spinal MNs, or the one of OCN, impairs locomotor function and reduces choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) levels. Mechanistically, OCN signaling through GPR158 fine-tunes autophagy, mitophagy and mitochondrial activity in spinal MNs. Restoring any of these processes, by pharmacologically inducing mitophagy or chemogenetically activating mitochondria, is sufficient to rescue the locomotor deficits of Gpr158-deficient mice. Finally, OCN restoration in aged mice reverses age-related locomotor decline through a mechanism that requires MN autophagy and mitophagy. This study reveals that through OCN, the skeleton influences motor functions by fine-tuning motoneuronal mitochondria, and suggests that age-related motor decline is, at least in part, reversible.

Article.Title: Neural Evidence of Early Sensitivity to Text in Pre-reading Toddlers
Article.Authors: Kherbawy, N.; Potter, C. E.; Jaffe-Dax, S.
Article.Abstract: Learning to read leads to widespread changes in brain organization, but it is not yet known when text first becomes a privileged stimulus. To test whether neural sensitivity to text can appear prior to reading instruction, 31 monolingual toddlers in Israel (2.1-3.6 years) not yet enrolled in school were presented with displays of real, native text and visually matched non-text symbols. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy, we found different patterns of activity in response to text vs. non-text across multiple cortical regions. Most notably, text elicited more activity in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, a region often associated with language processing. These results suggest that through implicit sensitivity to regularities in their input, toddlers may be able to discover that text is a meaningful stimulus and could begin to develop associations that will allow them to build connections between language and text.

Article.Title: The Effective Visual Acuity of Butterflies in Flight
Article.Authors: Supple, J. A.; Li, W.; Ilic, M.; Kos, M.; Lin, H.-T.; Belusic, G.; Krapp, H. G.
Article.Abstract: The spatial visual acuity of an eye is determined by both the spatial sampling density of the retina and the angular sensitivity of individual photoreceptors. In insect compound eyes, these are respectively characterised by the interommatidial angle, {Delta}{varphi}, and photoreceptor acceptance angle, {Delta}{rho}. During movement, however, finite photoreceptor integration times cause retinal image motion to broaden the effective acceptance angle, potentially degrading spatial resolution beyond its anatomical limit. This problem is especially acute in flying insects, which experience large rotational velocities during locomotion and must actively stabilise gaze to limit retinal image motion. Butterflies present a particularly demanding case because their flight is characterised by large, wingbeat-coupled thoracic oscillations. Here, we quantify how gaze stabilisation limits motion blur in freely flying Monarch butterflies Danaus plexippus by combining free-flight kinematic reconstruction of the head and thorax with separate intracellular measurements of photoreceptor acceptance angles and integration times from quiescent butterflies. We found that, without head compensation, thoracic oscillations would broaden the effective photoreceptor acceptance angle from its quiescent value of 2.17{degrees} to 9.38{degrees} during take-off. Compensatory head movements substantially reduced this motion-induced broadening, limiting the effective acceptance angle to 5.28{degrees}. Nevertheless, this 2.4-fold broadening of effective photoreceptor acceptance angle represents a substantial degradation of spatial acuity in flight, highlighting motion blur as an important constraint on the visual ecology of flying butterflies.

Article.Title: Reduction of complex dynamic touch information to a single stable perceptual feature
Article.Authors: Zamani, N.; Stephens-Fripp, B.; Tymms, C.; Chan, S.; Pardakhtim, R.; Culburtson, H.; Hartcher-O'Brien, J.
Article.Abstract: Dynamic touch requires the perceptual system to extract stable material properties from complex, evolving signals. Here, we examine potential material property features for a constrained dynamic-touch regime: brief taps, in which contact-induced vibratory transients are prominent and sustained deformation cues are reduced. Using a spectral-energy compensation method, we conducted five psychophysical experiments in two degraded-feedback scenarios: soft finger interfaces, in which fingertip stiffness was reduced by an inflatable silicone bubble, and compliant-surface interactions, in which participants tapped foam surfaces. Participants made explicit hardness judgments in two-alternative forced-choice tasks and identified rendered materials in multi-alternative matching and classification tasks. Under these tapping-based conditions, judgments scaled systematically with total spectral energy and were largely independent of waveform family. When spectral energy and dominant-frequency cues were placed in conflict, classifications predominantly followed spectral energy. These results identify total spectral energy as a robust cue for hardness judgments and material identification from brief taps, rather than as a complete account of hardness perception across all exploratory procedures. The findings provide a compact rendering principle for haptic interfaces in which contact-triggered vibrotactile feedback is available.

Article.Title: Voluntary engagement predicts recovery across rehabilitation time points after experimental spinal cord injury
Article.Authors: Griffin, J. M.; Papaioannou, P.; Menon, R.; Cheyne, O.; Kellaway, S.; Svirskis, D.; Jutzeler, C.; Aziz, A.; Bradke, F.
Article.Abstract:
Rehabilitation is the cornerstone of clinical care following spinal cord injury (SCI) and is frequently incorporated into preclinical studies to evaluate emerging therapies. However, the variables that influence the effectiveness of rehabilitation interventions in rodent models remain poorly characterized, limiting the translational value of preclinical research. Here, we performed a meta-analysis of 150 preclinical studies comprising more than 3000 rodents and 292 effect sizes to identify such factors associated with successful rehabilitation after SCI. Rehabilitation improved functional outcomes across multiple behavioral domains, with larger effects observed in thoracic than cervical injury models. Meta-regression identified environmental enrichment as the most effective strategy, particularly when combined with task-specific training. Longer rehabilitation duration was associated with improved recovery, whereas greater daily exposure to forced rehabilitation was associated with smaller gains. In contrast, prolonged access to voluntary rehabilitation did not show this relationship. Rehabilitation improved outcomes when initiated at all time points after injury, with greater benefits when initiated during the late subacute and intermediate phases. Rehabilitation approaches associated with higher stress burden produced reduced benefits, suggesting that stress may limit rehabilitation-induced recovery. Collectively, these findings identify rehabilitation type, duration, and delivery context as important determinants of recovery after SCI and support a broad therapeutic window for intervention. Our results favor low-stress, voluntary rehabilitation strategies that promote sustained engagement and provide principles for designing effective and biologically appropriate rehabilitation strategies, potentially improving translational success for emerging SCI therapies.
One Sentence SummarySustained voluntary rehabilitation promotes functional recovery across stages of experimental spinal cord injury, whereas prolonged forced training may reduce its benefits.

Article.Title: Intracranial electrophysiology reveals distinct neural representations of nociception and salience in the human brain
Article.Authors: Joshi, S.; Polat, M.; Pantis, S.; Garg, R.; Ahmed, S.; Huang, Y.; McGeoch, P. D.; Keller, C. J.; Buch, V. P.; Mackey, S.; Parvizi, J.; Ramayya, A. G.
Article.Abstract: Neuroimaging studies have shown close overlap between neural representations of nociceptive stimuli and non-nociceptive, salient stimuli (such as low-probability sounds), leading to the proposal that nociception and salience share a common neural substrate in the human brain. Here we use high-resolution intracranial recordings from 13 neurosurgical patients (2,018 total electrodes) to show that neural representations of nociception and salience are anatomically and functionally distinct in the human brain. 77% of 107 electrodes that encoded nociceptive stimuli did not encode low-probability sounds ("nociceptive representations"), whereas 23% encoded both nociceptive and low-probability sounds ("salience representations"). Nociceptive representations were distinct from salience representations in terms of anatomical prevalence (posterior insula, inferior parietal, and perirolandic cortex vs. anterior insula, thalamus, and inferior frontal gyrus), timing (nociception preceded salience by 120 ms on a trial-by-trial basis), and function (intracranial electrical stimulation was more likely to cause sensory experience when applied near nociceptive representations, as compared to salience representations). These results provide strong evidence that nociception and salience have distinct neural substrates in the human brain, and that selective measurement of these distinct processes may help understand patient-to-patient variability in chronic pain and develop personalized brain stimulation treatments.

Article.Title: Acceleration of vision changes object representations from infancy to adulthood
Article.Authors: Spriet, C.; Serraille, E.; Naderi, S.; Agrebi, M.; Bouyahia, Z.; Derrode, S.; Kaiser, D.; Papeo, L.; Hochmann, J.-R.
Article.Abstract: While much of the neural and cognitive machinery for visual perception is in place within weeks from birth, we identified and quantified a fundamental difference between infant and adult vision: the temporal rate at which meaningful visual information can be reliably extracted. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography with rapid serial visual presentation, we found that object categorization at 4 and 9 months is respectively seven times and two to three times slower than in adults. Using quantitative information from infants experiments, we created and presented accelerated visual streams to adults, to match infants perceptual experience. We used deep convolutional neural networks to identify object representations that match those elicited in adults when accelerating the information flow. Results show that acceleration compromises finer-grained object distinction while sparing broad, general object representations. We propose that slow vision is a design feature of early development for preserving and highlighting the most stable and general features of the world.

Article.Title: Larger Pre-Speech Auditory Modulation Is Associated With Smaller Corrective Responses To Auditory Errors
Article.Authors: Basciano, A.; Chao, S.-C.; Rogalsky, C.; Daliri, A.
Article.Abstract:
PurposeDuring speech planning, the brain predicts the auditory consequences of its movements and modulates the auditory system--a process called pre-speech auditory modulation (PSAM). We investigated the link between PSAM and behavioral error correction and determined how aging influences these mechanisms.
MethodsSeventeen young adults (18-32 years) and 13 older adults (50-85 years) performed a speaking task involving auditory feedback perturbations and a silent reading control. We measured electrophysiological responses (N1/P2) to auditory probes during speech planning and correlated these modulations with the magnitude of participants subsequent behavioral corrective responses.
ResultsBoth groups showed significant modulation of N1 and P2. However, N1 modulation correlated with corrective responses only in young adults. Older adults showed reduced behavioral corrections and smaller, delayed P2 components. Despite these age-related behavioral differences and the loss of the modulation-correction correlation, older adults maintained modulation magnitudes comparable to those of younger adults.
ConclusionsN1 modulation serves as a neural index of the brains predictive processes during speech planning. Aging appears to selectively disrupt the integration of these signals into motor output rather than the internal generation of the predictions themselves.

Article.Title: Rewiring the Human Brain: On the Fabric of Associative Thinking
Article.Authors: Czappa, F.; Kaster, M.; Kaiser, M.; Chen, X.; Butz-Ostendorf, M.; Wolf, F.
Article.Abstract: Concept cells are neurons in the medial temporal lobe that represent an abstract concept, such as a familiar person, in a context-independent way. They are activated by heterogeneous and potentially multimodal sensory input related to the concept, such as viewing a photo of the person, reading the person's name, or hearing the person's voice. Learning the concept implies connecting the cortical cells that are triggered when such features are perceived with the cells of the concept, resulting in an associative memory engram. Traditional models explain the formation of such an engram with Hebbian learning through synaptic plasticity, the strengthening of existing synapses in response to co-activation. However, the low edge density of the brain suggests that direct connections in the form of preexisting synapses between these cells are relatively unlikely, rendering such constructs inefficient and volatile. Instead, it is plausible that more persistent concept engrams rely on structural plasticity, involving the creation of synapses de novo. Yet, it remains unclear how neurons can find new postsynaptic targets over such a considerable distance. In this paper, we simulate the formation of such structural engrams in the connectomes of healthy subjects, offering a model hypothesis of how such engrams can be formed on a structural level. Based on our model, we further demonstrate how activating a concept can trigger related concepts through overlapping sensory associations, in a process we call a percept-concept loop.

Article.Title: BunDLe-Net: Learning minimal neural manifolds that represent only behaviourally relevant dynamics
Article.Authors: Kumar, A.; Gilra, A.; Meunier, A.; Grosse-Wentrup, M.
Article.Abstract: Neural manifold learning techniques represent high-dimensional neural dynamics in low-dimensional embeddings to reveal the intrinsic structure of neural manifolds. We introduce a novel neural manifold learning technique, BunDLe-Net, that learns a low-dimensional Markovian embedding of the neural dynamics which preserves only those aspects of the neural dynamics that are relevant for a given behavioural context. In contrast to other techniques that learn embeddings which allow a good reconstruction of the original data, BunDLe-Net eliminates neural dynamics that are irrelevant for decoding behaviour, effectively de-noising the data to reveal better the intricate relationships between neural dynamics and behaviour. We show that BunDLe-Net learns highly consistent manifolds across animals that reveal the building blocks of their neural manifolds on a variety of data sets, ranging from calcium imaging data recorded in the nematode C. elegans to spiking data from the rat hippocampus.

Article.Title: Sex influences gliovascular unit assembly and function in the developing mouse brain
Article.Authors: Lemale, L.; Abioui Mourgues, M.; Naule, L.; Alvear Perrez, R.; Rubio, M.; Vivien, D.; Becmeur Lefebvre, M.; Hourcade, T.; Boulay, A. C.; Mhaouty-Kodja, S.; Cohen-Salmon, M.; Delaunay-Piednoir, B.
Article.Abstract: The gliovascular unit (GVU), a specialized interface between the brain and the vascular system) assembles and matures after birth and establishes essential homeostatic functions, including blood brain barrier integrity, metabolic exchanges, fluid drainage, neurovascular coupling, and immune surveillance. Here, we compared the postnatal maturation of the cortical GVU in male vs. female mice. On P15, males exhibited more angiogenesis, a higher vessel density, and a higher level of aquaporin 4 expression in perivascular astrocyte processes. Females exhibited a higher density of perivascular macrophages and fibroblasts on P15 and P30 respectively, earlier development of the arterial vascular network, and a greater capacity to recruit cerebral blood flow. Transcriptomic profiling during the P5 P120 period revealed sex-specific developmental trajectories within the GVU, with the most prominent differences observed on P5. These dimorphisms were regulated at least in part by oestrogenic signalling. Taken as a whole, our results highlight pronounced sex-dependent differences in GVU assembly and maturation that might influence brain physiology and vulnerability to neurodevelopmental disorders.

Article.Title: Highlighting the strengths of new wearable fNIRS, precision accuracy microgenetic research designs, and new NeuroDOT processing algorithm to measure change over time in clinical populations for Speech-Language and Hearing Researchers
Article.Authors: Crow, S.; Segel, A.; Speh, E.; Eggebrecht, A. T.; Skolasinska, P.; Evans, J.
Article.Abstract: Fundamental to understanding the process of intervention among individuals with communication disorders is the ability to document behavioral changes over time. This technical report demonstrates the clinical applicability of wearable fNIRS systems and NeuroDOT processing pipelines for examining within-person cortical dynamics of learning. Using a microgenetic research design and a dense sampling approach, we examined changes in the prefrontal cortical hemodynamic response in an adult female participant who completed the same spoken sentence repetition and auditory fixation tasks across eight sessions. In addition to participant accuracy, hemodynamic data were collected with a continuous-wave, multi-channel fNIRS system (NIRSport2) using a prefrontal 20-channel optode montage. Data were processed using NeuroDOT (https://www.nitrc.org/projects/neurodot) (Eggebrecht & Culver, 2019) to: (i) standardize signal quality across the sessions to quantify motion levels and to ensure standardized brain map specificity, (ii) to examine both channel space fluctuations in the hemodynamic response and map changes in cortical activation patterns over the sessions. The signal quality met the predefined criteria for only the first five sessions. Participant's repetition accuracy did not improve over the five sessions. Channel-wise analysis revealed that HbO concentration differs significantly over right and left hemisphere channels over the course of the five sessions for the Sentence Repetition task, but not for the Auditory Fixation condition. Brain maps revealed qualitative differences in the pattern of prefrontal cortical activation across the five sessions. To fully document the mechanisms that drive changes in behavior, understanding the brain-behavior link is critical to identifying and discriminating between typical and atypical learning.

Article.Title: Striatal dopamine and serotonin release operate largely in parallel with limited, asymmetric crosstalk
Article.Authors: Chaudun, F.; Liu, Y.; Traba, J. E.; Hiver, A.; Luscher, C.
Article.Abstract: Dopamine and serotonin jointly regulate striatal functions that support reinforcement, decision-making and motivated behavior, yet whether activity in one system directly recruits release from the other remains unclear. Using anatomical tracing, cell type-specific optogenetics and genetically encoded fluorescent sensors, we measured dopamine and serotonin dynamics in the nucleus accumbens and dorsal striatum after cocaine administration and selective neuronal stimulation. Activation of ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons increased dopamine release without affecting serotonin. In contrast, activation of dorsal raphe serotonergic neurons robustly increased serotonin and weakly entrained dopamine signals without producing a sustained increase in dopamine amplitude. These findings indicate that striatal dopamine and serotonin release operate largely in parallel, with limited and directionally asymmetric crosstalk.

Article.Title: Disease-associated variants alter a novel physiological role of hnRNP H2 in neuronal development
Article.Authors: Lourinho, A.; Silva, M. S.; Tahiri, E.; D'Ambrosio, M.; Pinto, A. D.; Calvo Parra, S.; De Pietro, G.; Galvao, G.; Caniceiro, A. B.; Pereira de Almeida, L.; Pinheiro, P.; Moreira, I. S.; Nobre, R. J.; Mele, M.; Cwetsch, A. W.; Duarte, C. B.; Costa, R. O.
Article.Abstract: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein H2 (hnRNP H2) is a member of the hnRNP family of RNA-binding proteins that regulate neuronal function through multiple aspects of RNA metabolism. Mutations in the nuclear localisation signal (NLS) and quasi-RNA recognition motifs (qRRMs) of hnRNP H2 have recently been linked to a severe developmental syndrome, termed HNRNPH2-related neurodevelopmental disorder. Despite its emerging importance, the physiological roles of hnRNP H2 in neuronal development and synaptic maturation, and how disease-associated variants alter these processes to drive pathology, remain poorly understood. Here, we show that hnRNP H2 is expressed in hippocampal neurons and localises to the synaptic compartment. Knockdown of hnRNP H2 revealed essential roles of the protein in the regulation of neuronal morphology, dendritic spine maturation, synaptic transmission, and cortical neuronal migration in vivo. Disease-associated hnRNP H2 variants altered protein localisation and activity-dependent synaptic recruitment, resulting in defects in neuronal morphology, in vivo cortical neuronal migration and laminar orientation, dendritic spine maturation, and synaptic function. Together, these findings establish hnRNP H2 as a critical regulator of neurodevelopment and identify a molecular basis for HNRNPH2-related neurodevelopmental disorder.

Article.Title: Neuropeptide NLP-40 and Cognate G- Protein Coupled Receptor AEX-2 Regulate Behavioral Responses During Anoxia in Caenorhabditis elegans
Article.Authors: Watzinger, G. Z.; Bennett, H. L.
Article.Abstract: Background: Insufficient oxygen (hypoxia) or complete lack of oxygen (anoxia) causes cellular dysfunction and death in terrestrial animals. As a result, animals have developed homeostatic strategies, including changes in movement strategies to escape and survive stressful environments. Caenorhabditis elegans respond to changes in oxygen by increasing the frequency of reversals (backward movement) and increasing locomotor speed; these behaviors enable them to escape unfavorable environments and move to more suitable ones. The molecular and neural mechanisms underlying behavioral responses to low-oxygen environments are incomplete. Neuropeptides regulate C. elegans behaviors by modifying neural circuit function in response to hypoxia. Loss of function in C. elegans neuropeptide nlp-40 and its receptor aex-2 increased survival to anoxia [1]. However, the cells in which NLP-40 and AEX-2 function for anoxia, as well as the mechanisms underlying responses to anoxia, remain elusive. We hypothesized that NLP-40 and AEX-2 regulate anoxia by altering escape behaviors. Results: We found that neuropeptide NLP-40 functions in cholinergic neurons and AEX-2 functions in cholinergic or GLR-1 interneurons or motor neurons to regulate susceptibility to anoxia. We found that loss of either nlp-40 or aex-2 decreased locomotor activity and reversal frequency early during 48 hours of anoxia, suggesting that nlp-40 and aex-2 are required for the proper execution of these behaviors. We found that neuronal knockdown of nlp-40 recapitulated the behaviors observed in nlp-40 mutant animals and increased survival; however, restoring aex-2 function in glr-1 interneurons or motor neurons was sufficient to rescue behaviors to wild-type and restore vulnerability to anoxia. Conclusions: Overall, our results suggest that NLP-40 and AEX-2 likely function in cholinergic or glr-1 interneurons or motor neurons to regulate escape behaviors during anoxia. Escape behaviors are part of the homeostatic response and are typically protective in the wild; however, in our paradigm, we show that loss of either nlp-40 or aex-2 reduces escape responses and confers protection against 48 hours of anoxia. Collectively, these results highlight a new role for NLP-40 and AEX-2 in anoxia and shed light on mechanisms underlying the adaptive responses to anoxia.

Article.Title: Age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across time of day, chronotype, and testing format
Article.Authors: Maybury, J. S.; Simons, J. S.
Article.Abstract:
Older adults typically exhibit reduced episodic memory precision, while maintaining relatively preserved retrieval success. However, little is known about whether these age-related differences are influenced by internal biological factors (e.g., chronotype) or external testing conditions (e.g., experiment format, time of day).
To address this question, younger and older adults completed an object-location memory task online, either in the morning or evening, and either with or without video-based supervision. Memory performance was assessed using mean absolute error and Bayesian hierarchical mixture modelling, which dissociated memory precision ({kappa}) from the probability of memory-based responding ({theta}).
Immediate memory performance was high across age groups, irrespective of time of day. Greater encoding error predicted greater retrieval error, and participants tested in the video condition exhibited lower recall error and higher recognition performance than those tested without supervision. Consistent with prior studies, older adults exhibited reduced memory precision relative to younger adults, whereas retrieval success remained largely intact. However, Bayesian Hierarchical Modelling provided no evidence that time of day, experiment format, or their interactions with age influenced either memory precision or retrieval probability. Older adults reported stronger morning preferences than younger adults, and participants generally selected testing times that aligned with their chronotype. Nevertheless, alignment between chronotype and testing time did not modulate memory performance. The results indicate that age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across variations in testing context, including time of day, experiment format, and individual differences in chronotype.
More broadly, the results support the feasibility of remote and unsupervised testing for memory precision research and suggest that chronotype and testing time are unlikely to be major sources of variability in immediate object-location memory performance.

Article.Title: The effects of temporal smoothing and interpolation on EEG microstate parameters, syntax, and our view of resting-state brain dynamics
Article.Authors: von Wegner, F.; Hermann, G.; Toedt, I.; Todtenhaupt, I. K.; Laufs, H.
Article.Abstract: Microstate analysis studies dynamic brain activity through a discrete representation of electroencephalographic (EEG) signals and their topography. While the body of literature describing findings in diverse experimental and clinical settings is growing rapidly, the effects of several core components of the microstate algorithm are still insufficiently understood. This study systematically investigates how two common temporal smoothing algorithms, parametric smoothing and GFP peak interpolation, influence a wide range of microstate sequence parameters, and how they shape the integrated picture of brain dynamics inferred from these metrics. We study eyes-closed resting-state EEG recordings from N=201 healthy subjects from a public EEG database. For the elementary temporal metrics, we find that widening smoothing windows markedly increase microstate duration, reduce occurrence rates, but leave coverage mostly unaffected. In terms of simple syntax properties, smoothing windows above 30 ms yield an inconsistent picture with a memoryless, first-order Markov structure at short time scales, but a positive Hurst phenomenon suggestive of long-range correlations at long time scales. Evidence of asymmetry and non-equilibrium dynamics are suppressed by smoothing. At intermediate time scales, microstate periodicity was only observed up to a window size of 28 ms. Smoothing had a strong impact on the complexity metrics entropy rate and excess entropy, decreasing the former and increasing the latter. For most metrics, the effects of GFP peak interpolation were comparable to those of smoothing windows in the range between 28 ms and 44 ms. In conclusion, elementary and higher-order microstate parameters must be interpreted in the context of preprocessing, as many parameters change continuously with smoothing intensity. This limits the comparability of microstate parameters obtained with different preprocessing settings. Strong smoothing with a window size above 30 ms or GFP peak interpolation yields a fundamentally different picture of resting state brain dynamics, i.e. that of a memoryless, aperiodic, time-reversible first-order Markov chain. Since insights from other neurophysiological modalities suggest that time series memory and time-irreversibility are markers of normal brain activity, our recommendation is to avoid intense smoothing to minimize alterations of the initial sequences.

Article.Title: Neural latent representation of implicit perceptual decision confidence signatures from brain-wide intracranial EEG
Article.Authors: Mudavath, U. K. N.; Asadpour, A.; Gherman, S.; O'Connell, R. G.; Kelly, S. P.; Bickel, S.; Ahamed, S. R.; Wong-Lin, K.
Article.Abstract: Human perceptual decision confidence has been associated with brain-wide signalling, albeit with inconsistencies across studies. It remains unclear whether more robust neural latent representations exist, particularly for implicit confidence. We address this by applying complementary machine learning approaches to comprehensive, brain-wide intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) data acquired without explicit confidence reports. Using explainable feature selection methods, we elucidated key spatiotemporal iEEG components, especially in the frontal cortex, that readily distinguished confidence characteristics related to decision correctness, difficulty, and speed, and that were transferable across motor modalities. Despite inconsistencies in the features identified across methods and conditions, dimensionality reductions revealed robust low-dimensional neural latent representations. Furthermore, their neural trajectories within a shared subspace enhanced the distinguishability of confidence characteristics. Overall, our results uncover low-dimensional spatial and temporal neural latent representations underlying human implicit perceptual decision confidence that are robust to analytical methods and decision conditions.

Article.Title: Dual ecological-cultural pathways of sociocultural environment and resting state functional connectivity among Hispanic adolescents in the ABCD Study
Article.Authors: Laird, A. R.; Hampson, C. L.; Lembo, M.; Bottenhorn, K. L.; Sukumaran, K.; Cardenas-Iniguez, C.; Thompson, E.; Adise, S.; Sanchez, M.; Gonzalez, R.; Herting, M. M.; Meca, A.
Article.Abstract: Hispanic Americans face persistent health disparities rooted in complex sociocultural and bioecodevelopmental dynamics. Identifying early neurodevelopmental trajectories that confer risk or resilience during adolescence is critical for developing targeted health equity interventions. Grounded in the NIMHD Research Framework and bioecodevelopmental theory, data from 12- to 14-year-old Hispanic adolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study were analyzed (n=236). Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) was used to evaluate multivariate associations between sociocultural measures, spanning individual, family, and community levels, and resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) networks. Post hoc linear mixed-effects models examined how derived sociocultural-rsFC patterns predicted measures of physical and mental health, linking bioecodevelopmental patterns to adolescent well-being. PLSC revealed dual community- and family-level neural pathways of biological embedding, diverging from traditional nested bioecodevelopmental assumptions. The community pathway linked child opportunity and neighborhood disadvantage to connectivity across Cingulo-Opercular, Default, Dorsal Attention, Visual Networks. This community-rsFC profile was associated with lower respiratory functioning, reflecting an allostatic load marker of environmental stress. The family pathway linked caregiver ethnic identity and heritage acculturation to Default, Ventral Attention, Sensorimotor-Mouth, and Visual Networks connectivity, suggesting that the family system shapes neural systems underlying social attunement and identity formation. Structural community factors and familial culture impose distinct neurobiological demands on the adolescent connectome among Hispanic youth. Findings highlight respiratory health as a biological marker of environmental adversity and underscore the necessity of structural and culturally sustaining interventions to promote health equity among Hispanic youth.

Article.Title: Molecular basis of chemosensing by internal sensory neurons in Drosophila larvae
Article.Authors: Lu, S.; Qian, C. S.; Khair-Eldin, A.; Grueber, W. B.
Article.Abstract: Interoceptive neurons monitor the chemical and physical state of the body, providing critical information to the central nervous system that maintains homeostasis and promotes survival. The circuit and molecular basis for these interoceptive senses remain under active investigation. A population of larval Drosophila sensory neurons, the tracheal dendrite (td) neurons, extend dendrites along respiratory organs and provide a tractable model for investigating the cellular and molecular basis of internal chemosensation. Here, we show that partially overlapping populations of td neurons respond to decreases in O2 and increases in CO2. To define the molecular basis of these responses, we examined the roles of atypical soluble guanylyl cyclases (Gycs) and gustatory receptors (Grs). We found that Gyc88E/Gyc89Db were required for hypoxia-evoked activity, whereas Gr28b was required for responses to CO2. Targeted expression of Gr28b.c isoform in td neurons restored responses to CO2 in mutant larvae and conferred ectopic sensitivity to CO2 within the td network. We further found that gas-sensitive td neurons were activated upon prolonged larval burrowing, a natural-like feeding-associated behavior. Together, these findings reveal molecular mechanisms that enable interoceptive neurons to monitor respiratory gases and advance a Drosophila model for studying the neural and molecular basis of internal chemosensation.

Article.Title: A cortical signature of very preterm birth across development and its association with neurodevelopmental outcomes
Article.Authors: Liang, K.; Guo, Y.; Williams, L. Z. J.; Besenczi, R.; Sun, Z.; Leoni, M.; Ma, Q.; Rueckert, D.; Dazzan, P.; Edwards, D.; Robinson, E. C.; Nosarti, C.
Article.Abstract: Gestational age (GA) is a key determinant of neurodevelopment, and individuals born very preterm (VPT; [≤] 32 weeks' gestation) are at increased risk of cognitive and behavioural difficulties across the lifespan. A better understanding of the impact of VPT birth on cortical maturation trajectories may provide mechanistic insight into the origins of these neurodevelopmental sequelae. Here we compared cortical morphology between VPT individuals and full-term controls in three datasets spanning the neonatal period, childhood and adulthood. We identified a consistent cortical signature of VPT birth, characterized by reduced surface area and cortical folding in the frontal, temporal, parietal and insular regions, which were observed across development. Reduced surface area and cortical folding in the neonatal period were associated with clinical factors and poorer motor outcomes in toddlerhood. Furthermore, longitudinal analyses in a VPT cohort showed that greater cortical expansion from the neonatal period to childhood was associated with higher childhood IQ. Together, these findings demonstrate persistent cortical morphological alterations following VPT birth and their relevance to long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.

Article.Title: TDP-43 toxic gain of function links ALS, FTD and Alzheimers Disease through splicing dysregulation
Article.Authors: van Zuiden, W.; Meimoun, T.; Bar, C.; Siany, A.; Abarbanel, B.; Moshe, L.; Yacovzada, N. S.; Amzallag, E.; Rajkovic, A.; Alyagor, L.; Weizman, E.; Neumann, M.; Smith, C.; McDade, K.; Strange, A.; Siqueira Kazu, R.; Weinreich, M.; Buchman, A. S.; Wang, Y.; Bennett, D. A.; Zhao, B.; Jiang, L.; Bi, J.; Snyder, M. P.; Morderer, D.; Garcia Morato, J.; Rossoll, W.; Reeves, M. M.; Dickson, D. W.; Prudencio, M.; Nelson, P. T.; Glass, J. D.; Trautwig, A. N.; Chung, M.; McEachin, Z. T.; Seyfried, N. T.; Cooper-Knock, J.; Hornstein, E.
Article.Abstract: TDP-43 proteinopathy is a hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). It is also common in Alzheimers disease (AD), but its functional consequences are unclear. Here, we show that TDP-43 pathology in AD is broadly associated with splicing abnormalities. We define a conserved TDP-43-dependent splicing signature in AD and identify AD-relevant TDP-43-dependent mis-spliced mRNAs, including amyloid precursor protein (APP). TDP-43 drives the formation of elongated APP isoforms, disrupting alternative splicing across ALS, FTLD-TDP and AD, thus providing a compelling mechanism for a long-standing observation of APP isoform dysregulation. APP isoform imbalance correlates with and partially mediates the association between TDP-43 pathology and A{beta} burden pathology and is depicted spatially with pTDP-43 and malspliced STMN2 in LATE hippocampus. Contrary to a pure nuclear loss-of-function model, mis-splicing is driven by cytoplasmic TDP-43 gain-of-function that co-sequesters RNA-binding proteins involved in the regulation of splicing. Knockdown of TDP-43-associated RNA-binding proteins recapitulates disease-relevant splicing changes in AD and ALS/FTLD-TDP; furthermore, at least some of these proteins colocalize with cytoplasmic pTDP-43 in neuropathological samples. Together, our findings establish cytoplasmic TDP-43-driven splicing dysfunction as a key component of neurodegeneration, define sets of disease-relevant mis-spliced RNA across AD, and unite AD with ALS/FTLD-TDP through a shared mechanism of splicing factor sequestration.

Article.Title: A novel analysis pipeline and experimental design for measuring expanded repeat instability
Article.Authors: Smith, C.; Peter Durairaj, R. R.; Randall, E. L.; Aston, A. N.; Heraty, L.; Elsayed, W.; Murillo, A.; Dion, V.
Article.Abstract: The expansion of short tandem repeats is a feature of over 60 different human diseases. Ongoing somatic instability throughout a patients lifetime can influence disease progression and has emerged as a therapeutic target. Understanding its mechanism is essential for the identification of both drug targets and therapeutic interventions. A major obstacle towards this translational goal has been to measure changes in repeat size distributions. To address this we provide a new analysis method and accompanying software that generates delta plots, extracts the instability frequency from targeted long-read sequencing data, the instability bias, and the average size of the changes. It further provides statistical analysis for comparison between treatments. We show its applicability to non-dividing cells and in vivo datasets. Moreover, we have developed a streamlined experimental design for dividing cells, Single Clone-based Instability Assay (SCIA), that saves weeks in assessing the effect of a gene knockout on repeat instability and is ideal for an initial screen. We have validated the approach using FAN1, PMS1, and MLH1 knockouts in cell lines and induced pluripotent stem cells. We find that FAN1 knockout clones showed, as expected, an increased frequency of repeat expansion but the size of the expansions were smaller. This highlights the wealth of information that can be extracted and the potential for novel insights into the mechanism of repeat instability.

Article.Title: Computer mouse weight is associated with one-week motor skill improvement in a large naturalistic video game cohort
Article.Authors: Listman, J. B.; Mackey, W. E.
Article.Abstract: Computer mouse weight has been proposed to influence human motor performance, but existing evidence comes largely from small, short-duration controlled studies, leaving its relationship to performance during naturalistic gameplay unresolved. We analyzed one-week skill improvement in Aimlabs, a popular first-person shooter aim-training and assessment platform, among 9,067 players whose telemetry recorded a mouse-model change (switchers) during self-directed game use, using a 21-day baseline and 7-day follow-up; 4,991 players with a single mouse model (non-switchers) observed over matched pseudo-anchor intervals provided a secondary contextual comparison. Post-switch mouse weight was represented by eight bands spanning 35-124 g. The primary multivariable generalized additive regression model accounted for baseline skill, pre- and post-switch practice intensity, and pre- and post-switch mouse sensitivity, and allowed the association between weight band and improvement to vary with baseline skill, post-switch practice, and post-switch sensitivity. For each weight band, predicted mean one-week improvement was standardized to the observed distribution of these covariates among switchers and reported in percentile-rank points. Statistical significance was evaluated using 1,000 permutations in which observed mouse weights were randomly reassigned among switchers without replacement and the model was refitted to generate empirical null distributions for the weight-related test statistics. Predicted improvement differed significantly across the eight weight bands (p = 0.001). Pairwise comparisons identified significant differences between bands (p < 0.05), but no single band was associated with significantly greater predicted improvement than all seven others. In this large naturalistic cohort, predicted improvement was highest for players with 35-44 g mice, followed by 45-54 and 55-64 g, and several pairwise comparisons showed significantly greater improvement in lighter than in heavier weight bands. Across the examined baseline-skill profiles, the lowest predicted improvements occurred in either the 85-99 or 115-124 g band. Predicted improvement differed across weight bands at the 25th-percentile and median baseline-skill values (p = 0.002 and p = 0.003) but not at the 75th percentile (p = 0.153). However, the weight-band x baseline-skill interaction was not significant (p = 0.181), indicating that the analysis did not establish that weight-related differences varied by skill level.

Article.Title: PTEN Subcellular Localization Dictates Function
Article.Authors: Desmet, N. M.; Griffin, C. F.; Seo, H.; OuYang, A.; Tir, P.; Prina, M. L.; Wang, W.; Li, M.; Luikart, B. W.
Article.Abstract: Mutations in phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) drive unregulated activation of the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) pathway, resulting in neuronal hypertrophy, and are strongly associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Several PTEN mutations alter subcellular localization, yet how localization governs PTEN function in developing neurons remains unclear. Although PTEN has been reported broadly distributed throughout neurons, here, live imaging of HaloTagged PTEN reveals dynamically regulated localization, suggesting spatial control of its signaling. We then used retroviral-mediated genetic manipulation to delete endogenous Pten in developing hippocampal neurons while simultaneously expressing PTEN fused to defined localization motifs, allowing us to directly test how subcellular targeting regulates neuronal morphology. Loss of Pten produces neurons characterized by enlarged somata, more elaborate dendritic arbors, and increased spine density, length, and head area. Nuclear-excluded PTEN fully rescued these phenotypes, whereas targeting PTEN to filopodia via fusion to the FBAR domain of srGAP3 or to the postsynaptic density via Homer1C corrected or corrected all morphological abnormalities in PTEN-deficient neurons and simplified dendritic arborization compared to wild-type. In contrast, nuclear-localized PTEN produced only partial rescue, normalizing soma size and spine head area but not dendritic complexity or spine density. These findings indicate that PTEN acts locally to restrain growth and structural connectivity, whereas regulation of spine head size can be mediated by PTEN both inside and outside the nucleus, potentially through transcriptional or splicing-dependent mechanisms. Together, our results identify subcellular localization as a critical determinant of PTEN function and reveal spatially distinct mechanisms through which PTEN sculpts neuronal development.

Article.Title: Accelerated spike-triggered non-negative matrix factorization reveals coordinated ganglion cell subunit mosaics in the primate retina
Article.Authors: Zapp, S. J.; Khani, M. H.; Schreyer, H. M.; Sridhar, S.; Ramakrishna, V.; Krueppel, S.; Mietsch, M.; Protti, D. A.; Karamanlis, D.; Gollisch, T.
Article.Abstract: A standard circuit motif in sensory systems is the pooling of sensory information from an upstream neuronal layer. A downstream neuron thereby collects signals across different locations in stimulus space, which together compose the neuron's receptive field. In addition, nonlinear transformations in the signal transfer between the layers give rise to functional subunits inside the receptive field. For ganglion cells in the vertebrate retina, for example, receptive field subunits are thought to correspond to presynaptic bipolar cells. Identifying the number and locations of subunits from the stimulus-response relationship of a recorded ganglion cell has been an ongoing challenge in order to characterize the retina's functional circuitry and to build computational models that capture nonlinear signal pooling. Here we present a novel version of spike-triggered non-negative matrix factorization (STNMF), which can extract localized subunits in ganglion cell receptive fields from recorded spiking responses under spatiotemporal white-noise stimulation. The method provides a more than 100-fold speed increase compared to a previous implementation, which can be harnessed for systematic screening of hyperparameters, such as sparsity regularization. We demonstrate the power and flexibility of this approach by analyzing populations of ganglion cells from salamander and primate (marmoset) retina. For the marmoset retina, we find that the sets of subunits obtained from analyzing populations of midget or parasol ganglion cells, respectively, form separate mosaics that tile visual space. Moreover, these subunit mosaics show alignment with each other for ON and OFF midget as well as for ON and OFF parasol cells, indicating a spatial coordination of ON and OFF signals at the bipolar-cell level. Thus, STNMF can help reveal organizational principles of signal transmission between successive neural layers.

Article.Title: Retrospective attention strengthens a report-independent neural signature of visual perception
Article.Authors: Li, Y.; Wan, X.; Mao, M.; Jin, L.; Cai, Y.; Zhang, X.
Article.Abstract: Visual perception can remain modifiable after a stimulus has disappeared, but it is unknown at which processing stage a post-stimulus cue operates: on the lingering sensory trace, on the perceptual representation, or on later decision and report processes. We used masked retrospective cues to establish the behavioral effect and a Report/No-report EEG design to locate its processing stage. In Experiments 1 and 2, retrospective cues improved orientation discrimination even when masking reduced cue-location accuracy to near chance. In Experiment 3, valid cues increased EEG evidence for the target in a late interval, without the early enhancement expected from an early, additive sensory interaction.
