We also discuss key challenges complicating bioinformatic analysis, including limited human viral sequences, co-circulating viral lineages, viral dark matter, reference database limitations, large data volumes, and methodological biases, as well as emerging computational approaches aimed at improving wastewater sequencing analysis and interpretation.
Article.Keywords: bioinformatic analysis; metagenomic sequencing; sequencing; targeted sequencing; viruses; wastewater; wastewater-based surveillance

Article.Title: Data-driven burst shape analysis for functional phenotyping of neuronal cultures
Article.Authors: Schäfer T.; Giannakakis E.; Schmidt-Barbo P.; Levina A.; Vinogradov O.
Article.Abstract: Cultures of neurons in vitro are instrumental for studying network dynamics under normal and pathological conditions. Mature networks typically exhibit network bursting activity, traditionally quantified by simplified features such as inter-burst intervals and burst durations. These features have advanced our understanding of development, disease phenotypes, and drug effects. However, they overlook the temporal structure within bursts, which is highly sensitive to network changes and can thus reveal additional physiological or pathological effects. Here, we developed a comprehensive framework to quantify burst shapes, the time-course of network firing during bursts. On four datasets, including rodent- and human pluripotent stem cell-derived cultures, we show that burst shapes contain rich information about the underlying network dynamics. We quantify this information by classifying conditions (genetic disorders, pharmacological agents) using traditional and burst-shape features, and find that including shape features significantly improves accuracy. We provide an open pipeline for burst shape characterization, introducing burst shape as a complementary functional phenotyping feature that expands the analytical toolkit for disease modeling and drug screening.
Article.Keywords: CACNA1A haploinsufficiency; blocked inhibition; burst shape; human pluripotent stem cell; micro-electrode arrays; network dynamics; neural cultures; rodent

Article.Title: Assessing machine learning prediction of recycled aggregate concrete strength with a tabular foundation model
Article.Authors: Fan J.; Bharati R.; Zhang G.; Zhang H.; Zhang N.; Zhang Y.; Liang A.; Pokhrel M.
Article.Abstract: Recycled aggregate concrete (RAC) supports more sustainable construction, but recycled concrete aggregate (RCA)'s heterogeneity complicates compressive-strength prediction. This study evaluates the Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) against nine conventional machine-learning models using a standardized literature-derived database of 833 RAC mixtures. Cube strengths were converted to equivalent cylinder strengths, with conversion sensitivity also assessed. Among conventional models, CatBoost achieved the highest accuracy (R2 = 0.843), whereas TabPFN achieved R2 = 0.870, mean absolute error (MAE) = 3.924 MPa, and root mean squared error (RMSE) = 5.551 MPa. TabPFN also produced a lower RMSE than CatBoost across all four RCA replacement intervals without extensive task-specific hyperparameter tuning. Feature importance and Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) analyses identified effective water-to-cement ratio, aggregate-to-cement ratio, RCA density, and RCA absorption as key predictors, while RCA replacement level alone had limited influence. The moderate improvement over CatBoost indicates that further gains depend on improved RCA characterization.
Article.Keywords: Shapley additive explanation; TabPFN regressor; machine learning; recycled concrete aggregate; tabular foundation model

Article.Title: IL-4 and arginine synergy accelerates early bone regeneration via enhanced efferocytosis and ameliorated microenvironment
Article.Authors: Meng L.; Liu R.; Wang S.; Wang J.; Vinnikov I.; Yang R.; Song X.; Zhang H.; Wang J.; Zhang W.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Host bone microenvironment is a critical factor for successful bone regeneration during implantation. In this work, we identified a spatiotemporal mismatch at drilling-induced injury sites where initial apoptosis outpaces macrophage recruitment, leading to apoptotic cell accumulation and oxidative stress that impairs osteogenic differentiation. To mitigate this phenomenon, we developed a synergistic strategy co-delivering interleukin 4 (IL-4) and arginine (Arg) to reprogram the microenvironment. Mechanistically, IL-4 recruits and polarizes macrophages toward a pro-reparative M2 phenotype, while Arg fuels the arginase-1 metabolic pathway to sustain continual efferocytosis and secretion of pro-regenerative cytokines. In a mouse bone injury model, transcriptomic and histological analyses confirmed that this strategy accelerates apoptotic clearance and establishes an M2-dominant environment, significantly enhancing early bone regeneration. Altogether, this work proposes a novel therapeutic paradigm targeting macrophage efferocytosis to resolve early microenvironmental imbalances, providing a promising therapeutic approach to promote bone defect healing and offering novel insights into optimizing host microenvironments for osseointegration following implantation.

Article.Title: PXT3003: Lessons for therapeutic development in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A and related neuropathies
Article.Authors: Burns J.
Article.Abstract: Most drug development stories end predictably: promising compounds either succeed or fail. Occasionally, however, a therapy repeatedly returns from apparent extinction. PXT3003 for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A) represents one such example. More than a decade after early promise, the program has survived formulation instability, interrupted clinical development, regulatory uncertainty, and controversy surrounding efficacy before re-emerging with renewed evidence of clinical benefit. Yet, as with many therapeutic development programs, interpretation of the available evidence is influenced by the extent to which findings are publicly accessible. In a recent issue of iScience, a phase 3 clinical trial evaluated PXT3003, a combination of baclofen, naltrexone, and D-sorbitol, versus placebo over 15 months in participants aged 16-65 years with mild-to-moderate CMT1A across 25 sites in China. PXT3003 is not simply the story of one drug; it highlights the scientific, methodological, operational, and reporting challenges of developing disease-modifying therapies for slowly progressive inherited neuropathies.
Article.Keywords: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease; PXT3003; biomarkers; clinical outcome assessments; clinical trials; neuromuscular disorders; peripheral neuropathy

Article.Title: Monotropein mitigates atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability through circ_0140736/miR-495/SIRPα-mediated efferocytosis
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Wu Z.; Huang B.; Ye W.; Xu S.; He W.; Lan Y.; Xiao C.; Qin C.; Gao W.; Ye Z.
Article.Abstract: Efferocytosis is a biological process in which phagocytic cells engulf and degrade senescent, damaged, or dead cells to prevent secondary necrosis and inflammation. This process is implicated in various diseases, including atherosclerosis (AS). Enhancing efferocytosis efficiency may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for managing AS. Consequently, increasing attention is being paid to pharmacological agents that can promote efferocytosis. Monotropein (MON), the predominant iridoid glycoside in Morinda officinalis, has demonstrated anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties in previous studies. However, its role in regulating atherosclerotic plaque stability remains unclear. In this study, we show that MON enhances plaque stability in AS. The expression of circ_0140736 was found to be elevated in unstable atherosclerotic plaques. MON suppressed circ_0140736 expression and alleviated miR-495 sequestration via a competing endogenous RNA mechanism, thereby increasing miR-495 levels and downregulating signal regulatory protein α (SIRPɑ) expression. In conclusion, MON exerts its anti-atherosclerotic effects by promoting efferocytosis through the circ_0140736/miR-495/SIRPɑ axis, suggesting its potential as a promising therapeutic candidate for AS.
Article.Keywords: SIRPα; atherosclerosis; circ_0140736; efferocytosis; monotropein

Article.Title: Development of proteome-derived cyclic peptide libraries via ortho-phthalaldehyde-assisted cyclization
Article.Authors: Wei Y.; Feng K.; Hou W.; Tian X.; Xue Y.; Zhang W.; Deng H.
Article.Abstract: Cyclic peptides possess unique structural features and binding capabilities that make them attractive scaffolds for molecular recognition. However, strategies for generating functionally diverse libraries directly from natural proteomes remain comparatively underdeveloped. Here, we present a proteome-informed approach for constructing cyclic peptide libraries by integrating cysteine-enrichment protocols with ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA)-mediated macrocyclization. This method enables direct library generation from proteome digests and is compatible with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based annotation and downstream functional screening. We systematically identify key parameters governing OPA-mediated cyclization topology and develop a rule-based pipeline for automated library annotation of OPA-cyclized peptides. Applying this strategy, we generate a library of over 15,000 unique cyclic peptides and perform target-specific screening against human IgG. This yielded cyclic peptide binder candidates, including one lead peptide showing cyclization-dependent IgG-binding potential. Our study establishes an OPA-enabled, proteome-informed workflow for cyclic peptide library construction and annotation.
Article.Keywords: IgG-binding peptide; OPA; cyclic peptide library; mass spectrometry; ortho-phthalaldehyde; protein recognition

Article.Title: Stress induced hyperphagia in C. elegans as a genetic model for binge eating disorders
Article.Authors: Pucci M.; Cifani C.; D’Addario C.; Swoboda P.
Article.Abstract: Binge eating (BE) is often triggered by stress, dieting, and adverse environmental factors, and represents a common precursor to eating disorders such as anorexia, bulimia, and BE disorder. Stress-induced hyperphagia captures core features of binge-like feeding and shares neurobiological substrates will BE disorder, making it a useful behavioral readout for dissecting underlying mechanisms. We used the genetically tractable worm Caenorhabditis elegans to examine how starvation and stress interact to drive feeding, quantifying pharyngeal pumping as a measure of food intake. Combined starvation and heat stress increased feeding beyond starvation alone, with effects shaped by stress timing, food quality, and sex. Feeding phenotypes were separable from locomotor and feeding-capacity defects. Mutations in evolutionarily conserved homeostatic and hedonic feeding-pathway genes showed distinct hyperphagic responses, implicating that conserved neuronal circuits govern stress-induced feeding across species. This model offers a platform for genetic screening and drug testing to accelerate discovery of therapeutics for binge-like feeding disorders.
Article.Keywords: Caenorhabditis elegans; Feeding behavior; Stress-Induced Hyperphagia; binge-like feeding; compulsive eating; neuro-genetics; neuronal mechanisms; pharyngeal pumping

Article.Title: Pharmacological protection from a sugar-rich diet through inhibition of Ras/MAPK signaling
Article.Authors: Laskovs M.; Cook J.; Pitt A.; Spickett C.; Slack C.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Consumption of sugar-rich diets adversely affects health and reduces life expectancy through the excessive production and storage of triacylglycerides (TAGs), leading to metabolic dysfunction. Here, we show that in Drosophila , pharmacological inhibition of Ras/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling using the highly specific MEK inhibitor, trametinib, mitigates several of the detrimental effects of a high-sugar diet by reducing TAG accumulation, restoring TAG composition, and increasing survival. Notably, Ras/MAPK activity is required for the transcriptional response to elevated sugar intake, including expression of the glucagon-like hormone, Akh . We further demonstrate that adipokinetic hormone (AKH) is essential for the protective effects of trametinib under high-sugar conditions. Together, our findings support Ras/MAPK signaling as an important link between dietary sugar and metabolic dysfunction and show that its pharmacological inhibition can uncouple excess sugar intake from adverse metabolic outcomes.

Article.Title: Contrasting fate and GHG emissions of algal vs. manure DOM under light and microbes in lakes
Article.Authors: Tao Y.; Wang Q.; Bao M.; Tian Y.; Lu L.
Article.Abstract: Summary: The escalating dissolved organic matter (DOM) inputs from algal (ADOM) and livestock manure (MDOM) sources are altering lake ecosystems, yet their fate under light and microbes in steppe lakes is unclear. Using microcosms, we found that photodegradation suppressed ADOM bioavailability by 4.8% via substrate competition and reactive oxygen species (ROS) inhibition (especially singlet oxygen), while light enhanced MDOM bioavailability by 5.4%. ADOM mineralization released 1.6× more CO 2 than MDOM. Multi-group structural equation modeling (SEM) indicated that efficient ADOM microbial transformation drove higher CO 2 emissions, whereas light-induced ROS shifted microbial communities and transformation pathways. ADOM and MDOM inputs predominantly enhanced CO 2 emissions and water browning, respectively. These processes are interconnected—exogenous MDOM can promote algal blooms and subsequent greenhouse gas release. For eutrophic steppe lakes, integrated management combining exogenous load reduction and endogenous bloom suppression is critical to mitigate ecological risks and greenhouse effects.

Article.Title: Boid inclusion body disease in Boa constrictor: Unraveling the myth of immunosuppression
Article.Authors: Dervas E.; Czirják G.; Michalopoulou E.; Liesegang A.; Novacco M.; Schwarzenberger F.; Hetzel U.; Hepojoki J.; Baggio F.; Kipar A.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Boid inclusion body disease (BIBD) is an infectious disease of captive boid snakes of major relevance since the 1970s. It is caused by reptarenaviruses and characterized by intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in most cell types. Affected snakes frequently develop secondary bacterial infections, suggesting virus-associated immunosuppression. To investigate this, we analyzed peripheral blood from 48 Boa constrictor with confirmed BIBD, three infected snakes without disease, and 84 reptarenavirus-negative snakes, assessing hematology, biochemistry, stress parameters, and immune function. A functional phagocytosis assay on peripheral blood revealed a significantly reduced proportion of phagocytic cells (Iba1 + monocytes/azurophils) in BIBD-positive and reptarenavirus-infected snakes compared to uninfected animals, indicating impaired phagocytic capacity. In addition, BIBD-positive snakes showed reduced cholesterol and total immunoglobulin concentrations, while virus-specific IgY and IgM levels were elevated. These findings indicate selective impairment of innate and humoral immune components, providing mechanistic evidence for increased susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections in BIBD.

Article.Title: Inhibitory receptor profiles for joint prediction of benefit and toxicity in immune checkpoint blockade
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Xiong D.; Duan B.; Ding G.; Huang Y.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed cancer therapy, but durable benefit is limited to a subset of patients and can be accompanied by immune-related adverse events. This Review evaluates inhibitory receptor profiles as candidate biomarkers for predicting both antitumor benefit and immune toxicity. We examine how receptor abundance, co-expression, cellular lineage, clonality, spatial context, and treatment-induced dynamics shape interpretation across tissue imaging, cytometry, bulk transcriptomics, single-cell multi-omics, and spatial profiling, with particular attention to organ-specific toxicity and time-dependent analytical bias. Current evidence supports context-dependent associations, especially for multi-receptor T-cell states and early on-treatment changes, but not universal thresholds or stand-alone clinical use. Because benefit and toxicity share pathways yet arise from partly distinct biological determinants, they should remain separate model outputs. We propose a staged path from mechanistic discovery to a locked minimal assay, external validation, and prospective evaluation of clinical utility.

Article.Title: Endometriosis and chronic pain syndrome: The role of stress mechanisms
Article.Authors: Reis F.; Vannuccini S.; De Logu F.; Pisani I.; Nassini R.; Petraglia F.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Patients with endometriosis report increased levels of perceived stress, which correlates with disease severity and pain intensity, creating feedback loops that perpetuate the cycle of endometriosis inflammation, chronic pain syndrome, and pathological stress response. Stress and chronic pain form an integrated biopsychosocial system in which neuroendocrine dysregulation, central sensitization, neuroinflammation, large-scale network reorganization, and maladaptive threat learning mutually reinforce each other. Sex differences, developmental experiences, and resilience factors modulate this interaction. Chronic pain in endometriosis emerges as the result of a progressive integration of peripheral inflammation and central nervous system plasticity. Thus, mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for endometriosis-associated pain should address both peripheral drivers and central amplification processes. Further research is needed to better understand whether chronic stress is a contributing cause for the onset of endometriosis and whether there is an opportunity to modify this risk factor before endometriosis is fully established.

Article.Title: Association between human genomes and mycobacterial genomes contributes to severity and transmissibility of pulmonary tuberculosis
Article.Authors: Tantivitayakul P.; Kunhapan P.; Boonbangyang M.; Chaichoompu K.; Wilantho A.; Sawaengdee W.; Ruangchai W.; Thawornwattana Y.; Yanai H.; Wattanapokayakit S.; Disratthakit A.; Miyahara R.; Nedsuwan S.; Imasanguan W.; Kantipong P.; Chaiyasirinroje B.; Phelan J.; Clark T.; Hibberd M.; Tokunaga K.; Mahasirimongkol S.; Palittapongarnpim P.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) remains a major infectious disease globally. This study aimed to identify determinants of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) transmission clustering, treatment outcome, and pulmonary cavitation by simultaneously analyzing host and pathogen genomic data. Whole-genome sequencing of 1,960 MTB isolates identified four major lineages (L1–L4). Host population stratification by principal component analysis of genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) classified 899 patients (70%) into a genetically homogeneous main group for genome-wide association study (GWAS). Multivariate regression demonstrated that MTB lineage was the primary determinant of transmission clustering, rifampicin resistance was the dominant predictor of unfavorable treatment outcome, and host genetic group was independently associated with pulmonary cavitation. GWAS identified novel loci in collectin subfamily member 10 ( COLEC10 ), CTNNA3 , and long intergenic non-coding RNA 2775 ( LINC02775 ) associated with clustering, treatment outcome, and cavitation, respectively, with the association of COLEC10 also found in the remaining group of patients. These findings highlight the importance of integrating bacterial and human genomic analyses to understand tuberculosis host-pathogen interaction.

Article.Title: Rhizobacterial biocontrol of potato late blight and genomic insights into disease suppression and growth promotion
Article.Authors: Kelbessa B.; Ghosh S.; Ghadamgahi F.; Catara V.; Whisson S.; Ortiz R.; Vetukuri R.
Article.Abstract: No preview available

Article.Title: Climate vulnerability and governance impact the payoff of policy drivers for SDG 7 outcomes in BRICS countries
Article.Authors: Sinha A.; Jindal A.; Abbas S.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Achieving Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) in large emerging economies requires energy policies that operate under diverse institutional and climatic conditions. We examine BRICS countries over 2000–2022 to assess how climate vulnerability and governance quality condition the estimated marginal effects of environmental policy stringency, innovation, financial development, inequality, and demographic structure on energy access, renewable energy, and energy efficiency. A two-stage empirical framework combines moderated GLS estimation with post-estimation evaluation of marginal-effect surfaces across contrasting governance-vulnerability regimes and country-specific conditions. The results show that stronger governance and lower climate vulnerability are generally associated with more favorable estimated effects of finance, innovation, and policy stringency, while weak governance and high vulnerability can weaken or reverse these relationships. Policy priorities also differ across SDG 7 subgoals and BRICS economies. These findings support context-specific energy policies that align institutional strengthening and climate resilience with SDG 7 implementation.

Article.Title: Impacts of trail running and mountain biking: Resilience of a Mediterranean mountain ecosystem
Article.Authors: Gómez-Prieto F.; Tejedo P.; Faucha M.; Escudero A.; Leung Y.; Valladares F.; Benayas J.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Rising outdoor activities have created major challenges for managing protected natural areas due to uncertain ecological effects. This study analyzes the impacts of two expanding sports, trail running and mountain biking, on flat and sloped terrains in a Mediterranean mountain setting in the Sierra de Guadarrama National Park, where transects were subjected to different use intensities. Early short-term impacts and subsequent recovery were monitored over a year using biotic and abiotic indicators: soil compaction, vegetation (total cover, Simpson’s diversity index, and composition), bacterial colony-forming units, and edaphic microfauna. Results show that soil compaction and vegetation cover are the most affected among the variables analyzed, with significant alterations when applying a high number of passes on foot or by bicycle, but without significant differences between the two sports. Vegetation recovered faster than soil compaction, and Mediterranean seasonality strongly modulates impacts. Management measures are proposed to balance recreation and conservation.

Article.Title: Inducible dCas12a system expands CRISPRi/a capabilities for functional genomics in malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum
Article.Authors: Lucky A.; Li X.; Kobakhidze G.; Gonzales J.; Wang C.; Cui L.; Dong G.; Miao J.
Article.Abstract: We developed inducible dead Cas12a (dCas12a)-based CRISPR interference/activation (CRISPRi/a) systems for Plasmodium falciparum , expanding the gene regulation toolkit beyond dCas9. Our previous systems fused dCas9 to the catalytic domains of PfSir2a or PfGCN5 under DiCre/ loxP regulon, enabling conditional gene regulation but remaining constrained by Cas9's NGG protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) requirement. Unlike dCas9, dCas12a recognizes T-rich PAMs and processes a single transcript into multiple sgRNAs via its RNase activity, allowing multiplexed regulation of one or multiple genes. Functional validation targeting EBA175 and ATG18 demonstrated that single sgRNAs mediated CRISPRi/a's active gene regulation, while multiplexed sgRNA arrays enhanced CRISPRi activities. Using this platform, we showed that conditional repression of the histone methyltransferase gene PfSET7 impairs schizont egress and merozoite invasion, highlighting its critical role in parasite multiplication, consistent with its Toxoplasma homolog TgADTM1 . Altogether, these results establish dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a as a versatile platform for conditional and multiplexed gene regulation in P . falciparum .

Article.Title: Dysregulation of neuronal androgen receptor signaling by divergent collaborative transcription factors in Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Takayama K.; Suzuki Y.; Saito Y.; Suzuki T.; Tsutsumi S.; Aburatani H.; Inoue S.
Article.Abstract: Summary: The transcriptional mechanisms through which androgens and androgen receptor (AR) exert specific effects on human tissues remain elusive. Here, we demonstrated that neuronal cell-specific transcription factors (TFs) may play an important role as epigenetic modifiers that shape the AR cistrome during neuronal activity. The binding of GATA3 to specific regulatory sequences in human neuronal cell models is associated with enhanced AR-mediated transcription. AR-binding sites (ARBSs) are enriched in regions overlapping with super-enhancers (SEs) that encode critical neuronal factors. Furthermore, AR signaling in aged human male brains indicates its role in supporting neural function and declines during the progression of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). The expression levels of AR-associated TFs were dysregulated during aging and AD development. Altered expression of TFs may contribute to disruption of AR signaling. Thus, collaborative TFs could contribute to the neuronal androgen response and epigenetic regulation involved in aging and the progression of dementia.

Article.Title: Resveratrol-mediated Fe(III)/peroxydisulfate activation for ofloxacin degradation at circumneutral pH
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; Yang W.; Zeng Y.; Huang D.; Dong W.; Monfort O.; Motola M.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Iron-mediated peroxydisulfate (PDS) activation is limited by slow Fe(III)/Fe(II) redox cycling under circumneutral conditions. Here, resveratrol (RES), a natural stilbene polyphenol, was introduced as a low-dose redox mediator to promote Fe(II) formation from Fe(III) for enhanced PDS activation. The Fe(III)/RES/PDS system showed higher ofloxacin (OFL) degradation than the corresponding single-reagent and binary systems and achieved approximately 90% OFL degradation at pH 6.5. Chemical quenching and competition-kinetic analysis indicated that sulfate radical (SO 4 ·− ) was the major contributor to OFL degradation, while hydroxyl radical ( · OH) played a secondary role. Matrix experiments showed that Cl − and NO 3 − had minor effects, whereas NO 2 − strongly inhibited OFL degradation. This work provides a case study of RES-mediated Fe(III)/PDS activation for antibiotic degradation under near-neutral conditions.

Article.Title: Lateralized vagal oxytocin receptor signaling separately controls feeding and socioemotional functions via hypothalamic oxytocin neurons
Article.Authors: Iba K.; Masuda Y.; Kitano R.; Ohbayashi K.; Ago Y.; Nagai H.; Furuyashiki T.; Abe C.; Iwasaki Y.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Oxytocin neurons in the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH Oxt ) regulate feeding, anxiety, and social behaviors. Activation of Oxt receptor (Oxtr)-expressing vagal sensory neurons engages these PVH Oxt neurons and improves hyperphagic obesity; however, their roles in anxiety and sociability remain unclear. Here, we activated vagal Oxtr-expressing neurons in male mice using a single intraperitoneal (IP) Oxt injection or chemogenetics. IP Oxt reduced anxiety-like behavior, enhanced social interaction, and suppressed feeding while activating both vagal sensory neurons and PVH Oxt neurons. These effects were abolished by chemogenetic inhibition of PVH Oxt neurons or central Oxtr blockade. Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy revealed lateralized functions: right-side vagotomy eliminated anxiolytic and prosocial effects, whereas left-side vagotomy blocked feeding suppression. Consistently, chemogenetic activation of left-sided neurons suppressed feeding, while right-sided activation reduced anxiety and increased sociability. These findings identify Oxtr-expressing vagal sensory neurons as a major peripheral pathway in which left- and right-sided inputs differentially control feeding and socioemotional behaviors.

Article.Title: Massive histone H3 phosphorylation without mitotic chromosome condensation
Article.Authors: Ustun I.; Borsò M.; Kochanova N.; Forne I.; Reid C.; Prevo B.; Samejima K.; Xie L.; Paulson J.; Imhof A.; Earnshaw W.
Article.Abstract: No preview available

Article.Title: Small-molecule activators of the Staphylococcus aureus ClpC/ClpP AAA+ protease
Article.Authors: Jenne T.; Viliuga V.; Uhrig U.; Jehle B.; Schwan M.; Kopp J.; Flemming D.; Seebach E.; Sinning I.; Bukau B.; Mogk A.
Article.Abstract: Summary: The central AAA+ ClpC/ClpP protease in Gram-positive bacteria is crucial for virulence and stress resistance and has been recognized as drug target. Natural cyclic peptides deregulate the essential Mycobacterium tuberculosis ClpC1 and cause cell death. Similarly, overactivated mutants of the non-essential Staphylococcus aureus ClpC homolog cause uncontrolled proteolysis and severe toxicity in vivo . However, no chemical modulators of S. aureus ClpC have been described. Here, using a biochemical high-throughput screen, we identify eight distinct bona fide small molecules that stimulate ClpC ATPase and proteolytic activity in vitro . Structural, computational, and mutational analyses define two ligandable regulatory sites within the ClpC N-terminal domain (NTD) as compound targets: a conserved hydrophobic groove and an allosteric pArg1 pocket, both engaged in substrate recognition. These findings establish S. aureus ClpC as chemically targetable and provide mechanistic insight into its regulatory architecture, enabling future development and optimization of chemical probes to deregulate AAA+ protease control.

Article.Title: Short term overfeeding disrupts small intestinal barrier integrity and activates hepatic immunity in healthy men
Article.Authors: Nägele N.; Suppli M.; Gilliam-Vigh H.; Petersen N.; Hartmann B.; Knop F.; Lund A.; Jensen B.
Article.Abstract: Twenty healthy men underwent a 2-week hypercaloric diet (~4,600 kcal/day) combined with a sedentary lifestyle (<5,000 steps/day). Plasma biomarkers from a targeted Gastrointestinal Uptake and Translocation (GUT) panel, along with buffy coat 16S rRNA, were measured at baseline, post-intervention, and after 8 weeks of return to habitual lifestyle. The repository contains data from the plasma and buffy coat analyses related to the above mentioned manuscript.

Article.Title: Species-specific inflammatory responses of chondrocytes: Toward evidence-based model selection in OA research
Article.Authors: Kidtiwong A.; Arteaga M.; Tarasova K.; Gültekin S.; Rothbauer M.; Gerner I.; Jenner F.
Article.Abstract: Summary: To inform evidence-based osteoarthritis model selection, this study compares inflammatory responses of articular chondrocytes from six species (human, horse, sheep, rabbit, rat, and mouse) under standardized IL-1β and TNF-α stimulation in 2D and 3D culture. Chondrocytes were assessed for viability, proliferation, wound healing, and transcriptomic changes via RT-qPCR and 3′RNA sequencing. Marked interspecies differences were observed in morphology, proliferation, and inflammatory gene activation, with only two genes ( SOD2 , NFKBIA ) conserved across all species. Human, horse, and rat chondrocytes shared pathways including acute phase response, deubiquitination, and class-A/1-GPCR signaling. Species-specific responses included matrix remodeling in horses, rheumatoid arthritis-related pathways in sheep, and mixed inflammatory-regenerative profiles in rats. While no species fully replicates human OA, equine and rat chondrocytes best reflect key aspects of human inflammation. These findings underscore the need for molecular criteria in model selection and advocate for human cell-based models when interspecies differences limit the translational value of animal models.

Article.Title: Evidence for exposure to and infection with H5 clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses among polar bears inhabiting Alaska
Article.Authors: Ramey A.; Mangipane L.; Atwood T.; Stimmelmayr R.; Rotstein D.; Ahlstrom C.; Simac K.; Coburn S.; Kim Torchetti M.; Stallknecht D.; Poulson R.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) have become widespread among wildlife including within the Arctic. We summarize histopathological findings for three cases of HPAIV infection among polar bears ( Ursus maritimus ) inhabiting Alaska, genomically characterize viruses causing disease, and assess probable non-lethal exposures. Polar bears found dead and infected with HPAIVs exhibited meningoencephalomyelitis and neuronal necrosis, consistent with neurologic disease. Genomic sequence information obtained for H5N1 and H5N5 subtype HPAIVs associated with two cases supported epidemiologically independent spillovers. Serologic testing provided evidence for antibodies reactive to H5 and N1 antigens among most polar bears inhabiting Alaska during 2023–2024, consistent with contemporary non-lethal exposures, whereas antibodies were not found among bears sampled during 2013. These data indicate that HPAIV infection may represent an emerging threat to polar bear health within the Alaska Arctic; though, population immunity seems to be building and may protect this species from widespread demographic impacts of disease.

Article.Title: Low-frequency non-destructive adaptive fastest pulse preheating for lithium-ion batteries
Article.Authors: Li C.; Mao S.; Gao M.; He M.; Sun Y.; Wang D.; Han X.; Xia C.; Wang X.; Lu Y.; Gao W.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Low-temperature polarization sharply reduces lithium-ion battery capacity and power, limiting electric vehicles and energy storage systems in cold regions. Bidirectional pulsed current (BPC) self-heating exploits increased internal resistance to enable efficient, rapid, and uniform heating, but high-rate pulses may induce lithium plating. Although high-frequency (>100 Hz) BPC suppresses plating, it requires additional power components. Here, we propose an adaptive, non-destructive BPC heating strategy that adjusts pulse current with temperature and state of charge (SOC), enabling the fastest heating within the lithium-plating-free boundary at low frequencies (<1 Hz). Using parameters optimized with three-electrode cells, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries were heated from −15°C to 10°C while maintaining the negative electrode potential above 0 V (vs. Li/Li + ). After 100 heating cycles, neither chemistry showed capacity degradation, and post-heating analysis revealed no lithium plating, confirming safe and non-destructive low-temperature heating without compromising battery performance or requiring high-frequency auxiliary power electronics.

Article.Title: Cancer cell-intrinsic rewiring of the colorectal cancer secretome
Article.Authors: Witsen M.; Foskolos T.; Dijkstra J.; Parra-Martinez M.; Catsman J.; van Royen P.; Ignacio B.; Bleijerveld O.; Kuiken M.; van Vliet A.; Monkhorst K.; Theelen W.; Peeper D.; van de Haar J.; Bonger K.; Vermeulen M.; Voest E.; Dijkstra K.
Article.Abstract: Secreted factors are essential mediators of cellular communication that are exploited by tumors to control their environment and evade immune attack. However, how cancer cells rewire their secretome is unclear due to challenges in reliably profiling cancer cell-specific secreted factors. Here, we apply a click chemistry-based approach to selectively profile the secretome of patient-derived colorectal cancer (CRC) and healthy colon organoids. We observe cancer cell-intrinsic rewiring of the secretome during malignancy, with clear separation between microsatellite stable (MSS) and instable cancers. We then leverage this secretomics dataset to identify secreted factors that mark immune-excluded cancers, revealing NOTUM as a marker of decreased T cell infiltration across four independent datasets. Overall, our study provides an in-depth characterization of the cancer cell-intrinsic secretome of MSS-CRC and nominates NOTUM as a secreted factor marking immune-excluded colorectal cancers. This provides a scalable framework to link cancer cell-derived secreted factors to relevant tumor phenotypes.
Article.Keywords: CRC; NOTUM; immune evasion; organoids; secretome

Article.Title: Multiscale cross modal fusion and cascaded signal propagation for drug target interaction prediction
Article.Authors: Wang B.; Xie X.; Zou H.; Peng S.
Article.Abstract: Accurate prediction of drug-target interaction (DTI) facilitates the translation of lead compounds into clinical therapeutics. Despite progress in deep learning, two challenges remain: the representation gap between heterogeneous drug and protein modalities and insufficient use of complementary knowledge from pretrained encoders. To address these issues, we propose SF-DTI, a unified framework that integrates multi-encoder protein fusion, structure-semantic drug alignment, and progressive cross-modal refinement for DTI prediction. Specifically, SF-DTI captures global protein semantics from multiple pretrained protein language models, aligns graph-based structural features with pretrained semantic embeddings for drugs under subspace constraints, and progressively refines drug-protein interaction representations through cascaded cross-modal signal propagation. Experiments on six benchmark datasets under standard, cold-start, and cross-domain settings demonstrate that SF-DTI achieves competitive performance relative to seven state-of-the-art baselines across evaluation scenarios. These results suggest that SF-DTI is a promising framework for DTI prediction and may support virtual screening, drug repositioning, and drug discovery.
Article.Keywords: chemical language model; drug-target interaction prediction; multiscale fusion; protein language model; subspace alignment

Article.Title: FKBP12 determines ligand-specific SMAD signaling in individual living endothelial cells
Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Lenhardt S.; Snyder P.; Bulldan A.; Hausch F.; Loewer A.
Article.Abstract: Summary: The BMP signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in regulating the formation and maintenance of our vascular system, employing a diverse set of ligands, receptors, and cytoplasmic mediators. However, little is known about how the interplay of these elements is regulated dynamically in individual living endothelial cells. Here, we developed fluorescent reporter to quantify BMP signaling and used a combination of time-resolved microscopy and computer-aided analysis to demonstrate ligand-specific dynamics of SMAD1, SMAD5, and SMAD9. Using this approach, we identified FKBP12 as a critical regulator of receptor complex activity that determines the balance of SMAD1/5/9 and SMAD2/3 signaling upon treatment with angiogenic ligands such as BMP7 and Activin A. This provides insights into the regulation of the BMP pathway in endothelial cells and offers a potential node for modulating vascular pathologies where the SMAD1/5/9-SMAD2/3 balance is disrupted.

Article.Title: Patent insights on advanced polymer composites for transport systems
Article.Authors: D B.; V B.; S S.; S D.; M V.
Article.Abstract: No preview available

Article.Title: Energy absorption of multicell thin walled structures filled with polyurethane infiltrated open cell aluminum foam
Article.Authors: Zhang P.; Chen Y.; Shi Y.; Zhao R.; Guo T.; Guo H.; Chen L.; Yu P.
Article.Abstract: This dataset characterized the energy absorption behavior of hybrid structures combining multi-cell thin-walled aluminum alloy tubes with aluminum foam (AF) and aluminum foam/polyurethane composites (AF/PU). The underlying hypothesis was that integrating lightweight cellular materials into multi-cell structures could synergistically enhance crashworthiness by optimizing deformation modes and increasing energy absorption performance parameters. Data were derived from quasi-static compression and dynamic drop-weight impact tests, supplemented by validated finite element simulations. Key findings revealed that the S3 configuration (MTS + AF1/PU) exhibited superior overall performance, significantly mitigating the initial peak force while increasing the mean crushing force and specific energy absorption (SEA) compared to empty tubes. The dataset included force-displacement curves, processed metrics (EA, MCF, SEA, CFE), and SEM and micro-CT images, enabling users to interpret deformation patterns, validate numerical models, or optimize hybrid structures for automotive and aerospace crashworthiness applications.

Article.Title: Viral persistence and immune dysfunction in chronic hepatitis B: Mechanisms of post-treatment antigen asynchrony
Article.Authors: Du S.; Wang H.; Zhou B.; Jin Q.
Article.Abstract: Summary: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global health burden. Following antiviral therapy, the dynamics of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) may become discordant, a phenomenon referred to as post-treatment asynchrony. This review summarizes the three principal forms of post-treatment asynchrony and examines their underlying mechanisms. We integrate the limitations of current antiviral targets, host immune dysfunction, virological characteristics, and host genetic factors into a unified framework to explain the discordant dynamics between HBsAg and HBV DNA. A better understanding of post-treatment asynchrony may help refine the interpretation of serological markers and inform patient stratification and individualized therapeutic strategies. Overall, this review provides an integrated perspective on the mechanisms and clinical significance of post-treatment asynchrony in CHB.

Article.Title: The effectiveness of sound-based interventions on promoting sleep quality in hospitalized patients: A systematic review
Article.Authors: Henriques H.; Silva M.; Guerreiro R.; Mendonça S.; Durão C.; Rosario Pinto M.; Teixeira J.
Article.Abstract: No preview available

Article.Title: Resilience assessment of lithium ion battery supply chains under critical mineral shortages
Article.Authors: Liu X.; Huang H.; An F.; Dong X.; Fang W.; Wang Y.; Zhang H.; Liu Y.; Liu H.
Article.Abstract: Summary: The energy transition and transportation electrification have increased the reliance of lithium ion battery supply chains on critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Here, we construct a multi-tier interfirm supply network of nine major battery manufacturers and develop a propagation recovery model to assess mineral shortage impacts and recovery pathways. Lithium shortages generate the largest cascading losses, followed by cobalt and nickel shortages. Recovery is primarily achieved through cross-tier resource reallocation, which contributes approximately 70% of total recovery, whereas newly established supply links provide a smaller contribution. Manufacturer resilience varies across minerals, reflecting heterogeneous supply chain exposure and recovery capacity. These findings identify mineral-specific risk pathways and recovery mechanisms, providing insights for resilient supply chain management and critical mineral governance during energy transitions.

Article.Title: A multimodal in situ framework for spatial characterization applied on SARS-CoV-2 live-attenuated vaccines in the nasal mucosa
Article.Authors: Britzke T.; Schön J.; Halwe N.; Ulrich L.; Kochmann J.; Corleis B.; Klopfleisch R.; Beer M.; Hoffmann D.; Breithaupt A.
Article.Abstract: Respiratory viruses frequently initiate infection in the nasal mucosa, where virus-host interactions shape disease progression and transmission. Yet this site remains undercharacterized due to anatomical and technical challenges. Spatially resolved technologies are limited by cost and complexity, leaving most studies reliant on bulk or descriptive approaches lacking spatial context. We present a framework for spatially resolved investigation of infections in the nasal cavity. Using wild-type SARS-CoV-2 and two live-attenuated vaccines (OTS-206, OTS-228) as model viruses in Syrian hamsters, we integrate standardized sampling, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, multiplex RNA in situ hybridization, and quantitative image analysis across spatial scales, including tissue, single-cell and subcellular resolution. We identified distinct infection patterns and graduated tissue damage from wild-type to OTS-228. Despite limited infection, OTS-228 induces a robust tissue-preserving immune response. Subcellular analysis shows that both vaccines exhibit a primarily cytoplasmic distribution of host antiviral transcripts, whereas WT infection is characterized by predominantly nuclear RNA localization

Article.Title: Network-based characterization of latent co-testing patterns in antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Article.Authors: Awotoro E.; Anžel A.; Anyabolu C.; Willrich N.; Hattab G.
Article.Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance depends on antimicrobial susceptibility testing, yet antibiotic panels vary by pathogen cohort, specimen, year, ward, and care setting. We term these empirically reconstructed testing architectures shadow antibiograms: structures that shape which susceptibility results enter surveillance datasets and which resistance relationships can be observed. We analyzed approximately 13 million bacterial isolates from Germany's National Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance system (2019-2023) across six WHO BPPL-aligned operational cohorts. Co-testing networks were constructed using Jaccard, Dice, cosine, and phi-coefficient similarity, evaluated with Fisher's exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and partitioned with multi-resolution Louvain community detection. Networks contained three to four dominant co-testing communities; false discovery rate (FDR) retention ranged from 89 to 100% across cohorts and specimen types. Jaccard provided the best balance of coherence, stability, antimicrobial-class alignment, interpretability, and edge retention. This work provides one of the first national-scale empirical characterizations of shadow antibiogram structure, supporting diagnostic stewardship and bias-aware AMR surveillance interpretation.
Article.Keywords: antimicrobial resistance; co-testing patterns; community detection and antimicrobial susceptibility testing; diagnostic stewardship; network analysis; shadow antibiograms; similarity metrics

Article.Title: Multimodal imaging reveals no evidence for magnetite-based magnetoreceptors in the mole-rat eye
Article.Authors: Moritz L.; Nath K.; Walsh E.; Sternberg A.; Becher E.; Lange A.; Falkenberg G.; Brückner D.; Diwoky C.; Bredies K.; Brammerloh M.; Howard D.; Paterson D.; Medjoubi K.; Irsen S.; Wolf-Kümmeth S.; Zhang L.; Daniel M.; Simpson D.; Begall S.; Malkemper E.
Article.Abstract: Magnetoreception is widespread across animals, but its sensory mechanism remains unresolved. One leading hypothesis proposes that single-domain magnetite is coupled to mechanosensitive ion channels. In subterranean Ansell's mole-rats, such receptors have been proposed to reside in the cornea or retina. We screened for magnetite in the mole-rat eye by combining iron imaging via enhanced Prussian blue staining and synchrotron X-ray fluorescence microscopy (XFM) with magnetic imaging via MRI-quantitative susceptibility mapping (MRI-QSM) and quantum-diamond microscopy. The retina and cornea contained little iron, most of which co-localized with titanium or chromium, indicating a non-biogenic origin. Iron-enriched lines in the cornea did not show ferrimagnetic signals. MRI-QSM revealed the highest susceptibility in the ciliary body, where iron-rich pigmented cells were identified. A targeted TEM-screen, however, failed to detect single-domain magnetite particles. In conclusion, we found no evidence of magnetite-based magnetoreceptors in the cornea or retina, suggesting other tissues or mechanisms underlie mole-rat magnetoreception.
Article.Keywords: animal navigation; biometals; cornea; magnetoreception; magnetosensation; microscopy; retina

Article.Title: Reconstructing tropical cyclone intensity in southeastern China over the past century using tree-rings
Article.Authors: Bing X.; Fang K.; Zhou F.; Dong Z.; Xing H.; Altman J.
Article.Abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) significantly impact coastal forests, yet long-term records remain scarce. In this study, we investigate the influence of TC frequency and intensity on the radial growth patterns of three dominant tree species in natural forests of southeastern China. Using tree-ring data, we reconstruct historical TC intensity and explore its relationship with the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Our findings reveal that anomalously high TC wind speeds during the late 1950s and late 1980s led to enhanced radial growth in the studied trees due to improved light conditions caused by TC impact. The reconstructed TC wind speeds since the 1920s indicate that the intensity of landfalling TCs in southeastern China increased during El Niño phases. These results demonstrate that tree-growth anomalies can serve as a reliable proxy for reconstructing TC activity beyond the instrumental record, providing valuable insights into the linkages between TC variability and large-scale climate oscillations.
Article.Keywords: El Niño-southern oscillation; Taiwan strait; growth release; reconstruction; tree-ring; tropical cyclone wind speed

Article.Title: Trimodal ultrasound imaging of brain-tumor interaction
Article.Authors: Rabut C.; Shivaei S.; Heiles B.; Daghlian G.; Shapiro M.
Article.Abstract: Brain tumors cause debilitating neurological dysfunction by disrupting brain tissue and altering local and global neurovascular activity and blood flow. Studying tumor-brain interactions in animal models is challenging, as no single method captures tumor growth, neurovascular activity, and vascular remodeling over time. Here, we overcome this limitation with a multimodal ultrasound platform combining nonlinear imaging of acoustic reporter gene-expressing tumors, functional hemodynamic imaging of brain activity, and super-resolution vascular microscopy. Applying it to a U87 glioblastoma xenograft model, we followed individual animals across their disease lifetimes. Co-registration of all three readouts linked the displacement and weakening of the lateral geniculate nucleus to the molecularly defined tumor and the vascular remodeling around it. We also identified a tumor-intrinsic hemodynamic signal, spatially uniform and uncoupled from surrounding networks, that hemodynamic imaging alone could not distinguish from displaced tissue. This platform provides a foundation for mechanistic studies in more invasive glioma models.
Article.Keywords: ULM; acoustic reporter genes ultrasound localization microscopy; brain-tumor interactions; fUSI; functional ultrasound imaging; glioblastoma; longitudinal in vivo imaging; neurovascular coupling; tumor angiogenesis

Article.Title: MED26 facilitates Mediator-Pol II complex assembly and promotes nuclear stress body formation during heat stress
Article.Authors: Li K.; Furugori K.; Suzuki H.; Abe R.; Sawatsubashi S.; Yasui N.; Ike Y.; Horiuchi K.; Takahashi H.
Article.Abstract: Cells adapt to environmental stress by reprogramming gene expression. During heat stress, the transcription factor heat shock factor 1 (HSF1) translocates into the nucleus and activates heat shock-responsive loci, including the long non-coding RNA HSATIII, promoting nuclear stress body (nSB) formation. We show that the Mediator complex subunit MED26 enhances HSATIII transcription and nSB formation through a mechanism distinct from its role at heat-shock response (HSR) genes. Under heat stress, MED26-containing Mediator is recruited to HSR genes and nSBs through interactions with HSF1 and MED15. Phosphorylation of the intrinsically disordered region of HSF1 appears to facilitate Mediator recruitment to nSBs. Acute loss of MED26 leads to the dissociation of the Mediator and RNA polymerase II (Pol II) from HSR gene promoters, whereas the Mediator remains bound to HSATIII despite Pol II dissociation. These results suggest that MED26 acts as molecular switch, thereby facilitating Mediator-Pol II complex assembly at nSBs and promoting nSB formation during heat stress.
Article.Keywords: HSF1; MED15; MED26; Mediator; nuclear stress bodies

Article.Title: Hyperopic reserve, early myopia risk and screening strategies in children: A multi-regional analysis from the CREAM-KIDS consortium
Article.Authors: Pan W.; Harrington S.; Lingham G.; Moore M.; Foo L.; Kneepkens S.; van Hemert D.; Saunders K.; McCullough S.; Willams K.; Pärssinen O.; Baraas R.; Hagen L.; French A.; Saw S.; Yam J.; Klaver C.; Flitcroft I.; Lan W.
Article.Abstract: Reduced hyperopic reserve (HR) in early childhood is a strong predictor of future myopia. A harmonized dataset from the CREAM-Kids Consortium was utilized to assess regional differences in HR. Among 7-year olds, mean (SD) HR was 1.44 (1.17) D in Europe, 1.32 (0.80) D in Australia, 0.78 (0.89) D in Hong Kong, and 0.59 (0.66) D in Singapore (p < 0.001). The annualized decline in HR was -0.12 D/year among European-Australian followed from age 6.73 (0.64) to 11.64 (1.49), and -0.35 D/year among Asian followed from age 7.71 (0.77) to 10.71 (0.77). In European-Australian aged 6-7, the sensitivity and specificity of myopia screening was 67%-75% and 98%, and in Asian aged 4-9, 92%-99% and 70%-77%, respectively. Asian children demonstrated substantially lower HR and a faster consumption than their European and Australian peers, placing a larger proportion of Asian children at higher risk for early-onset myopia.
Article.Keywords: CREAM-KIDS; Myopia; hyperopic reserve; regional; screening

Article.Title: Reprogramming bone homeostasis: The recoupling-oriented framework of bidirectional regulation strategies for osteoporosis
Article.Authors: Niu J.; Li Z.; Zou Y.; Wang Z.; Kang J.; Zhang Y.; Wang S.; Liu R.; Han X.
Article.Abstract: Current osteoporosis treatments reduce fracture risk by suppressing bone resorption, stimulating bone formation, or combining both effects. Yet these clinical benefits do not show whether formation has resumed at sites where bone was previously resorbed. This Review uses a remodeling recoupling framework to examine this resorption-to-formation transition. We define recoupling as restoration of the sequence from resorption through reversal to osteoblast recruitment and bone formation. This differs from bidirectional regulation, in which osteoblast activity increases and osteoclast activity decreases without evidence that the two responses are linked. We review the cellular communication, signaling pathways, cell-survival mechanisms, and systemic conditions that influence this transition. We also assess candidate targets and treatments according to the strength of clinical, human, animal, and mechanistic evidence. The available evidence is strongest for established therapies and several human-supported pathways, whereas many proposed targets and delivery approaches remain preclinical. This framework may help guide treatment sequencing, patient selection, bone-targeted delivery, and the development of measures that determine whether formation follows resorption.
Article.Keywords: bidirectional regulation; bone homeostasis; osteoporosis; remodeling coupling; remodeling recoupling

Article.Title: When grooming stalls: Assessing communicative repair, negotiation, and progressivity in chimpanzees
Article.Authors: Kolff K.; Pika S.
Article.Abstract: Human social interaction is built on progressivity (the forward flow of interaction), which communicative breakdowns may disrupt. Communicative repair (resolving communicative troubles) and negotiation (a collaborative sequence to resolve communicative breakdowns) may both serve as processes to restore progressivity following breakdowns. Here, we investigated gestural redoings(reproduction of a previous signal in any form), negotiation, and progressivity in grooming interactions (N = 311) among male East African chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) in the wild. These chimpanzees produced gestural redoings as repetitions, substitutions, and modifications (N = 158) occurring at delayed temporal gaps relative to grooming turn-taking latencies. Both substitutions and negotiations (N = 219) were associated with restored progressivity. Strongly bonded pairs showed a higher likelihood of compromise outcomes during negotiation. These findings indicate that these chimpanzees employed repair-like processes associated with restored progressivity, bearing certain resemblances to those observed in human conversation-raising the possibility that such capacities may have evolutionary roots predating the emergence of language.
Article.Keywords: Pan troglodytes; communication; cooperation; gestures; social interactions; turn-taking

Article.Title: Procedural circulatory support-enabled intracoronary cell delivery in advanced dilated cardiomyopathy
Article.Authors: Ramaseshan R.; Hussain M.; Perera D.; Hamshere S.; Kelham M.; Pinto P.; Whiteford J.; Moseley T.; Reid A.; Bastos S.; Russell J.; Andiapen M.; Wynne L.; Davies C.; Keeble T.; Fawaz S.; Martin J.; Ariti C.; Jones D.; Mathur A.
Article.Abstract: Advanced heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) has limited treatment options. Although intracoronary autologous cell therapy may improve cardiac function, its use in patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction is limited by procedural risk. This exploratory study investigated whether temporary mechanical circulatory support with an Impella device could enable safer therapy delivery. Twenty patients with DCM and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of ≤35% received granulocyte colony-stimulating factor pretreatment followed by Impella-supported intracoronary infusion of autologous bone marrow mononuclear cells. The procedure was feasible, well tolerated, and not associated with major complications. After three months, mean LVEF increased by 2.9%, with numerically greater gains in those with more severe baseline impairment. Participants also experienced symptomatic, exercise capacity, and quality of life improvements. Changes in microvascular function and circulating soluble receptor for advanced glycation end-products (sRAGE) suggested potential mechanistic pathways. As a single-arm study, these findings are hypothesis generating and support further evaluation in randomized controlled trials.
Article.Keywords: cell therapy; circulatory support; clinical trial; dilated cardiomyopathy; heart failure

Article.Title: Deep brain stimulation mechanisms in comorbid pain and emotional dysregulation from animal models
Article.Authors: Si T.; Han H.; Zhang Y.; Zhou Z.; Li Z.; Cao J.; Zang W.
Article.Abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a potent neuromodulatory intervention for chronic pain and comorbid affective disorders. This review synthesizes preclinical evidence detailing the neural circuits and molecular cascades engaged by DBS in models of pain and emotional dysregulation. We delineate how DBS-targeting regions like the prefrontal cortex (PFC), thalamus, and nucleus accumbens (NAc) recruit the prefrontal-midbrain-spinal axis to facilitate endogenous opioid release and modulate neurotransmission, thereby attenuating nociception. Concurrently, stimulating the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) or lateral habenula (LHb) ameliorates affective deficits by restoring serotonergic (5-HT) and dopaminergic (DA) tone and stabilizing circuit dynamics. By mapping these convergent and divergent mechanisms, we highlight how DBS fine-tunes reward, anti-reward, and descending antinociceptive pathways. This mechanism-based framework outlines a translational roadmap for personalized neuromodulation, guiding symptom-specific target selection and the development of biomarker-driven, closed-loop DBS systems to concurrently treat pain and affective pathologies.
Article.Keywords: circuits; deep brain stimulation; depresssion; molecular pathways; pain

Article.Title: Long non-coding RNAs in tuberculosis: Immune regulation and clinical biomarker potential
Article.Authors: Tian N.; Lin J.; Ju D.; Tan Y.; Zhu J.
Article.Abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains the leading infectious cause of mortality worldwide, with an estimated 1.25 million deaths in 2023. Despite therapeutic advances, the lack of precise early screening tools continues to impede epidemic control. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as essential modulators of host anti-Mtb immunity, and elucidating their functional mechanisms is pivotal for developing effective interventions. This review systematically synthesizes lncRNA-mediated immune regulation during Mtb infection, with emphasis on their roles in modulating immune cell death, extending beyond apoptosis to encompass necrosis and pyroptosis. Importantly, we provide a comprehensive analysis of lncRNAs and related gene polymorphisms as predictive biomarkers for anti-TB drug-induced adverse reactions. Current research gaps and future priorities are also discussed. Together, the dual potential of lncRNAs as molecular diagnostics and candidate targets for host-directed therapy represents a promising frontier in TB management.
Article.Keywords: Mycobacterium tuberculosis; biomarker; long non-coding RNAs

Article.Title: Strongly coupled cogeneration increases the competitive value of nuclear reactors for industrial process heat
Article.Authors: Achireko K.; Senga J.; Parsons J.
Article.Abstract: We incorporate the thermodynamic efficiency benefits of cogeneration into an evaluation of the competitiveness of alternative nuclear reactor designs in supplying heat to a sample of industrial facilities in two regions of the US. Earlier work by Vanatta et al. had captured the capacity utilization benefits but had not incorporated the efficiency gain. Doing so increases the number of facilities for which nuclear supply is competitive. Doing so also reorders which design is most competitive for any specific industrial facility.
Article.Keywords: SMR; cogeneration; decarbonization; energy efficiency; industrial heat; nuclear power

Article.Title: Morphological plasticity facilitates lung adaptation and dynamic immune remodeling in Mycobacterium abscessus infection
Article.Authors: Chen Y.; Miao Q.; Hu L.; Pan J.; Gu X.; Qin L.; Fang T.; Hu B.
Article.Abstract: Mycobacterium abscessus pulmonary disease (Mab-PD) shows rising global incidence and low cure rates. Mab exhibits marked phenotypic heterogeneity, with infection outcomes likely dependent on strain-specific host interactions. Through in vivo morphotype switching, we obtained a rough strain (Mab-R) that showed higher virulence, bacterial loads, and lung pathology than the smooth morphotype. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that Mab-R adapts to macrophage functional states by modulating virulence and metabolic genes, promoting intracellular survival. Single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered dynamic macrophage reprogramming during infection. In acute infection, alveolar macrophages and C1qa+ interstitial macrophages cleared Mab-R via programmed cell death, while newly recruited monocytes showed strong phagocytic capacity but incomplete bacterial clearance. During chronic infection, enhanced T cell immunity and resident-like macrophage dominance facilitated inflammation resolution. These findings reveal host-pathogen interplay driving Mab-R persistence and identify bacterial metabolic adaptation and macrophage reprogramming as potential therapeutic targets for chronic Mab-PD.
Article.Keywords: Mycobacterium abscessus; alveolar macrophage; chronic pulmonary infection; single-cell RNA sequencing; virulence

Article.Title: Neurofibrillary tangle deposition in primary idiotypic isocortices using flortaucipir PET in histopathologically confirmed Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Josephs K.; Weigand S.; Satoh R.; Lavrova A.; Tapia A.; Graff-Radford J.; Machulda M.; Kantarci K.; Boeve B.; Petersen R.; Jack C.; Dickson D.; Nguyen A.; Reichard R.; Lowe V.; Whitwell J.
Article.Abstract: Tau deposition in Alzheimer's disease (AD) spreads throughout the brain in a stereotypical pattern captured by the Braak neurofibrillary tangle staging scheme. While involvement of primary isocortex defines the highest stage, it is unclear whether flortaucipir PET uptake differs among primary isocortical regions. We determined relationships between flortaucipir uptake in primary visual, auditory, motor, and somatosensory isocortices and Braak stage in 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with AD. Flortaucipir uptake was observed starting at Braak stage V, with visual and auditory isocortices showing greater and faster increases in uptake than somatosensory and motor; age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake. Flortaucipir uptake and change in primary isocortices were similar in the lateral temporal cortex but different in the entorhinal cortex. Findings suggest that tau deposition in primary isocortices in AD occurs earlier than currently emphasized, although there are differences among them. Given these findings, clinical correlations of primary isocortical involvement in AD need to be evaluated.
Article.Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease; braak stage; flortaucipir; isocortex; motor cortex; tau

Article.Title: Sonocavitation therapy for pancreatic cancer: Research progress, clinical application and future perspectives
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Yang S.; Shama S.; Zhao R.; Liang X.
Article.Abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, characterized by a dense desmoplastic stroma, an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and poor response to conventional therapies. Sonocavitation therapy, based on ultrasound microbubble (USMB) technology, has emerged as a potential strategy to improve intratumoral drug delivery, remodel the tumor microenvironment (TME), and enhance chemotherapy, immunotherapy, gene therapy, and radiotherapy. Proposed mechanisms include sonoporation, cascade cavitation, vascular normalization, and mechano-acoustic remodeling of the stroma. Early clinical studies suggest that USMB-assisted chemotherapy is feasible and may improve disease control, although the evidence remains heterogeneous and is based largely on small, single-center or early-phase studies. Major barriers to translation include nonstandardized acoustic parameters, pharmacokinetic mismatch between microbubbles and co-administered drugs, incomplete representation of human disease in preclinical models, and limited long-term safety data. Future work should prioritize standardized acoustic dosing, biomarker-guided patient selection, clinically practical formulations, rigorous pharmacokinetic and biodistribution studies, and adequately powered randomized trials. This review summarizes the mechanistic rationale, preclinical evidence, and clinical progress of sonocavitation therapy in pancreatic cancer and outlines priorities for its clinical translation.
Article.Keywords: clinical translation; drug delivery; pancreatic cancer; sonocavitation therapy; ultrasound microbubbles technology

Article.Title: Robust multimodal emotion recognition under incomplete modalities via transformer conditional variational autoencoders
Article.Authors: Wang S.; Li J.; Wu Z.; Wang B.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MER) has gained increasing research interest owing to its ability to integrate complementary emotional cues from textual, acoustic, and visual modalities. However, real-world applications often suffer from incomplete multimodal inputs caused by sensor failures, communication disruptions, or noisy environments, resulting in missing modalities or corrupted features. To address these challenges, this study proposes RMM-TCVAE, a robust MER framework based on a Transformer-based Conditional Variational Autoencoder. The framework combines modality-specific encoders, a conditional Transformer Reconstruction Network for recovering missing modalities, and a Gated Multimodal Fusion Network for adaptive cross-modal integration. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and IEMOCAP demonstrate that RMM-TCVAE consistently outperforms strong baselines under incomplete multimodal conditions, achieving 84.8% accuracy on CMU-MOSEI and yielding improvements of up to 2.9 percentage points in Acc and 3.1 percentage points in WAF across fixed missing-rate experiments. Ablation and visualization analyses support the effectiveness of RMM-TCVAE under incomplete multimodal conditions.
Article.Keywords: conditional variational autoencoder; cross-modal fusion; incomplete multimodal learning; multimodal emotion recognition; robust representation learning; transformer

Article.Title: Targeted neuronal stimulation modulates working memory via astrocytic interactions: Insights from a spiking neuron-astrocyte model
Article.Authors: Naghieh P.; Amiri M.; Peremans H.
Article.Abstract: Brain stimulation offers promising avenues for cognitive enhancement, yet conventional paradigms often overlook the active role of astrocytes and treat stimulation as an all-or-none intervention without considering spatial information or competition among temporal dynamics. We present a spiking neuron-astrocyte network model integrated with 2D recording and stimulation arrays to investigate how targeted neuronal stimulation modulates working memory (WM) via neuroglial interactions. WM depends on a temporal hierarchy: rapid neuronal spiking, synaptic glutamate release, and slow astrocytic calcium signaling. In three experiments we demonstrate: (1) targeted excitatory stimulation restores WM in synaptically impaired networks by reactivating astrocytic calcium dynamics; (2) inhibitory stimulation disrupts WM maintenance by blocking the necessary neuroglial feedback loop; and (3) excitatory stimulation during the sample phase augments WM encoding for novel patterns. Our findings underscore the importance of spatiotemporal precision in stimulation protocols and establish astrocytes as pivotal mediators, providing a new framework for bio-inspired memory systems.
Article.Keywords: Biocomputational method; Cognitive neuroscience; Neural networks; Neuroscience

Article.Title: Preventive trial-and-error model is associated with improved breech delivery skills and training transfer in midwifery interns
Article.Authors: Zhuge Y.; Yao X.; Deng X.; Yao H.
Article.Abstract: Breech delivery requires midwifery trainees to integrate technical skills, clinical decision-making, and error prevention in time-sensitive situations. We evaluated a preventive trial-and-error model using high-fidelity simulation among 89 midwifery interns in a quasi-experimental study. Over 4 weeks, the intervention incorporated structured exposure to simulated errors, guided correction, preventive strategy discussion, and feedback, whereas the control group received conventional demonstration-based training. Compared with controls, the intervention group achieved higher breech delivery skill scores (89.65 ± 3.42 versus 85.53 ± 2.64) and training transfer scores (25.83 ± 1.78 versus 22.88 ± 1.62). These findings suggest that structured error-based simulation may support short-term skill acquisition and perceived transfer of learning in midwifery education. The approach provides a practical framework for integrating error prevention and reflective learning into simulation-based training when opportunities for repeated clinical exposure are limited.
Article.Keywords: breech delivery; high-fidelity simulation; midwifery education; preventive trial-and-error model; trial-and-error learning theory

Article.Title: Impact of health education on quality of life in patients with chronic kidney disease
Article.Authors: Vicente-Garrido C.; Vicente García T.; Sánchez Aguadero N.; González Sánchez J.; Alonso Domínguez R.; Recio Rodríguez J.; Bermejo Gil B.; Coello González E.; Sánchez-Tocino M.
Article.Abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with lower quality of life (QoL) than the general population, and health education is widely proposed to help patients manage the disease. We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of studies published between 2014 and April 2024 evaluating educational interventions in adults with CKD using a validated QoL instrument. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted data, resolving disagreements with a third reviewer; risk of bias was assessed with RoB2 and ROBINS-I. Twelve studies met inclusion criteria. Educational interventions were generally associated with improvements in QoL and clinical parameters, more consistently for mental than physical health, although certainty of evidence was limited by heterogeneity in design, populations and outcomes, and by a predominance of studies with some concerns or high risk of bias. Health education appears a valuable component of CKD care, but well-designed, prospectively registered trials are needed before firm recommendations can be made.
Article.Keywords: PRISMA; chronic kidney disease; health education; health-related quality of life; quality of life; systematic review

Article.Title: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor in diabetes: A promising target for cognitive restoration
Article.Authors: Chandak G.; Kumar B.; Kumar S.; Ashique S.; Bhui U.; Pandey N.; Debnath B.; Al-Salem F.; Yasmin S.; Brady M.; Ansari M.
Article.Abstract: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays an essential role in neuronal growth and maturation, as well as in maintaining synaptic plasticity. Dysregulated BDNF levels significantly increase the risk of neurological and metabolic disorders. In type 2 diabetes mellitus, several pathological mechanisms, including prolonged hyperglycemia, oxidative damage, chronic inflammation, and impaired insulin sensitivity, are known to drive neurodegenerative processes and deterioration of cognitive function. Impaired BDNF signaling can result in compromised synaptic transmission and gradual loss of neurons, with the hippocampus being particularly vulnerable. A growing body of evidence points to a strong correlation between diminished BDNF levels and diabetes related cognitive decline. Findings from both human clinical trials and animal studies have consistently reported reduced BDNF concentrations in brain tissues and systemic circulation in diabetic conditions. Therapeutic strategies aimed at upregulating BDNF expression and modulating its downstream signaling pathways hold considerable promise for preventing or mitigating diabetes associated cognitive deficits.
Article.Keywords: BDNF; T2DM; anti-depressant; anti-diabetes; brain-derived neurotrophic factor; cognitive function; neuroprotective

Article.Title: Local electricity price effects of Bitcoin mining in renewable-rich energy systems
Article.Authors: Gill M.; Stinner J.; Tyrell M.
Article.Abstract: Load-shifting is increasingly important in renewable-rich energy systems. Bitcoin mining is often cited as a large, theoretically flexible load. Despite electricity consumption rivaling medium-sized industrial economies, the energy market behavior and impacts of Bitcoin miners remain largely unexplored. We exploit the large-scale relocation of Bitcoin mining to Texas, which became the world's largest mining hub following China's 2021 ban, to estimate its effects on local wholesale electricity prices. Combining a hand-collected dataset on mining facility locations with high-frequency wholesale price data, we identify price impacts using a DiD design. We find that miners select into renewable-rich, high-GDP per capita counties with initially lower electricity prices on average. Entry has no robust effect on daytime prices but raises nighttime prices by 19.9%. Price separation widens most in already-stressed hours. Miners may curtail under extreme scarcity, but do not shift load across ordinary price cycles to complement renewable generation.
Article.Keywords: Bitcoin mining; demand flexibility; electricity markets; energy and sustainability

Article.Title: Research on the transmission characteristics and fabrication process of photonic lanterns
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Chen Z.; Liu T.; Sun Z.; Li X.; Jiang Z.
Article.Abstract: As a waveguide device capable of realizing low-loss adiabatic transition from multiple single-mode fibers to a multimode fiber, the photonic lantern exhibits broad application prospects in fields such as mode division multiplexing communication, high-power laser manipulation, and astronomical observation. This paper systematically investigates the physical mechanism of mode evolution, numerical modeling methods, and transmission characteristic characterization of photonic lanterns. The full-process fabrication technology, including material pretreatment, bundle arrangement, tapering optimization, precision cleaving, and dissimilar splicing, is detailed, with key process factors analyzed. Comprehensive characterization shows transmission efficiency exceeding 98% at low power, while mode field tests verify mode evolution laws consistent with simulations, laying a theoretical foundation and technical support for the engineering application of photonic lanterns.
Article.Keywords: mode evolution; neural network; optical fiber processing; photonic lantern; transmission matrix

Article.Title: Dual functions of NPC1L1 for cholesterol transport: Cholesterol capture and regulation of inner-leaflet cholesterol accessibility
Article.Authors: Yamanashi Y.; Kitani M.; Kumamaru M.; Fukaya T.; Sugita R.; Takada T.
Article.Abstract: Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1) is essential for intestinal cholesterol absorption, but the detailed mechanisms underlying its non-vesicular cholesterol transport remain unclear. Using fluorescent cholesterol probes, we found that NPC1L1 decreased accessible cholesterol in the outer leaflet while increasing it in the inner leaflet in an ezetimibe-sensitive manner. This activity was independent of outer-leaflet sphingomyelin levels and was unaffected by a dysfunctional mutation in the N-terminal domain (NTD), which mediates extracellular cholesterol binding and insertion into the outer leaflet. In contrast, mutations in the sterol-sensing domain (SSD) abolished NPC1L1-dependent redistribution of accessible cholesterol between plasma membrane leaflets. These findings support a two-step model in which the NTD captures and inserts cholesterol into the outer leaflet, whereas the SSD promotes its redistribution toward the inner leaflet. Our study identifies a previously unrecognized step in NPC1L1-mediated non-vesicular cholesterol transport and provides mechanistic insight into SSD function.
Article.Keywords: SSD; accessible cholesterol; cholesterol probe; cholesterol uptake; transporter

Article.Title: EGaIn-based liquid-metal electrodes for electronic interfaces and contact engineering
Article.Authors: Kim G.; Lee H.; Bang M.; Mun S.; Lee Y.; Park B.; Kang J.
Article.Abstract: Liquid metals offer a unique combination of metallic conductivity and fluid-like deformability, but their practical implementation as electrodes requires precise control over dynamic and chemically active interfaces. This review examines eutectic gallium-indium (EGaIn) as a representative gallium-based liquid metal and analyzes how its native oxide skin, wetting behavior, reactive alloying, and contact mechanics govern electrical contact formation, interfacial stability, and device integration.
