Article.Abstract: Thermal and solute transport enhancement is a requirement of several industrial and engineering processes like thermal and cooling systems, thermal radiators, nuclear reactor cooling, HVAC and refrigeration, etc. The rheological constitutive relations, the Stefan-Boltzmann law for thermal radiation effects, Ohm's law, and a set of Maxwell equations, together with conservation laws in the presence of magnetic body and buoyancy forces, are used to develop the governing equations. The coupled momentum, energy, and concentration equations are simplified using boundary-layer approximations. The resulting partial differential equations are reduced by similarity transformation to a dimensionless system, which is then numerically solved using the finite element method (FEM). The linear shape functions are used for approximating the solutions in a one-dimensional domain. The stiffness elements are used in the Galerkin approximations. Picard linearization is an effective technique for nonlinear algebraic systems that converges quickly when functions have a linear shape. Therefore, the Picard approach is implemented in this case. FEM solutions are further used for capturing thermal enhancement in both mono and hybrid nanofluids. The resulting nonlinear algebraic system is then linearized using Picard linearization and solved under a convergence tolerance of 10 −5 . The present results are validated by comparing with already published benchmark 46 . To clarify the impact of important physical parameters on thermal transport properties, parametric simulations are carried out. Temperature distribution decreases when the thermal radiation parameter increases because an increase in \(Nr\) corresponds to an increase in intensity of thermal radiation, and an increase in thermal radiation implies an increase in electromagnetic waves that escape heat away from the fluid.

Article.Title: A high-efficiency non-isolated bidirectional converter for power exchange between PV array and battery
Article.Authors: Shahidi N.; Salary E.
Article.Abstract: This paper proposes a high-efficiency non-isolated bidirectional DC-DC converter for power exchange between a photovoltaic (PV) array and a battery energy storage system. The proposed topology is designed to achieve an extended voltage conversion range while maintaining a simple circuit structure, continuous input current, and reduced semiconductor voltage stress. Compared with the conventional bidirectional buck–boost converter, the proposed converter provides an asymmetric voltage conversion ratio, achieving a voltage gain of $$\:\frac{\text{D}}{2}$$ in buck mode and $$\:\frac{2}{1-\text{D}}$$ in boost mode. Synchronous rectification is employed to reduce conduction losses and improve overall conversion efficiency. The operating principles and steady-state characteristics of the converter are analyzed in detail and validated through simulation and experimental investigations. Furthermore, the converter is integrated into a PV-battery power management system, where continuous input current improves compatibility with photovoltaic sources and reduces input filtering requirements. To ensure stable bidirectional power transfer and effective energy management, a sliding mode control (SMC) strategy is implemented, providing fast dynamic response, robust operation, and accurate maximum power point tracking (MPPT) under varying environmental conditions. Experimental results obtained from a laboratory-scale prototype verify the feasibility of the proposed design and demonstrate peak efficiencies of 98.3% in buck mode and 98.4% in boost mode. The combination of extended voltage gain, low device stress, high efficiency, and simple implementation makes the proposed converter a promising solution for PV-battery energy storage systems and other renewable energy applications.

Article.Title: Identification and analysis of obesity-cellular senescence associated key genes in metabolic syndrome based on transcriptomic data
Article.Authors: Zhang L.; Zhang H.; Wang Q.; Zhang Y.; Yuan X.; Gao L.; Deng F.; Liao X.
Article.Abstract: The Intricate relationship between obesity, cellular senescence, and metabolic syndrome (MetS) remains elusive. This study aimed to elucidate mechanisms involving obesity-related genes (ORGs) and cellular senescence-related genes (CSRGs) in MetS. Transcriptomic profiles from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) distinguishing MetS patients from healthy controls. We then implemented weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to determine pivotal module genes correlated with ORGs and CSRGs, followed by intersecting DEGs to obtain target genes. Nine CytoHubba algorithms and expression validation were employed to identify potential biomarkers. Based on potential biomarkers, a nomogram model were developed and assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Additionally, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and therapeutic target prediction were performed. Ultimately, potential biomarkers expression levels were confirmed through reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analysis. CCL2, CXCL2, HAVCR2, and TLR5 were identified as potential biomarkers, demonstrating significant associations with obesity and cellular senescence in MetS. The nomogram exhibited promising predictive capability for MetS risk. Furthermore, GSEA showed that NOD-like receptor signaling pathway was enriched by potential biomarkers. Several potential therapeutic drugs were predicted on potential biomarkers, including mifamurtide and plozalizumab. Finally, the expression of CCL2, CXCL2, and HAVCR2 was significantly lower in the MetS group, while TLR5 had the converse results. This study preliminarily suggests that CCL2, CXCL2, HAVCR2, and TLR5 are potential biomarkers for MetS and may be associated with obesity and cellular senescence. These findings provide candidate targets for subsequent functional validation and mechanistic studies. However, their clinical diagnostic value, risk predictive performance, and biological functions still require further validation in larger independent cohorts and functional experiments.

Article.Title: Structural, electronic, spectroscopic, and thermodynamic properties of gentisic acid: solvent and temperature effects using DFT and TD-DFT approaches
Article.Authors: Kena E.; Hordofa A.; Dadi D.; Evstigneev M.; Gemta A.
Article.Abstract: Gentisic acid (GA) is a naturally occurring phenolic compound known for its anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and anticancer properties. Despite some reports, a systematic assessment of solvent- and temperature-dependent electronic, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties has not yet been investigated. In this study, we employed semi-empirical PM6, Hartree-Fock, and DFT (B3LYP/6-311++G(d,p)) with IEF−PCM Continuum solvation to examine the effect of solvent polarity. The results indicate that increasing solvent polarity modifies the electronic structure of GA and narrows the HOMO−LUMO energy gap. The natural bond orbital (NBO) analysis reveals that oxygen lone-pair donation and $$\pi$$-electron delocalization are important contributors to the molecular stabilization. Charge distribution analyses displayed non-uniform redistribution of electron density in the gas phase and aqueous environment. The TD-DFT calculations show slight solvent-dependent shifts, with the UV−Vis data showing consistency with the previous experimental data. The FTIR vibrational frequencies were also evaluated and show good agreement with previous experimental measurements. The calculated thermodynamic properties over the temperature range of 100−1000 K show systematic increase in enthalpy, heat capacity, and entropy in both the gas and aqueous phases. The gas phase thermodynamic properties are slightly greater than those in water, due to enhanced translational and rotational degrees of freedom in the gas phase. In general, the results of this work provide a systematic computational description of solvent- and temperature-dependent behavior of GA, offering valuable insights into its potential relevance to drug development and molecular spectroscopy.

Article.Title: Practical reliability-aware temporal state correction for depth-assisted RGB-skeleton action recognition
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhang M.; Wang X.; Tong S.
Article.Abstract: RGB-D action recognition benefits from skeleton motion, RGB appearance, and depth geometry, yet auxiliary modalities are not equally helpful for every sample. We present a reliability-aware temporal state correction method that treats the skeleton representation as the primary temporal state and RGB and local depth features as corrective evidence. A low-cost state-unreliability proxy combines class-normalized prediction entropy with temporal variation between unit-normalized hidden states; both components are dimensionless and bounded before fusion. A monotonic sigmoid gate then controls sample-wise RGB correction, while skeleton-guided local depth features provide a subordinate geometric residual. On NTU RGB+D 60, the full model achieves 93.7%/96.0% under the cross-subject/cross-view protocols; on NTU RGB+D 120, it achieves 90.2%/91.8% under the cross-subject/cross-setup protocols. Under a strictly matched NTU RGB+D 60 cross-subject decomposition, reliability-conditioned RGB correction improves naive integration from 91.8% to 93.1%, and local depth further raises accuracy to 93.7%. The combined proxy obtains an error-detection AUROC of 0.72 on the held-out validation split. We interpret this score only as an empirical conditioning proxy, not as Bayesian or calibrated uncertainty.

Article.Title: A robust model for improving digital marketing using sentiment analysis and two-agent off-policy proximal policy optimization
Article.Authors: Yarjanli M.; Mahdinasab N.
Article.Abstract: Understanding consumer sentiment is important in digital marketing because it strongly influences brand perception and purchasing decisions. This paper proposes a novel two-agent off-policy proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework. Unlike standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) approaches, the proposed framework uses a two-agent off-policy PPO design. It combines an active learning (AL) agent for sample selection with a sentiment analysis (SA) agent to improve labeling efficiency and classification robustness. Current SA methods often face challenges related to labeling efficiency, feature selection, class imbalance, generalization, and hyperparameter optimization. Unlike existing SA approaches that tackle these challenges independently, the proposed framework addresses them within a unified learning workflow. To address these challenges, the proposed two‑agent framework has the first agent select the most informative unlabeled samples for annotation. This reduces labeling costs. The second agent then performs SA. Within the second agent, local interpretable model‑agnostic explanations (LIME) guides feature selection. Augmented rewards are also used to improve the recognition of underrepresented classes. A relational generative adversarial network framework enhanced with gradient signal exclusion (RelGANGE) is used for online data augmentation. To increase sample diversity, the generator in RelGANGE ignores gradients from samples that receive high discriminator weights. Hyperparameters are optimized using Bayesian optimization hyperband (BOHB). Comprehensive evaluations on the Amazon Instant Video (AIV), Amazon Apps and Games Reviews (AA), and Yelp datasets were conducted using 5-fold cross-validation. The proposed framework achieved F-measure scores of 95.163%, 95.580%, and 93.054%, respectively. These results significantly outperformed traditional and transformer-based baselines. Statistical analyses confirmed that the improvements were significant ( p < 0.01). The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for e-commerce recommendation systems (RSs) and decision-support applications.

Article.Title: Automated brain MRI image classification through machine learning and deep learning approaches
Article.Authors: Kamarujjaman N/A.; Das S.; Majumdar D.; Das J.; Alam S.; Pal A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Tumors within the human brain cause severe effects on the cerebral system. Therefore, the early detection of such abnormalities needs to be accurately performed, and classifications of such cells also play a pivotal role in planning further treatment procedures. Timely detection and classification of brain tumors remain challenging, motivating the investigation of machine learning and deep learning approaches for computer-assisted image analysis. To serve the purpose, Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, U-Net, and k-Nearest Neighbors models for the identification and correct categorization of the brain tumors have been considered. The models have been trained and tested using the brain MRI images. The considered models are implemented in Python, and the outcomes of the models are observed critically to select the best model for the computer-aided diagnosis system. Among the models, Random Forest and k-Nearest Neighbors have illustrated the highest classification accuracy and computational efficiency of 94.44% and 93.89%, with runtimes of 0.073s and 10.97s, respectively, in correct identification and categorization of the brain tumor through MRI images.

Article.Title: PITRM1-AS1 attenuates the ferroptosis of gastric cancer via TAF1-mediated KDM3B transcription
Article.Authors: Shen C.; Liu H.; Zhou F.; Wang Z.; Wang Y.; Shao J.; Guo J.; Shi Z.; Zhou G.
Article.Abstract: This study aimed to identify ferroptosis-related lncRNAs in gastric cancer (GC), with a view to providing novel insights into GC therapy by inducing ferroptosis. Bioinformatics analysis was conducted to screen ferroptosis-related lncRNAs and further identified their expression at the tissue and cellular levels. The malignant phenotypes and ferroptosis characteristics of GC cells were measured by CCK-8, colony formation, transwell assays as well as iron, Fe 2+ , MDA detection. The molecular mechanism mediated by PITRM1-AS1 was probed through co-expression analysis, RNA immunoprecipitation, dual-luciferase reporter, and rescue experiments. Besides, the nude mouse model was applied to verify the ferroptosis effect caused by PITRM1-AS1 in vivo. PITRM1-AS1 was identified as a ferroptosis-related lncRNA highly expressed in GC. Knockdown of PITRM1-AS1 significantly weakened the proliferation and metastatic abilities of GC cells while promoting ferroptosis. Co-expression results presented that KDM3B was a downstream target gene positively regulated by PITRM1-AS1. Moreover, mechanism studies demonstrated that PITRM1-AS1 directly bind to transcription factor TAF1 and promoted TAF1-mediated transcription of KDM3B. Furthermore, rescue studies confirmed that KDM3B overexpression partially abrogated the ferroptosis effect and tumor suppression induced by PITRM1-AS1 silencing. In summary, these results revealed the function of PITRM1-AS1 in GC and disclosed a novel PITRM1-AS1-mediated TAF1/KDM3B/SLC7A11 regulatory axis. Our findings offer novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying ferroptosis-related GC.

Article.Title: Multivariate analysis and genetic diversity for tuber yield and quality traits in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.)
Article.Authors: Thakur N.; Sood S.; Kumari M.; Dipta B.; Mankar P.; Kaur R.; Mangal V.; Bhardwaj V.; Kumar V.; Singh B.
Article.Abstract: The present investigation was conducted to assess the genetic variability, stability and adaptability of potato genotypes across multiple environments for yield and quality improvement. A total of 357 genotypes including advanced breeding lines and released cultivars were evaluated during 2022-23 and 2023-24 at two locations using an augmented block design. Significant genotypic variation was observed for agro-morphological traits across environments, indicating substantial genetic variability. The phenotypic coefficient of variation was higher than genotypic coefficient of variation for most traits indicating influence of environment on trait expression. High heritability coupled with moderate to high genetic advance was observed for traits processing grade yield percent, dry matter, specific gravity, tuber shape, skin color, eye depth and flesh color indicating the predominance of additive gene effects. Strong positive phenotypic and genotypic correlation was observed for total tuber yield and marketable tuber yield, while dry matter content exhibited a negative association with yield traits. Path coefficient analysis revealed that marketable tuber yield had strong positive direct effect on total tuber yield. Cluster analysis grouped the genotypes into four major clusters, whereas principal component analysis explained 84.50% of the total cumulative variance through the first four components having eigen value greater than one. BLUP and AMMI stability analysis identified stable and high- performing genotypes across environments. Based on the combined performance across yield and quality traits, CP2390, CP3412, Kufri Sadabahar and CP2086 were identified as superior ideotype genotypes with potential for further advancement in potato breeding programme.

Article.Title: Evaluation of a robust and asymmetric class of nonlinear regression models under censoring
Article.Authors: Moatani O.; Maleki M.; Zare K.; Mahmoudi M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Censored nonlinear regression models are often based on Gaussian errors for analytical convenience. However, real data—such as income levels, HIV viral loads, or agricultural yields—often exhibit asymmetry, heavy tails, outliers, and censored observations, making classical Gaussian models inadequate. In this study, we extend censored nonlinear regression (CNLR) using the two–piece scale mixture of normal (TP–SMN), a flexible distribution that accommodates both asymmetry and excess kurtosis. We develop an EM–type algorithm that allows exact maximum likelihood estimation without stochastic EM methods. The method’s effectiveness is demonstrated on simulated and real datasets, including Ultrasonic and Oil data. The results show that the proposed TP–SMN–CNLR models are robust against asymmetric behavior, outliers and censoring, providing accurate and reliable inference even under challenging data conditions.

Article.Title: Chloroplast genome assembly of Thalassia testudinum from the Caribbean Sea, and its evolutionary analysis with related genera
Article.Authors: Colón Colón A.; Rosario G.; Vázquez Fuentes D.; Batista R.; Rivera-Vicéns R.; Núñez-Marrero Á.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Seagrass meadows, composed of submerged marine angiosperms, provide a critical framework for studying biodiversity and ecological adaptations. The widely distributed genus Thalassia holds significant promise for sustainable environmental development. Moreover, a notable gap remains in the analysis of the Thalassia testudinum from the Caribbean, which is essential for accurately evaluating evolutionary distances between Thalassia species. To address this, a recent study utilized Minion long-read sequencing to analyze the chloroplast (cp) genome of T. testudinum collected from Guánica, Puerto Rico. In addition, a comprehensive genomic cp comparison to uncover evolutionary relationships with other T. testudinum and T. hemprichii populations. The sequenced Guánica cp genome was 179,257 base pairs in size, containing 141 protein-coding genes, and comparisons revealed a high degree of genetic conservation across Thalassia species. Furthermore, Simple Sequence Repeats (SSRs) analysis highlighted strong similarities among geographically related populations, with genetic variability primarily isolated to mononucleotide compositions and specific dinucleotide and tetranucleotide repeat motifs. The phylogenetic placement within the Hydrocharitaceae family confirmed the relation of T. testudinum of Guánica to Florida. Ultimately, these findings establish a foundational understanding of the evolutionary relationships of T. testudinum cp from Puerto Rico to other Thalassia species.

Article.Title: TRIM3 functions as a tumor suppressor and predicts prognosis in triple-negative breast cancer: a multi-omics study with clinical cohort validation
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Tao Y.; Zhang Q.; Shi M.; Ye B.; Wang K.; Tian J.; Zhang C.; Yuan X.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype with poor prognosis and limited treatment options. Tripartite motif-containing protein 3 (TRIM3), an E3 ubiquitin ligase, has been implicated as a tumor suppressor in several cancers; however, its biological role and clinical significance in TNBC remain unclear. TRIM3 expression was analyzed using TCGA, bc-GenExMiner, CPTAC, and GEO datasets, and survival associations were evaluated with Kaplan–Meier Plotter and bc-GenExMiner. Functional assays, including CCK-8, colony formation, Transwell migration, xenograft tumorigenesis, and RNA sequencing, were performed in TRIM3-overexpressing TNBC cells. A p53-knockdown rescue experiment and immunofluorescence staining of gamma-H2A.X were also performed. Downstream pathways were explored using principal component analysis, differential expression, KEGG enrichment, EggNOG classification, gene set enrichment analysis, and protein–protein interaction networks. TNBC intrinsic molecular subtypes (BL1, BL2, M, LAR) were stratified, and the correlation between TRIM3 and immune checkpoints was analyzed. Immunohistochemistry assessed TRIM3 and TP53 expression in clinical TNBC samples, and a prognostic nomogram with a RiskScore model was constructed using Cox regression. The RiskScore model was externally validated in the METABRIC TNBC cohort. TRIM3 was significantly downregulated in TNBC compared with non-TNBC subtypes at both mRNA and protein levels. Low TRIM3 expression predicted worse survival outcomes and was strongly associated with TP53 mutation and genomic instability–related pathways. TRIM3 overexpression suppressed TNBC cell proliferation, migration, and tumor growth in vivo. Notably, TRIM3 expression was lowest in the BL1 subtype and highest in LAR, and was negatively correlated with multiple immune checkpoints. P53 knockdown reversed the tumor-suppressive effects of TRIM3 overexpression. Clinically, TRIM3 loss was more pronounced in TP53-mutated tumors. The TRIM3-based RiskScore effectively stratified patients, with high-risk individuals showing markedly poorer survival (HR = 18.42; AUC = 0.83 at 5 years and 0.90 at 10 years). The RiskScore model was further externally validated in the METABRIC cohort (HR = 1.016; 5-year AUC = 0.647). TRIM3 functions as a tumor suppressor in TNBC and is linked to TP53 mutation, genomic instability, and adverse clinical outcomes, highlighting its potential as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target.

Article.Title: A hybrid framework combining enhanced fields and consistent spatial features for stroke lesion segmentation in MR images
Article.Authors: Li M.; Lian F.; Zhai R.; Shan C.
Article.Abstract: Stroke lesion segmentation plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis, prognosis and rehabilitation treatment. However, this task remains highly challenging due to inter-subject differences, shape variations, noise and artifacts in MR images, which hinder the accurate extraction of stroke regions. This work proposes a novel hybrid framework for accurate stroke lesion segmentation from MR images termed HFFS-net. To enhance spatial consistency between the segmented stroke regions and the original ones in MR images, we introduce an adversarial architecture as an auxiliary encoder, which extracts high-dimensional distribution features of stroke lesions, ensuring improved consistency between the spatial distributions of original MR images and segmented outputs. To further capture fine-grained details of stroke lesions, we enhance the receptive fields of kernels in convolution framework, enabling robust extraction of representative features from target stroke lesions. Additionally, we design a multi-dimensional framework with hierarchical enhanced fields to comprehensively aggregate diverse stroke-specific information from MR images. The proposed model was rigorously evaluated on datasets comprising stroke lesions of varying sizes to comprehensively assess its segmentation performance and generalization capability. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing segmentation methods, attaining a Dice score of 84.33% and a Recall of 85.44%. These results confirm that the proposed framework is capable of effectively capturing diverse and discriminative features, thereby enabling accurate stroke lesion segmentation.

Article.Title: Reliable multimodal signals for in-vehicle heartbeat detection
Article.Authors: Bollmann J.; Warnecke J.; Ji D.; Baumgärtel D.; Flormann M.; Henze R.; Deserno T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Continuous and unobtrusive cardiac monitoring during driving is medically attractive but technically challenging due to motion artifacts, contact variability, and changing illumination. Building on our previously developed multimodal sensing platform that integrates steering wheel electrocardiography (ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and a camera (RGB), in this paper, we (i) propose an improved electrode design for steering wheel ECG acquisition, (ii) integrate infrared and thermal cameras, and (iii) combine these modalities for robust heartbeat detection under real-world driving conditions. We record data from 23 healthy adults on a standardized 55 km route that includes urban, rural, and highway segments. During each drive, we acquire a ground truth ECG using electrodes attached to the driver’s upper body. We use convolutional neural network models with early fusion, signal-based late fusion, sensor-based late fusion, and hybrid fusion. The steering wheel ECG achieves the highest single-modality performance (F1-score = 91.92%). Augmenting ECG with iPPG-RGB and iPPG-IR raises the F1-score to 92.14%. The vision-based signals provide limited complementary information but do not compensate for complete steering wheel electrocardiogram (ECG) loss. In future work, we will increase the reliability of physiological recordings by using data from the vehicle’s controller area network (CAN) bus.

Article.Title: ATLAS: an adaptive threat learning and analysis system using heterogeneous federated deep learning and FedNova aggregation for multi-cloud environments
Article.Authors: Khan S.; Panwar A.; Jain A.; Qamar S.; Alomran A.; Alsharif M.; Alomary F.; Alsolai H.
Article.Abstract: The proliferation of multi-cloud architectures has intensified challenges in phishing detection, as security intelligence becomes fragmented across heterogeneous cloud infrastructures governed by stringent privacy regulations and data sovereignty constraints. Conventional centralized threat detection paradigms necessitate aggregating sensitive data from disparate sources, thereby introducing substantial privacy risks, regulatory compliance burdens, and communication bottlenecks. This paper introduces ATLAS (Adaptive Threat Learning and Analysis System), a privacy preserving threat intelligence framework leveraging Heterogeneous Federated Deep Learning (HFDL) for collaborative multi-cloud cybersecurity. Unlike traditional federated learning approaches that presuppose uniform model architectures across participants, ATLAS accommodates diverse client models specifically, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU), and XGBoost classifier each trained on disjoint feature subsets representing distributed cloud observations. To reconcile objective inconsistencies and heterogeneous local training dynamics, ATLAS evaluates multiple aggregation strategies: FedAvg (naive probability averaging), FedProx (performance weighted aggregation), FedNova (normalized averaging accounting for local update heterogeneity), and a meta-learning ensemble. Comprehensive experiments on the PhishNet phishing detection dataset reveal that ATLAS with FedNova aggregation attains 95.21% accuracy and 95.19% F1-score, surpassing FedAvg (94.57% accuracy) with statistical significance confirmed via McNemar’s test ( \(\chi ^2=4.97\) , \(p=0.026\) ). Performance approaches that of centralized learning (96.79% accuracy) while achieving approximately 80.6% reduction in communication overhead and negligible aggregation latency (0.00025 ms/sample), thereby enabling real-time deployment. These findings establish heterogeneous federated learning as a viable, scalable, and privacy preserving paradigm for collaborative threat detection in distributed multi-cloud environments, effectively balancing detection efficacy with data sovereignty requirements.

Article.Title: Five degree of freedom modulation parameters for three level dual active bridge converter
Article.Authors: Prabhu Deva Kumar S.; Akashe S.; Upadhyay G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract To improve the performance of isolated bidirectional DC/DC converters, this article investigates an enhanced control strategy for the multilevel (ML) dual active bridge (DAB) topology. Compared with the conventional DAB structure, the ML structure supports the use of lower voltage rating switches and provides more control degrees of freedom. The five degree of freedom modulation strategy used here, in which the optimal duty cycles are determined from the fundamental and third harmonic components of the high frequency bridge voltages by means of vector diagrams and without complex node analysis. The contribution of the present study is the implementation of that established framework: the conventional look-up table based realisation is replaced by an offline trained function fitting neural network that predicts the five duty ratios directly from the measured operating point, avoiding both multi-dimensional tables and iterative online optimisation. The inductor current is significantly reduced at light loads by the proposed modulation strategy and neural network. Moreover, this optimization method does not require complex optimization tools. All results reported in this paper are obtained from MATLAB/Simulink simulations of a 100 kW three-level NPC DAB converter, and no experimental prototype has been built. Within this scope, the simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method in reducing the inductor current. Compared with single phase shift (SPS) modulation, the proposed strategy reduces the inductor current RMS value by up to 34.8% at light load (10 kW) and by about 22% at 50 kW, while the three strategies converge at the rated 100 kW, which indicates that the proposed method is a promising candidate for next generation power conversion systems, subject to experimental confirmation.

Article.Title: AdaptDelivery: a polymer informatics platform for predicting structural properties of polymers via machine learning
Article.Authors: Parajdi L.; Toth I.; Farcas A.; Balint Z.; Kiraly A.; Farcas A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Polymers are highly versatile and cost-effective materials with a wide range of tunable physicochemical properties, making them indispensable across numerous technological and biomedical applications. However, their intrinsic chemical heterogeneity and complex structural organization pose significant challenges for the rational design of advanced systems, particularly in gene and pharmaceutical delivery. To address these limitations, the emerging field of polymer informatics leverages data-driven and computational approaches to enable efficient prediction of material properties and accelerate design processes through machine learning techniques. A data-driven polymer informatics framework is developed by integrating molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning models to enable rapid and accurate prediction of key structural descriptors, including the radius of gyration and solvent-accessible surface area. The models establish quantitative relationships between polymer chain length and the corresponding structural descriptors across a diverse range of polymer architectures. Recognizing that different properties may require different model configurations, property-specific neural network architectures are employed to enhance predictive performance. The resulting models are deployed within an accessible online platform, , designed to streamline polymer design workflows through real-time prediction and visualization. Ongoing developments focus on expanding the chemical space and incorporating additional properties, thereby increasing the platform’s applicability across scientific and technological domains.

Article.Title: Explainable artificial intelligence-based prediction of electrical characteristics in GAA MOSFETs
Article.Authors: Gupta R.; Gupta N.; Agarwal S.
Article.Abstract: In this paper, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) based prediction is used for gate all around (GAA) MOSFET to predict its electrical behaviour. The data set is produced using TCAD simulations by changing device parameters like channel length (L g ), Radius of silicon pillar (R), work function (Φ m ), doping concentration (N d ), oxide thickness (t ox ) and drain bias (V ds ). The Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm is considered for training. The R 2 of 99.5% is achieved for threshold voltage prediction. The contribution of each device parameter to the model predictions at the global and local levels is determined by using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for the purpose of model interpretability. SHAP measures the relative relevance of input factors for the overall dataset, while LIME explains individual predictions through the construction of local surrogate models. SHAP analysis revealed that gate length was the most influential parameter with a mean absolute SHAP value of 0.1. This was followed by the metal gate work function, drain bias, nanowire radius, channel doping concentration and oxide thickness with mean absolute SHAP values of 0.065, 0.05, 0.041, 0.026 and 0.015 respectively. The concordance between the SHAP, LIME and the well-established electrostatic principles of GAA MOSFETs confirm that the proposed XAI framework delivers accurate, transparent and physically interpretable predictions, making it a potential tool for AI-assisted design and optimization of semiconductor devices.

Article.Title: A hybrid CNN-transformer network with global-local context feature aggregation for lung medical image segmentation
Article.Authors: Sun Z.; Dai M.; Liu H.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Accurate lung segmentation is a key prerequisite for computer-aided diagnosis of pulmonary diseases on chest CT and X-ray images. Lung segmentation, however, remains highly challenging due to the complex anatomy of the lung, ambiguous lesion boundaries, low tissue contrast, and the marked appearance gap across imaging modalities. In this work, we propose HGCANet, a hybrid CNN-Transformer network for lung segmentation based on global-local context feature aggregation. The encoder of HGCANet combines CNN and Transformer layer to extract local and global features and incorporates three proposed key modules: (1) A Cross-branch Global-Local Feature Aggregation block consists of three parallel transformation branches to effectively fuse global and local features; (2) A Deep Multi-Scale Attention block, which captures multi-scale contextual information through multi-branch dilated convolutions and jointly applies spatial and channel attention to enhance the response of salient regions; (3) A Global Context Collaborative Attention block, which integrates multi-scale perception with global channel-spatial attention to realize adaptive deep fusion between encoder and decoder features. Comparative experiments conducted on two public and two in-house lung-image datasets demonstrate that HGCANet achieves accurate and efficient lung-region segmentation, showing potential for clinical lung-segmentation applications.

Article.Title: Endoplasmic reticulum stress and glucose metabolism gene signature associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus
Article.Authors: Shi Y.; Chen S.; Zhou X.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) involves pancreatic β-cell dysfunction, systemic insulin resistance, and dysregulated cellular stress responses. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and glucose metabolism are closely interconnected in pancreatic islets, but their combined value for transcriptomic-based diagnostic modeling remains unclear. Public pancreatic islet transcriptomic datasets were analyzed. GSE76894, including 19 T2DM and 84 control samples, was used as the training dataset, and GSE38642, including 9 T2DM and 54 control samples, served as an independent validation dataset. Differentially expressed genes were intersected with curated ER stress and glucose metabolism–related gene sets. Functional enrichment and machine-learning analyses were performed to identify candidate diagnostic genes. A total of 2,781 differentially expressed genes were identified in the training dataset, including 1,322 upregulated and 1,459 downregulated genes. Intersection with curated pathway-related gene sets yielded 20 ER stress and glucose metabolism–related differentially expressed genes. Enrichment analysis highlighted metabolic regulation, kinase activity, carbohydrate metabolism, and FoxO, HIF-1, and MAPK signaling pathways. Logistic regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression, and support vector machine analysis identified a nine-gene signature consisting of EP300, IRS1, IL1B, IAPP, AKT1, IGF1, VEGFA, HNF1A, and HSPA5. The model showed high classification performance in the training dataset and moderate discriminatory performance in the validation dataset. Exploratory immune-infiltration analysis suggested an association between IL1B and immune-related signals in pancreatic islets. This study identified a pathway-informed nine-gene signature associated with T2DM status in pancreatic islet transcriptomic datasets. These findings support the potential value of integrating ER stress and glucose metabolism gene sets for molecular classification and provide a basis for future biomarker validation.

Article.Title: Fast dynamic reconfiguration for large-scale distribution networks via decision-oriented spatiotemporal integrated reduction
Article.Authors: Zhou G.; Yu T.; Wu Y.; Pan Z.; Liu Q.; Zhou Y.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Dynamic reconfiguration (DR) is essential for the secure and economic operation of active distribution networks. However, DR is commonly formulated as a computationally demanding mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem. Existing studies often improve tractability through period division and spatial key switch selection. These approaches are usually driven by load-profile similarity and do not fully account for topological characteristics or decision consistency across time steps. Static key switch selection also cannot adapt to time-varying optimal topologies, which can lead to suboptimal reconfiguration decisions. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a decision-oriented spatiotemporal dimensionality reduction method. First, a multi-objective reconfiguration model is formulated to minimize network loss and the load balancing index. Second, an integrated reduction framework is developed. By quantifying multi-time-step decision interoperability and incorporating switch operation similarity, the proposed method jointly determines the period division and period-wise critical switches. This design reduces the solution space in both temporal and spatial dimensions while preserving decision quality. The method is validated on standard 16-node and 72-node systems and on a real-world 395-node network in Southern China. Simulation results show that the proposed approach achieves a favorable trade-off between solution quality and computational efficiency compared with traditional reduction methods.

Article.Title: Machine-learning modelling of regional landslide susceptibility in eThekwini, South Africa
Article.Authors: Petersen C.; Mhangara P.; Naidoo L.; Gidey E.
Article.Abstract: The occurrence of landslides, particularly within urban landscapes, has gained significant research interest because of their devastating impacts on infrastructure, resulting in casualties, displacement, and economic losses. This study aimed to examine the probability of landslide events and landslide-prone areas within the eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality in KwaZulu-Natal Province, South Africa. To achieve this, robust machine learning models, including Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machines (SVM), combined with geospatial tools and key landslide-triggering factors, were considered in the analysis and characterised based on susceptibility indexes ranging from very low to very high based on various carefully chosen thresholds. The results indicate that land use, elevation, NDVI, and lithology are important landslide-influencing factors. In contrast, land use parameters, such as cultivated land and built-up areas, were associated with high susceptibility zones. Furthermore, RF yielded slightly higher overall accuracy scores than SVM, with accuracy scores of 99.45% and 98.63%, respectively. The SVM susceptibility output was further analysed based on the spatial distribution of formal and informal housing types. The results confirmed that only a small percentage of each housing type fell within the high-susceptibility zones, calculated as 1.33% and 2.41% for formal and informal housing, respectively. Although SVM is one of the strongest models, RF shows higher accuracy in landslide susceptibility modelling. Furthermore, its slightly higher recall score compared to its precision score is deemed most applicable for identifying landslide-prone areas. The study suggested that human-engineered land-use activities, such as road and property development, contribute significantly to increased landslide susceptibility within the eThekwini area.

Article.Title: Sub-millisecond precision and variability in a cricket calling song pattern
Article.Authors: Hedwig B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nightly calling songs of male Gryllus bimaculatus start with bouts of activity which gradually increase in intensity until a stable singing pattern is generated. The temporal pattern of the calling song consists of loud chirps with 3–6 sound pulses and subsequent silent inter-chirp intervals. The chirp rate is close to 3 Hz; the pulse rate between 26 and 36 Hz. Pulse periods occur with millisecond or sub-millisecond jitter driven by rapid membrane potential depolarisations of pattern generating neurons, making them one of the most precise insect motor patterns. In contrast inter-chirp intervals occur with a considerable variability and jitter, due to an underlying slow ramp depolarisation driving the pattern generating neurons and centrally initiating a new chirp period. Comparing a European and a Japanese line, reveals clear differences in the timing of the pulse pattern. Japanese males generate shorter pulse periods and pulse durations. This is linked to their significantly higher calling song frequency as compared to the European line, indicating signs of allopatric speciation. Males singing in earshot do not adjust their chirp or pulse pattern in respect to the song of their neighbour. Their individualistic behaviour does not provide support for possible chorusing or alternate singing strategies in populations.

Article.Title: Gut microbiome features associated with PIK3CA-mutated colorectal cancer: A nationwide pan-cancer genomic and microbial profiling study (MONSTAR-SCREEN)
Article.Authors: Boku S.; Sakai S.; Sawada K.; Horasawa S.; Yoshikawa A.; Nakamura Y.; Fujisawa T.; Yamashita R.; Satake H.; Komatsu Y.; Nishina T.; Shiozawa M.; Kudo T.; Matsuhashi N.; Yamazaki K.; Yamaguchi T.; Yasui H.; Takahashi N.; Kadowaki S.; Denda T.; Yoshino T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Purpose To characterize the landscape of gut microbiota associated with oncogenic driver mutations across multiple solid tumors, with a specific focus on the clinical and biological implications of PIK3CA mutations in colorectal cancer (CRC). Methods We analyzed fecal 16S rRNA sequencing and tumor genomic profiles from 1,414 patients with advanced solid tumors enrolled in the nationwide MONSTAR-SCREEN study in Japan. To ensure microbiota integrity, patients with recent antibiotic exposure were excluded. Diversity indices and functional pathways were compared based on somatic mutation status. Results In the pan-cancer cohort, PIK3CA mutations were specifically associated with significantly reduced gut microbial diversity in CRC (effect size: -0.87; p = .018), a finding not consistently observed in other tumor types. Among 84 CRC cases, PIK3CA -mutated tumors (n = 10; 11.9%) exhibited a marked depletion of Desulfovibrio (effect size: -0.36; p = .046) and Oscillospira (effect size: -0.31; p = .027). Functional inference predicted a significant enrichment of both primary and secondary bile acid biosynthesis pathways (effect size: 0.37; p = .045) in the PIK3CA -mutant group. Conclusion PIK3CA -mutated CRC represents a distinct clinicomolecular entity characterized by profound gut dysbiosis and altered bile acid metabolism. These findings suggest that the gut microbiome is a key feature of PIK3CA -driven tumorigenesis in the colon, identifying this patient subgroup as a potential candidate for microbiota-targeted therapeutic interventions.

Article.Title: Smoking exposure and overall survival in nasopharyngeal carcinoma: a multicenter cohort from non-endemic northern China with an exploratory meta-analysis
Article.Authors: An Q.; Qian Y.; Zhang J.; Zhang Y.; Liu S.; Su J.; Han X.; Wang P.; Wang Z.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Smoking exposure is routinely documented in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), but its prognostic relevance in non-endemic regions is uncertain. We analyzed a multicenter retrospective cohort of 1022 patients with non-metastatic NPC treated with definitive-intent intensity-modulated radiotherapy in northern China using Kaplan–Meier and multivariable Cox methods, and conducted a secondary exploratory meta-analysis of seven published studies reporting adjusted overall-survival estimates. Among 980 patients with known smoking status, 244 were never, 182 former, and 554 current/recent smokers. Five-year overall survival was 83.0%, 80.6%, and 74.9%, respectively. After adjustment for age, sex, late-stage disease, hospital tier, diagnosis year, and diagnostic delay, the adjusted HRs were 1.35 for current/recent versus never smoking (95% CI 0.97–1.88; P = 0.074) and 1.31 for ever versus never smoking (95% CI 0.96–1.79; P = 0.094). The meta-analysis yielded a pooled adjusted HR of 1.96 (95% CI 1.41–2.73; I-squared = 74.5%). In the multicenter cohort, smoking was associated with poorer unadjusted survival; however, the fully adjusted estimates were attenuated and imprecise. Published adjusted estimates indicated higher mortality hazards but substantial between-study heterogeneity. These observational findings warrant cautious interpretation and more standardized smoking assessment.

Article.Title: Mechanics-informed neural network for predicting the axial compressive strength of short circular concrete-filled steel tube columns
Article.Authors: Boonlertnirun P.; Su R.; Sutha A.; Gao W.; Tangaramvong S.
Article.Abstract: This study proposes a mechanics-informed neural network (MINN) model for predicting the axial compressive strength of short circular concrete-filled steel tubular (CCFST) columns by incorporating mechanics-based knowledge describing confinement effects, composite action and established mechanical relationships into the learning process. An experimental database comprising 1,071 short CCFST column specimens was collected from previously published studies and randomly divided into training and testing datasets at proportions of 75% and 25%, respectively. K-fold cross-validation was employed during model development to assess robustness and reduce dependence on a single training–validation split. The proposed MINN demonstrated excellent predictive performance, achieving a testing R 2 of 99.47% and a mean predicted-to-experimental strength ratio of 1.051. To evaluate the interpretability of the developed model, SHAP, sensitivity and elasticity analyses were conducted. The results indicated that incorporating mechanics-based knowledge improved the mechanical interpretability of the model and enabled the MINN to capture mechanically meaningful relationships between the input variables and axial compressive strength. Furthermore, the analyses identified the outer diameter as the most influential parameter, followed by the steel tube thickness and material strengths, whereas the length-to-diameter ratio exhibited a comparatively minor influence, consistent with the expected behavior of short CCFST columns.

Article.Title: Tourism, energy use, and resource rents as determinants of ecological footprint in SAARC: cross-sectionally robust evidence
Article.Authors: Musa M.; Rahman P.; Liu Y.; Liu X.; Hui J.; Huang Y.
Article.Abstract: Tourism is now one of the world’s fastest-growing industries, with measurable consequences for energy demand and natural resource use, and SAARC economies are no exception. Despite this exposure, no prior study has applied a cross-sectionally robust panel framework to jointly assess tourism, energy, natural resources, and growth as determinants of environmental quality in the region, leaving policymakers without reliable evidence on the region’s key drivers of ecological pressure. This study examines how economic growth, energy consumption, tourism, and natural resource exploitation jointly affect the ecological footprint across six SAARC countries from 1995 to 2024. We apply the Driscoll-Kraay regression model, which is robust to cross-sectional dependence, and the Dumitrescu-Hurlin causality test, which accommodates heterogeneous panels, with robustness checks via Augmented Mean Group and Feasible Generalized Least Squares estimators. Four findings emerge. First, economic growth is currently worsening the ecological footprint. A quadratic extension confirms the inverted U-shaped Environmental Kuznets Curve and improves model fit, with no support for the N-shaped dynamics reported elsewhere in the region; however, the estimated income turning point, and whether any SAARC economy has crossed it, is sensitive to estimator choice. Second, energy consumption is the primary driver of ecological degradation, reflecting the region’s heavy dependence on fossil fuels. Third, tourism is associated with a reduction in the ecological footprint, a result that diverges from the CO2-based literature and points to a measurement-driven discrepancy. Fourth, natural resource rents are positively associated with the ecological footprint, and rising ecological degradation itself Granger-causes greater resource extraction, rather than the reverse. SAARC governments should prioritize renewable energy transitions and cap natural resource rents to decouple growth from ecological harm.

Article.Title: RNA with Azvudine incorporated one nucleotide upstream of 3’-end resists cleavage by SARS-CoV-2 proofreading exonuclease
Article.Authors: Yue Y.; Lin K.; Tao C.; Li X.; Peng S.; Teplova M.; Kumar S.; Morozova I.; Kalachikov S.; Russo J.; Patel D.; Ju J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The cytidine analog Azvudine (Azv) showed promising therapeutic effects against Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infections, leading to its conditional authorization as a COVID-19 treatment in China. Once Azvudine enters infected cells, it is converted to the active form, Azvudine-triphosphate, which has been shown to inhibit polymerases of several viruses. Here we show that when Azvudine is incorporated into RNA by the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), it hinders incorporation of the subsequent nucleotide, but this hindrance can be partially overcome in the presence of natural nucleotides. Moreover, the 3’-Azv-terminated RNA does not show any resistance to the SARS-CoV-2 proofreading exonuclease (ExoN). However, we found that the incorporation of Azvudine at the penultimate position of the RNA prevents RNA cleavage by the ExoN. Because Azvudine partially terminates RNA synthesis and 3’-Azv-terminated RNA does not show any ExoN resistance, the penultimate ExoN-resistant RNA configuration is a less frequent event. Although these finding do not establish a direct RdRp-mediated inhibition as the primary reason for reported Azvudine’s therapeutic effect, the position-dependent ExoN resistance observed here provide mechanistic insight for the development of novel nucleotide analogs that potentially inhibit RdRp and resist the viral proofreading mechanism of coronaviruses.

Article.Title: Vibration identification and reduction of a reciprocating compressor suction bottle with long cantilever structure
Article.Authors: Li S.; Yin X.; Yin G.; Chen J.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Excessive vibration in reciprocating compressor systems can threaten equipment reliability, operational safety, and production continuity. In this study, the root cause and reduction of excessive vibration in a compressor suction system were investigated through vibration testing, modal analysis, transient flow-field analysis, and buckling analysis. Vibration measurements and modal analysis demonstrated that the excessive vibration was not caused by mechanical resonance. Transient flow-field analysis revealed that the intermittent suction process generated significant fluid-induced excitation forces, with the dominant excitation force reaching 63–68 kN in the vertical direction. Buckling analysis showed a minimum critical buckling load of only 6.463 MPa in the horizontal direction, indicating that the long cantilever configuration of the suction bottle provided insufficient structural stiffness and stability. To mitigate vibration, a vibration reduction scheme was proposed that involved shortening the cantilever sections and relocating the inlet nozzle to the axial center of the suction bottle. These structural modifications increased the mechanical natural frequencies and enlarged the frequency separation margin from the compressor excitation frequencies. Moreover, the dominant fluid-induced excitation force in the vertical direction decreased from 63–68 to 51.6–55.1 kN, and the minimum critical buckling load in the horizontal direction increased by 52.57%, from 6.463 to 9.861 MPa. Field implementation verified the effectiveness of the proposed scheme, with vibration velocities reduced by more than 40% and all measured velocities decreasing to below the ISO 20816–1 limit of 18 mm/s. The proposed methodology provides a practical solution for vibration diagnosis, structural optimization, and vibration mitigation in reciprocating compressor systems.

Article.Title: Sowing date effects on allometric relationships and growth dynamics of quinoa for non-destructive leaf area estimation
Article.Authors: Taji M.; Karizaki A.; Biabani A.; Torabi B.; Alamdari E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Understanding the allometric relationships between leaf area and other plant traits is essential for non-destructive growth monitoring and efficient crop management. However, no comprehensive study has yet modeled leaf area in quinoa ( Chenopodium quinoa Willd.) using simple morphological traits across different sowing dates. This study aimed to quantify allometric relationships between leaf area and plant height, leaf dry weight, stem dry weight, panicle dry weight, and total dry matter, and to evaluate whether these relationships are modified by sowing date. A two-year field experiment was conducted with 12 sowing dates under a randomized complete block design with three replications. Leaf area index (LAI) dynamics were described using a logistic model, and allometric relationships were fitted using power-law equations. The results showed that LAI followed a logistic trend across all sowing dates, with maximum values ranging from 2.7 to 7.9. Plant height provided the most reliable prediction of leaf area (R 2 = 0.83, b = 1.2), followed by leaf dry weight (R 2 = 0.72, b = 0.97). The allometric coefficients for stem dry weight (b = 1.54, R 2 = 0.74) and panicle dry weight (b = 1.95, R 2 = 0.71) showed greater variability. A striking finding was the exceptionally high allometric coefficient (b = 4.95) recorded on May 6 of the second year, indicating a pronounced shift in resource allocation toward leaf area expansion. Total dry matter was a weak predictor (R 2 = 0.54), likely due to leaf fall during the growing season. The hypothesis that sowing date modifies allometric relationships was confirmed, as evidenced by considerable variation in allometric coefficients across sowing dates. This study provides, for the first time, a comprehensive set of allometric models for quinoa across multiple sowing dates. Plant height and leaf dry weight are recommended as simple, rapid, and non-destructive indicators for leaf area estimation, facilitating improved crop monitoring and management under diverse environmental conditions.

Article.Title: Scale-free dynamics and reservoir computing in a non-stationary Freedericksz model
Article.Authors: Shamraiz I.; Thivierge J.
Article.Abstract: Scale-free behavior is commonly associated with stationary dynamics and thresholded events, assumptions that are violated in many physical systems exhibiting slow drifts over time. Here, we investigate weakly and strongly driven regimes of Freedericksz dynamics in a model of nematic liquid crystals. To characterize the weakly driven, non-stationary regime without thresholding or stationarity assumptions, we use a squared temporal-increment measure of the director field. Numerical simulations show that this squared-increment activity follows a robust power-law distribution over several decades. Using mean-field avalanche theory as a scaling framework, we derive the associated exponent and show that it is largely independent of microscopic model parameters. We further demonstrate finite-size scaling, with distributions obtained for different system sizes collapsing onto a common scaling function after rescaling by a characteristic cutoff. As external forcing increases, scale-free statistics progressively break down and the system enters a strongly driven regime that can support reservoir computation. We implement the Freedericksz model as a reservoir for delayed prediction of time-series data and show that performance depends on physically interpretable parameters including elastic coupling, dielectric anisotropy, and applied electric field strength. Importantly, optimal performance occurs away from the regime exhibiting the strongest scale-free organization, indicating that scale-free dynamics alone are not sufficient for optimal computation. Together, these results show that scale-free organization can arise in non-stationary continuous-field dynamics without explicit event segmentation, while establishing Freedericksz liquid-crystal dynamics as a tunable model for relating changes in collective dynamical regime to physical computation.

Article.Title: The comparison of short-term outcome between tenecteplase and alteplase in minor acute ischemic stroke based on neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio stratification
Article.Authors: Xiang L.; Xu J.; Feng Z.; Li Z.; Zheng Y.; Li Y.; Zhu P.; Liu L.; Li M.
Article.Abstract: This study aims to compare the effects of intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) with alteplase versus tenecteplase (TNK) on short-term outcomes in patients with minor acute ischemic stroke (AIS) across different levels of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR). Patients with minor AIS (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score ≤ 5) who underwent IVT were prospectively and consecutively enrolled. A total of 234 participants were included, among whom 86 (36.8%) received alteplase while 148 (63.2%) received TNK. At discharge, 158 (67.5%) patients achieved an excellent outcome [a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) of 0–1 point]. Using the median NLR value of 2.34 (1.64, 3.89), participants were stratified into a low-NLR group (NLR ≤ 2.34) and a high-NLR group (NLR > 2.34). In the low-NLR group, IVT with TNK was associated with an excellent outcome (OR = 3.44, 95% CI: 1.25–9.47, p = 0.017) but was not associated with an excellent outcome (OR = 1.93, 95% CI: 0.80–4.69, p = 0.14) in the high-NLR group. For patients with minor AIS within 4.5 h of onset, TNK may be considered a preferred option for IVT In the low-NLR subgroup.

Article.Title: SS-AV-InDF: a self-supervised multimodal framework with local and global feature modeling for deepfake detection in Indian media
Article.Authors: Garg S.; Kaur S.; Singh P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Information integrity is seriously threatened by the growing number of deepfakes, but current detection techniques frequently have weak generalization and demographic bias due to the biasness of datasets. This research presents a two-stage self-supervised multimodal architecture that learns inherent audio–visual correspondence especially for Indian media. The proposed approach learns multimodal features both locally and globally using cross attention along with transformer-based CLIP and SimCLR modals. This contrastive learning based SSL technique uses InfoNCE loss to learn the representations during pretext task. This study compares the Transformer-based (CLIP/SimCLR) SSL designs with various SSL techniques, such as a ResNet-50 baseline, an Xception-based model, and custom handcrafted features with traditional classifier. Further, a comparative architecture analysis of the proposed SSL i.e. Transformer-based (CLIP/SimCLR) architectures with other methods for SSL has been conducted. To assess the resilience of the model for the Indian dataset, all SSL techniques are tested on the varied InDeepFake dataset. The suggested approach (CLIP+SimCLR, local pipeline) outperforms all architectures., based on corrected leakage-free performance, subject-disjoint stability, cross-dataset generalization, demographic fairness, and training efficiency. Our suggested framework outperforms ResNet-50, Xception, and handcrafted-feature baselines with significantly smaller demographic performance disparities, achieving 97.92% accuracy and 99.95% AUC on InDeepFake under a strict subject-disjoint evaluation protocol with zero identity overlap between training and test sets. These findings suggest that localized artifacts are the best way to characterize contemporary deepfakes, with patch-based detection addressing intrinsic instability for real-world implementation. Further to test the generalizability of the proposed SSL architecture, we used three datasets containing Indian languages and video i.e. InDeepFake, FakeAVCeleb and HAV-DF.

Article.Title: Real-world utilization, safety, and observed clinical outcomes of dapagliflozin among Sudanese patients with heart failure: a multicenter retrospective cohort study
Article.Authors: Nasreldeen M.; Mohamed T.; Babiker A.; Yousef B.; Siddig E.; Ahmed K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Dapagliflozin, a sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, provides glycemic control and has proven cardiovascular and renal benefits in large trials, but its real-world use in Sudan has not been described. This study aimed to describe clinical characteristics, safety, adherence, and outcomes among Sudanese patients prescribed dapagliflozin in routine care. A multicenter retrospective cohort study (April–July 2022) was conducted at three cardiac hospitals in Khartoum, Sudan. Adults ( n = 238) prescribed dapagliflozin for heart failure (HF) were enrolled. Data were obtained from medical records and structured patient interviews, capturing sociodemographic data, adverse events, adherence, hospitalizations, and deaths. Mean age was 60.7 ± 12 years; 55% were male. 96.3% of patients received dapagliflozin at a starting dose of 10 mg once daily. High adherence was reported in 86.1%. Common adverse events were polyuria (65.1%) and urinary tract infection (32.8%). Following dapagliflozin therapy, mean LVEF increased from baseline to follow-up by 5.98 ± 7.39% points among 213 patients with paired LVEF data (paired p < 0.001), whereas HbA1c showed a reduction of 0.91 ± 1.78% points among 158 patients with paired HbA1c data (paired p < 0.001). Cardiovascular death was observed in 4.6% of patients, and HF hospitalization occurred in 7.6%. In this first Sudanese real-world cohort, dapagliflozin was associated with good adherence, observed improvement in LVEF, and an acceptable safety profile, supporting its role in cardiac care in low-resource settings.

Article.Title: Postdiagnostic pretreatment risk stratification for chondrosarcoma survival using routinely available registry variables: a SEER-based temporal validation study
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Wang J.; Wang J.; Hu W.; Zhao H.
Article.Abstract: This study developed and temporally validated a postdiagnostic pretreatment survival risk-stratification framework for chondrosarcoma using routinely available variables from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results registry. Patients diagnosed from 2000 to 2015 formed the development cohort, and those diagnosed from 2016 to 2021 formed the independent temporal validation cohort. Discrimination, time-specific calibration, risk-group event enrichment, model interpretability, histological heterogeneity, missing-data sensitivity, model-selection stability, and competing risks were evaluated. Among 4066 eligible patients, the temporal validation cohort included 1168 patients and 215 overall-survival deaths. The locked Cox proportional hazards-random survival forest ensemble achieved a C-index of 0.861, with 1- and 3-year AUCs of 0.903 and 0.870. The high-risk group comprised 35.4% of the validation cohort but accounted for 80.5% of observed overall-survival deaths. In competing-risk analysis, the 1- and 3-year cumulative incidences of chondrosarcoma-attributed death in the high-risk group were 24.2% and 38.7%, respectively. Age, summary stage, tumor grade, and histological subtype were the leading permutation-importance variables; discrimination remained substantial after exclusion of histology and within the ICD-O-3 9220/3 chondrosarcoma NOS subgroup. Development-only repeated cross-validation showed that several leading configurations had near-equivalent performance, while the originally locked ensemble remained among the leading models. This registry-based framework demonstrated postdiagnostic risk enrichment in temporal validation but has not been shown to add prognostic value beyond expert multidisciplinary assessment. External validation and prospective workflow evaluation are required before clinical use.

Article.Title: Population genetic data for 23 STR loci of the Miskito ethnic group in Honduras
Article.Authors: Zuniga A.; Molina Y.; Amaya K.; Moya Z.; Soriano P.; Pineda D.; Pinto Y.; Garcia O.; Romero S.; Zablah I.
Article.Abstract: The Miskito constitute Honduras’s largest indigenous population (~ 80,000 individuals), yet population-specific genetic databases essential for accurate forensic analysis remain unavailable. Allele frequencies for 23 autosomal short tandem repeat loci were determined from 100 unrelated Miskito individuals (52 females, 48 males) from four settlements in Gracias a Dios department. DNA was amplified using the PowerPlex Fusion 6C System and analyzed by capillary electrophoresis. Statistical parameters were calculated using Arlequin v3.5.2.2 and Genepop v4.7.5. A total of 187 distinct alleles were observed (mean 8.13 ± 3.49 per locus). Expected heterozygosity ranged from 0.3872 (D2S441) to 0.9188 (SE33), with mean He = 0.7523. No locus deviated significantly from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium after Bonferroni correction (α = 0.0022). Linkage disequilibrium testing revealed no significant associations among the 253 locus pairs after Bonferroni correction (α = 0.0002). The combined match probability was less than 1 × 10 −15 , corresponding to a combined power of discrimination exceeding 99.9999%. The combined probability of exclusion reached 99.999%. AMOVA detected minimal population structure among settlements (FST = 0.003, p = 0.18). This first comprehensive genetic characterization of the Honduran Miskito population provides essential reference data for forensic casework and kinship analysis. Beyond its forensic utility, this dataset fills a long-standing gap in Central American population genetics and contributes to the comparative analysis of Chibchan-speaking populations of the isthmian corridor.

Article.Title: Monitoring and forecasting groundwater storage dynamics in arid Wadi systems using GRACE/GRACE-FO satellite observations and XGBoost machine learning: Wadi El-Assiuti, Egypt (2003–2030)
Article.Authors: Hagage M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Progressive groundwater depletion in arid regions represents one of the most critical water security challenges of the twenty-first century. Despite intensive agricultural abstraction in Egypt’s Wadi El-Assiuti since the 1990s, a continuous basin-scale assessment of groundwater storage dynamics has remained lacking. This study integrates GRACE/GRACE-FO Terrestrial Water Storage Anomalies (TWSA), GLDAS-2.2 soil moisture data, CHIRPS precipitation, and multi-temporal Sentinel-2/Landsat land-use datasets to derive monthly groundwater storage anomalies (GWSA) and cumulative variations over the period 2003–2024. Long-term trends were evaluated using the Mann–Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator, while relationships were quantified using Pearson correlation analysis. GRACE-derived estimates were evaluated against available piezometric records. An XGBoost machine learning model was trained on the period 2003–2016, independently validated over 2017–2024, and subsequently applied for a 72-month forecasting horizon extending to 2030. Results indicate statistically significant declining trends in both GWSA ( p < 0.001) and cumulative groundwater storage, with an average depletion rate of approximately − 987,000 m 3 yr⁻ 1 . Annual rainfall showed weak, non-significant correlation with groundwater storage ( p = 0.471) and no monotonic trend (Sen's slope = 2.08 × 10⁻ 7 mm month⁻ 1 ), confirming climatic variability is not the primary depletion driver. In contrast, agricultural land expansion increased by approximately 273% between 2003 and 2024 and showed a strong negative correlation with groundwater storage (r = − 0.76, p < 0001), confirming irrigation-driven abstraction as the dominant control on aquifer depletion. The XGBoost model demonstrated high predictive performance (R 2 > 0.92) and projected a continued depletion trajectory under current land-use conditions through 2030. Overall, the integrated framework indicates that anthropogenic land-use change is the dominant anthropogenic factor associated with groundwater decline in Wadi El-Assiuti. The approach is fully reproducible using open-access datasets and is readily transferable to data-scarce arid aquifer systems across the Middle East.

Article.Title: Vitamin B1 administration attenuates anxiety and depression-like behaviors induced by nicotine abstinence in chronically stressed rats
Article.Authors: Najafzadeh A.; Kakhki S.; Khatibi S.; Saadat S.; Ahmadi-Soleimani S.; Beheshti F.
Article.Abstract: The present study aimed to assess the effect of treatment by Vitamin B1 (Vit B 1 ) on behavioral manifestations of anxiety and depression in rats exposed to nicotine and/or unpredictable chronic mild stress (UCMS) during adolescence. Furthermore, several biochemical pathways and alcohol drinking behavior was also investigated in these subjects. 120 adolescent male rats (21 days of age) were randomly divided into eight experimental groups: (1) Vehicle (received saline+saline), (2) Nicotine (received Nicotine+saline, 2 mg/kg), (3) UCMS (UCMS+saline), (4) Nicotine-UCMS (Nicotine-UCMS+saline), 5–7) Nicotine-UCMS+ three doses of Vit B 1 (5, 10 and 15 mg/kg) 2) and 8) Vit B1 (received saline + Vit B 1 ). Anxiety- and depression-like behaviors were quantified by open field, elevated plus maze, marble burying and forced swimming tests. Furthermore, ethanol drinking behavior was assessed by the two bottle method. Animals in Nic, UCMS, and Nic-UCMS groups demonstrated heightened anxiety- and depression-like signs as well as increased ethanol consumption, compared to their control counterparts. Interestingly, these observations were associated with biochemical alterations in brain oxidative, inflammatory, neurotrophic and aminergic profile. Treatment with Vit B 1 remarkably restored balance in many of the mentioned behavioral and biochemical findings, particularly when treatment was applied at high dose (i.e. 15 mg/kg). Both nicotine and UCMS adversely affect the mood and reward-related behaviors in rats via affecting brain biochemical pathways and Vit B 1 supplementation could be a potential candidate to improve these complications by restoration of biochemical balance in cortex.

Article.Title: Automatizing the deep learning pipeline for out-of-distribution lung segmentation
Article.Authors: Gómez A.; Buccardi M.; Miguel-Ramiro N.; Soto-Montenegro M.; Stellari F.; Desco M.; Abella M.
Article.Abstract: Automatic segmentation of murine lungs is an integral part of the preclinical research pipeline. Being able to quickly and reliably segment the lungs across hundreds of samples is essential for extracting metrics of interest to study certain pathologies. However, the deep learning (DL) approaches proposed in the literature for this task are trained on homogeneous datasets, limiting their generalizability. This lack of diversity necessitates manual preprocessing and standardization, tasks that typically require expert intervention. To overcome these limitations, in this work we propose a multistage framework that performs automated normalization, localization, rotation and size standardization, followed by a robust lung segmentation. This method is integrated into AutoLung, an open-source, user-friendly toolbox that leverages Neural Architecture Search to fully automate the DL workflow, enabling researchers without programming expertise to fine-tune models on new data. The proposed method was trained on rodent data with different pathologies (including health, pulmonary fibrosis and cancer) acquired with three different scanners. Its performance was validated on an external dataset of fibrotic c57bl/6 and healthy BALB/c mice to ensure generalization across animal models. Furthermore, we demonstrate AutoLung’s generalizability by successfully applying it to human data, representing a significant out-of-distribution challenge.

Article.Title: Geochemical evaluation of subsurface hydrogen-brine-mineral interactions and hydrogen loss
Article.Authors: Muther T.; Kalantari Dahaghi A.; Fowle D.; Goldstein R.
Article.Abstract: Naturally occurring and stored hydrogen in subsurface pores in rocks can undergo abiotic reactions driven by interactions with minerals, formation water, and coexisting gases. These reactions may result in hydrogen loss, altering reservoir injectivity, mineral structure, and gas composition. To systematically evaluate these geochemical processes, this study integrates equilibrium modeling to assess the long-term thermodynamic stability of hydrogen and kinetic batch modeling to capture time-dependent hydrogen-mineral reactions. Within this modeling framework, key properties such as hydrogen solubility, pH variations, mineral dissolution and precipitation, and hydrogen loss mechanisms are analyzed under various thermodynamic conditions relevant to both hydrogen storage and natural hydrogen occurrences. The results demonstrate that hydrogen solubility in brine increases with pressure and temperature and decreases with salinity due to salting-out effects. In pure mineral systems, most silicate and carbonate minerals remain largely unaltered. However, sulfate-bearing minerals exhibit significant reactivity under hydrogen-bearing brine conditions, with anhydrite undergoing complete dissolution, resulting in H 2 S formation and additional hydrogen consumption associated with pyrite-pyrrhotite transformation. In mixed mineral systems, distinct responses emerge for sandstone and dolomitic limestone, with limited reactivity in silicate-dominated sandstone and enhanced carbonate and sulfide mineral reactions in dolomitic limestone, resulting in further hydrogen consumption. These findings clarify the key abiotic geochemical pathways governing hydrogen stability and retention in subsurface hydrogen storage and along hydrogen’s migration pathway when it is naturally occurring.

Article.Title: Developing and validating a productive thinking assessment for sustainable university science learning
Article.Authors: Sari R.; Saputro S.; Ramli M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Assessing productive thinking in sustainable science learning requires instruments that capture coordinated cognitive and metacognitive processes during authentic problem-solving. Existing higher-order thinking assessments often examine critical thinking, creativity, or metacognition separately and provide limited validity evidence in performance-based sustainability contexts. This study developed and evaluated a performance-based Productive Thinking Assessment (PTA) measuring three interrelated dimensions: critical–analytical, creative thinking, and thinking process management within microplastic and bioplastic contexts. A multi-method instrument development design was used to obtain complementary validity evidence. Content validation involved seven experts, while psychometric evaluation involved 200 pre-service elementary science teachers from three Indonesian universities. Response-process evidence was examined using Think-Aloud Protocols with six students. Content validity was evaluated using Aiken’s V, internal structure using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and PLS-SEM, item functioning using Rasch analysis, and scoring reliability using intraclass correlation coefficients. Aiken’s V coefficients ranged from 0.81 to 0.95. PCA supported the proposed three-dimensional structure, and PLS-SEM indicated high indicator reliability, internal consistency, and convergent validity. Rasch analysis showed acceptable item fit, with item difficulties ranging from − 0.829 to 1.289 logits and ordered, estimable rating-category thresholds. Inter-rater reliability ranged from moderate to good for individual ratings and from good to excellent for average ratings. The think-aloud findings illustrated evidence-based reasoning, solution generation, and metacognitive regulation during task completion. The findings provide complementary validity evidence supporting the interpretation of PTA scores for assessing productive thinking within sustainability-oriented science learning, while indicating the need for further validation across broader populations and science contexts.

Article.Title: Design of a single-layer compact multi-band frequency selective surface exhibiting angular and polarization stability for WLAN applications
Article.Authors: Deepa J.; Santhanam S.; Palavesam T.; Manikandan D.; Santhosh K.
